en: The Scripture on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha. Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Six Similes (I). Chapter One: The Six Similes.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Monastery in the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to receive offerings for three months. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the Saṃgha completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, the father of the Buddha, and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha’s paternal aunt, came to the monastic quarters to make offerings to the Saṃgha. Having completed their prostrations and presented tooth-sticks and cleansing powder, they called out to Ānanda, saying:
“We now wish to go to the place where the World-Honored One is; would this be acceptable?”
At that time, Ānanda immediately proclaimed these words to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When the Father King arrives, he will surely inquire about the wondrous Dharma. You must go and announce this to the entire community of bhikṣus, and go into the forest to summon Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kātyāyana, Aniruddha, and others, as well as Maitreya Bodhisattva, Bhadrapāla, and the sixteen virtuous men, so that they may all assemble here at once."
Thus the sound spread in all directions.
At that time, the lords of the devas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and nāgas, together with their retinues, had all assembled.
At that time, the King, his father, Śreṇika Bimbisāra, and three hundred million Śākyas entered the Buddha’s vihāra.

As they were entering, they saw the Buddha’s vihāra like a mountain of crystal; they prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and before their heads had even been raised, they saw a great lotus flower composed of various jewels before the Buddha, upon which was a great radiant terrace.
Upon seeing this, the King, his father, felt great joy in his heart and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; he circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the King rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"The Buddha is my son, and I am the Buddha's father. Now that I am in this world, I behold the Buddha’s physical body; yet I see only its exterior and do not perceive its interior.

When Siddhārtha was in the palace, the physiognomists all saw the thirty-two marks; now that he has attained Buddhahood, his radiance is even more manifest, surpassing what it was in former days by hundreds of thousands of millions of times."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should sentient beings of future generations contemplate the physical marks and color of the Buddha’s body, such as the constant reach of his radiance?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will [explain this].
"Now, for my sake and for future sentient beings, you should analyze and explain this.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of the Pure Body of Form; arising from that samādhi, he immediately smiled. According to the law of the Buddhas' smiles, there were rays of light of five colors.
At that time, the five-colored light transformed into five hundred colors and issued from the Buddha’s mouth, illuminating the crown of the King, his father;
from the King’s crown it illuminated the Hall of Radiance;
from the Hall of Radiance it illuminated the vihāra, pervading the entire Sahā world before returning to enter the crown of the Buddha’s head.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the King, his father, saying:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
The Tathāgata shall now speak of how sentient beings of future ages shall attain the vision of the Buddha-dharma.”
The Father King addressed the Buddha:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
I now pray that you will grant me your hearing."
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"In Jambudvīpa there is a lion king named Vimala."

Regarding the dharma of that lion, it is only after forty years have passed that the male and female mate; having mated once, it leaps and roars, rolling itself over until it collapses, yet its body remains without injury.
When his son, the lion cub, was in the womb, he was no different from his father, the king of beasts.
Your Majesty should know that it is impossible for one in the womb to be able to roar, fly, fall, run, or crouch.
The Father King addressed the Buddha:
"When the son of the Lion King was in his mother’s womb, were his head, eyes, tusks, and claws similar to those of his father?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"He is no different from his father, yet his strength and ability do not equal even a hundred thousand millionth part of his father's.
The Buddha told the King, his father: "So it is, so it is!"

In future ages, if any sons or daughters of good family, as well as all others, can with a sincere heart fix their mindfulness within, sitting upright in meditative absorption to contemplate the Buddha’s form-body, you should know that the minds of these people are like the Buddha-mind and are no different from the Buddha’s.
"Though he remains amidst afflictions, he is not obscured by various evils, and in future ages he will rain down the great Dharma-rain.
Furthermore, O King, it is like this:

suppose *eranda* trees grow together with sandalwood on Mount Malaya, and a *gośīrṣa-candana* tree grows within a thicket of *eranda*. While it has not yet grown large and remains beneath the earth, its sprouts, stems, branches, and leaves are like bamboo shoots in Jambudvīpa; people do not recognize them and say that this mountain consists entirely of *eranda* and contains no sandalwood."
Yet the stench of the eranda is like that of a bloated corpse, pervading forty yojanas; its flowers are red and exceedingly lovely, yet whoever eats them goes mad and dies.
Although the gośīrṣa-candana had grown in this forest, it could not emit its fragrance because it was not yet fully developed.

When the moon was full in the middle month of autumn, it suddenly emerged from the earth and became a candana tree. All the people then smelled the sublime and wondrous fragrance of the gośīrṣa-candana, and the foul stench of the eranda tree vanished forever.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"The mind that recollects the Buddha is likewise so!
By means of this mind, one is able to attain the roots of the three kinds of bodhi."
"Furthermore, O King!
Within Jambudvīpa and the four continents, there is a garuḍa named King Suparṇa, who has attained complete mastery over all birds."
By the karmic retribution of this bird, it ought to feed upon various nāgas; each day in Jambudvīpa it eats one nāga king and five hundred minor nāgas;
on the following day, in Pūrvavideha, it eats one nāga king and five hundred minor nāgas;
on the third day, in Aparagoyānī, it eats one nāga king and five hundred minor nāgas.
On the fourth day, he again went to Uttarakuru and ate one dragon king and five hundred minor dragons.
This cycle repeated itself for eight thousand years.

At that time, signs of death appeared upon the bird; the dragons spat forth poison so that it could find no way to eat. Pressed by hunger and wandering in distress, it searched everywhere for food but could find none. It roamed among the various mountains without ever finding peace, until it reached Vajra Mountain, where it finally stayed for a brief moment.

Descending directly from Mount Vajra to the edge of the great waters, and from the edge of the great waters to the edge of the wind-circle, they are blown by the wind back to Mount Vajra; thus it happens seven times before their life comes to an end.
When its life ended, because of that poison, fires simultaneously broke out upon the ten jewel mountains.

At that time, Nanda the Dragon King, fearing that these mountains would be consumed by fire, immediately sent down a great rain with torrents as thick as chariot axles. The bird's flesh was completely dispersed, leaving only its heart; this heart fell straight down seven times in succession, and only then did it return to rest atop the Vajra Mountain.
"The Dragon King Nanda took this bird’s heart to serve as a bright jewel, and the Universal Monarch obtained it to serve as a wish-fulfilling gem.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"O sons and daughters of good family!..."
If one contemplates the Buddha, the mind is likewise so!
"Furthermore, Great King, on Mount Himavat there is a tree named Aṅgada; its fruit is very large, yet its seed is very small."
Tracing its origin from beginning to end, it came from Mount Gandhamādana and reached the Snowy Mountains by the power of the wind.

During the intense cold of early winter, Rākṣasas and Yakṣas dwelt in secluded recesses within the mountain curves; their excrement and impurities flowed across the ground, and fierce winds blew snow to cover them. Gradually, this formed a trench fifty yojanas wide, and through the power of the manure, this fruit was able to grow. Its roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits flourished luxuriantly. In the third month of spring, when the sun’s warmth prevailed, winds rose simultaneously from all eight directions, melting away the ice and snow until only the fruit tree remained.
As for the color and shape of its fruit, nothing among the fruits of Jambudvīpa can serve as a comparison.

Its form is perfectly round and measures half a yojana. If a brahmin eats it, he immediately attains the Way of the Immortals, becoming fully endowed with the five supernatural powers; his lifespan lasts for one kalpa, and he neither ages nor dies.
If an ordinary person eats it, they will head toward the stage of Srotāpanna; if an Anāgāmin eats it, they shall become an Arhat, fully possessing the three insights and six supernatural powers.

There was a person who took its seeds to the fertile soil of Jambudvīpa, whereupon they sprouted; the tree grew to the height of one tala tree, named *kovidāra*, and its fruit was called *tāla*, resembling a five-dou measure jar. Those people of Jambudvīpa who ate it were able to eliminate febrile illnesses.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Good sons and good daughters!
It is likewise when one contemplates the realm of all Buddhas with right mindfulness!"
"Furthermore, Great King, it is like the Pārijātaka tree that grows in the Nandana Grove of Śakra.

When the celestial maidens see it, their bodies and minds are filled with such joy that they cannot contain themselves; when Śakra sees it, he immediately gives rise to thoughts of desire, and the eighty-four thousand court ladies likewise experience a sensation of bliss."

When this tree grows, its curved branches reach the ground; immediately beneath the earth, flowers bloom and fruits form. These fruits are golden in color, radiating brilliant light, and their petals and leaves never wither or fall. Possessing the ten colors, they manifest radiant light and produce various musical sounds. In the eighth month of autumn, it emerges from the earth, reaching a height of three million four hundred and fifty thousand yojanas.
"The gods who see this experience a joy that is not their usual state.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"The contemplation of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) while still within the stage of afflictions is also like this!"
When he was born, he was as magnificent and beautiful to behold as that precious tree.
Furthermore, Great King, it is like at the beginning of a kalpa, when fire arises for one kalpa, rain arises for one kalpa, wind arises for one kalpa, and earth arises for one kalpa.

"When the kalpa of the earth is formed, the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven travel through the world and bathe in the waters. Because of this bathing, the vital essence of the four great elements enters their bodies; due to the pleasure of physical contact, their semen flows into the water. Blown away by the eight winds, it falls into the mud and naturally forms an egg."
After eight thousand years, the egg finally opened, and a woman was born.
Her form was dark blue-black like muddy silt, and she had nine hundred and ninety-nine heads;
each head had a thousand eyes, nine hundred and ninety-nine mouths, and each mouth had four fangs from which fire issued forth like thunderbolts.
He has twenty-four hands, each grasping all manner of weapons;
his body is as tall and vast as Mount Sumeru, and he enters the great ocean to splash the waters for his own delight.

When the whirlwind blows upon the waters of the great ocean, if water enters her body, she immediately becomes pregnant; after eight thousand years have passed, she then gives birth to a son, whose body is four times taller and more magnificent than his mother’s.

The child had nine heads, each with a thousand eyes; fire issued from his mouths; he possessed nine hundred and ninety-nine hands and eight feet; he made sounds from within the ocean and was named Vemacitra, the Asura King.
This ghost’s way of eating consisted solely of consuming mud and the roots of lotuses.
As her son grew up, he saw the celestial maidens surrounding [the gods] and said to his mother:
"Everyone has a consort; why am I alone without one?"
His mother told him:

"On Mount Gandhamādana there is a deity named Gandharva; that deity has a daughter whose beauty is exquisite and whose complexion surpasses white jade. From all the pores of her body issue wondrous sounds that are most pleasing to my heart."
"Now I have betrothed you; does this fulfill your wish?
The asura replied, "Excellent, excellent!"
"I pray that you, Mother, will go and seek her.
At that time, the mother went to Mount Gandhamādana; having arrived at Mount Gandhamādana, she addressed the Kinnara king:
"I have a son of sovereign power and majesty, who has no equal throughout the four continents. Do you have a daughter who might be a suitable match for my son?"
Upon hearing this, the maiden joyfully wished to follow him to the asura realm.

When the asura had accepted her, his mind was at ease and he performed the marriage rites with her. Not long thereafter, she became pregnant; after eight thousand years had passed, she gave birth to a daughter. The girl’s appearance was upright and extraordinary, peerless among all beings in heaven or on earth. She adorned herself with the most exquisite of complexions, possessing eighty-four thousand marks of grace upon her face, eighty-four thousand on her left side, eighty-four thousand on her right side, eighty-four thousand on her front, and eighty-four thousand on her back.
The asuras, seeing her, considered her magnificent and extraordinary, like the moon among the stars, truly most marvelous.
When Kauśika heard of this, he immediately dispatched a messenger down to the asuras to seek this maiden.
The asura said, "By virtue of your heavenly merit, you have enabled me to ride upon a palace of the seven treasures and take your daughter as my wife.

Upon hearing this, Śakra’s heart leaped with joy; he immediately removed his jeweled crown and held it out toward the sea. Due to the retribution for his ten virtuous deeds, he caused the asura to sit upon the Victorious Palace (Vijayanta).
At that time, the asura leaped for joy and gave his daughter as a wife to him. Śakra then went to welcome her with six kinds of precious palaces.

Within the palace, there was a great lotus from which eighty-four thousand exquisite jewel-women were spontaneously born. In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, they arrived at Śakra’s Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā). At that moment, the celestial palace surpassed its former state by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; Śakra-devānām-indra established a name for her, calling her Manoharā.
When the devas saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; looking east, they forgot the west, and looking south, they forgot the north.
The thirty-two auxiliary ministers likewise beheld Manoharā with hearts and bodies filled with joy, such that even the hairs on their skin bristled with delight.
"When Śakra arrives at the Nandana Grove, he enters the pond with his various celestial maidens to sport there.
At that time, Manoharā becomes jealous and dispatches five yakṣas to inform her father, the King:
'Now this Śakra no longer shows me favor; he sports with his own celestial maidens.'"
Upon hearing these words, the father’s heart was filled with wrath; he immediately mobilized the fourfold army to attack Śakra.

Standing upon the great ocean waters and perched atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, his nine hundred and ninety-nine hands acted simultaneously, shaking the city of Sudarśana and rocking Mount Sumeru, so that the waters of the four great oceans surged at once.
Śakra Devānām Indra was struck with alarm and dread, not knowing where to turn.
At that time, a deity in the palace addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"Do not be so greatly alarmed. The Buddhas of the past have taught the *Prajñāpāramitā*; Your Majesty should recite and uphold it, and the ghostly armies will naturally shatter."
At that time, Śakra sat in the Hall of Good Dharma, burning various famous incenses and making this great vow:

"The Prajñāpāramitā is the great mantra of illumination, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra; it is true and not false. By upholding this Dharma, I shall attain the Way of the Buddha and cause the asuras to naturally retreat and disperse."

When these words were spoken, four sword-wheels appeared in the void; through the merit of Śakra, they descended spontaneously. As they came upon the asuras, the asuras’ ears, noses, hands, and feet all fell off at once, causing the waters of the great ocean to turn crimson like liquid madder.
At that time, the asuras were immediately struck with terror; having no place to flee, they entered the pores of lotus fibers.
"By the power of the ghosts of greed, hatred, and delusion, and by the power of illusion, they are still able to do such things!"
"How much more so, then, is the Buddha-dharma inconceivable?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"O sons and daughters of good family!

Focusing the mind to contemplate the realm of all Buddhas, one is also able to dwell securely within the ocean of samādhis; the merit of such a person is beyond measure or calculation, being equal to that of all Buddhas without distinction.
2. Introduction: Chapter on Contemplating the Grounds (1). Introduction: Chapter Two on Contemplating the Grounds. “What is meant by ‘contemplating the realm of all Buddhas’?
When the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, appear in the world, they adorn themselves with two kinds of dharmas.”
What are these two?
First, to first preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures so that all sentient beings may read, recite, and master them; such various acts as these are called the gift of Dharma.

Second, by means of his wondrous form-body, he manifests himself throughout Jambudvīpa and the worlds of the ten directions, causing all sentient beings to see the Buddha’s form-body fully adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, without any deficiency, so that their hearts give rise to joy.
“By observing these marks, what causes them to be attained?

They all arise from the hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices performed in previous lives, as well as the cultivation of the various *pāramitās* and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).”
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"If there are sentient beings who wish to mindfully recollect the Buddha, who wish to contemplate the Buddha, who wish to see the Buddha, who wish to discern the marks and signs [of the Buddha],
who wish to recognize the radiance of the Buddha, who wish to know the interior of the Buddha’s body, or who wish to study contemplation..."

Those who possess the Buddha-mind are those who study the contemplation of the Buddha’s crown protuberance, those who study the contemplation of the thousand-spoked wheel-mark beneath the Buddha’s feet,
those who wish to know the signs at the time of the Buddha’s birth, those who wish to know the time when the Buddha took a consort,

those who wish to know the time when the Buddha left the household life, those who wish to know the time when the Buddha practiced austerities, and those who wish to know the time when the Buddha subdued Māra.
If one wishes to know the time when the Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
if one wishes to know the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s turning of the wheel of Dharma; if one wishes to know the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s “Treasure Horse” mark (*aśva-kośa-lakṣaṇa*);
if one wishes to know the characteristics of the time when the Tathāgata ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, Lady Māyā; if one wishes to know—

Regarding the signs when the Tathāgata descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven: those who wish to know the marks of radiance within the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—of the Tathāgata;
those who wish to know the signs of the Tathāgata approaching Kuśinagara to subdue and deliver the Mallas;
and those who wish to know the marks of the light from the pores of the Tathāgata as he subdued the spirits of the wilderness.
The Buddha told the Father King:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others, wish to fix their mindfulness, wish to contemplate, wish to practice dhyāna, or wish to attain the correct reception of samādhi."
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"What is meant by 'binding the mindfulness'?
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s complete physical marks."
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating each individual mark and excellence among the Tathāgata’s various marks and excellences;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s marks and excellences in their sequential order;
and there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s marks and excellences in their reverse order.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the radiance of the Tathāgata;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the conduct of the Tathāgata;
and there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the dwelling of the Tathāgata.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata seated;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata reclining.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata begging for alms.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s initial birth;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata when he takes a consort;
and there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata when he leaves the household life.
There are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s ascetic practices;
there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s subjugation of Māra;
and there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood.
There are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata turning the wheel of Dharma;
there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother;
and there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata subduing the spirits and demons of the wilderness.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata at Nālandā when he subdued the nāgas and left his shadow;

there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata in the city of Kuśinagara when he subdued the six heretical teachers, the low-caste Niti, and those of evil discipline and grave wrong views.

"Thus it is, O Father King: after my parinirvāṇa, sentient beings will have various karmic actions and various intentions; their cognitions will differ. According to what each sentient being perceives through their own thoughts and minds, you should teach them to practice mindfulness in due order, so that they need not rely on mindfulness as they would while I dwell in the world."
It is like the rising of the sun: all who were in darkness see clearly, yet only those without eyes remain unable to behold it.
"In future ages, my disciples should cultivate three dharmas."
What are the three? First, reciting the profound sūtras.
Second, purely maintaining the prohibitive precepts and being without transgression in one's dignified conduct.
Third, binding one's mindfulness through contemplation so that the mind does not become distracted.
What is meant by "binding mindfulness"?
It refers, for instance, to those who bind their minds with desire to contemplate the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Some may fix their minds on contemplating the Buddha’s hair;
some may fix their minds on contemplating the Buddha’s hairline;
and some may fix their minds on contemplating the Buddha’s mark of a broad, even, and upright forehead.
Some wish to fix their minds on contemplating the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows;
some wish to fix their minds on contemplating the Buddha’s eyebrows;
and some wish to fix their minds on contemplating the Buddha’s mark of eyes like those of a bull king.
Some may wish to fix their minds on contemplating the Buddha’s straight nose as they practice;
some may wish to fix their minds on contemplating the Buddha’s hawk-like beak;
and there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mustache and beard, which are shaped like tadpoles and radiate forth light.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the space between the upper palate and the lips of the Tathāgata;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the color of the Tathāgata’s lips, which are as beautiful and red as the *bimba* fruit;

and there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s lower lip, which is like the stalk of a *padma* flower, crimson in hue and merging its color into that of the *bimba* fruit above.
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of forty teeth in his mouth;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of teeth that are white, even, and closely set;
and there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of the patterns of lines upon his teeth.
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the lines on the Tathāgata’s teeth;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the appearance of the Tathāgata’s upper palate, where eighty-four thousand lines are clearly and distinctly visible;
and there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s lower gums, which have the color of the stem of an *utpala* flower.
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s throat as being like a tube of lapis lazuli, appearing like a succession of lotus flowers;

there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad and long tongue as having the shape of a lotus petal, with five superior colors clearly distinguished in five hues, ten veins beneath the tongue from which various rays of light flow forth, and the mark of the tongue being so broad and long that it completely covers his face;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the three marks within the joints of the Tathāgata’s throat.
There are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s mark of the throat and chest, which is like the eye of a garuḍa;
there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s mark of the head;
and there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s mark of the eighty-four thousand hairs of the head.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s body hairs curling to the right;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding how each and every pore of the Tathāgata has a single hair growing in a spiral;
and there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s scalp.
There are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance;
there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s brain;
and there are sentient beings who take pleasure in beholding the Tathāgata’s ears hanging down as if in sleep.
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of the contours of the earlobes;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of the seven hairs spiraling upward from the ears;
and there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of the fullness of the clavicles, wherein a radiant pedestal spirals forth from within those bones.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s mark of the fullness of his armpits, wherein five pearls are suspended, like mani-jewels resting upon the Buddha’s armpits;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s arms, which are smooth, slender, and rounded like the trunk of an elephant king;

there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s elbow bones, which are like the coiled hair of a dragon king, their patterns unbroken, with the dragon coiling at the joints so that no trace is seen, while the fingers are set in varying positions without losing their proper order, and twelve wheels appear at the tips of each finger joint.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s copper-colored nails, which possess eight colors and are clearly distinct;

there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s webbed palms, which, when extended, show the fingers joined and not separated, appearing as clearly as a net of pearls, surpassing Jambūnada gold by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, its brilliance exceeding the range of the visual faculty, with a *svastika* symbol produced at the tip of each of the ten fingers, and between the points of these *svastikas* are thousand-spoked wheels, all marks fully perfected like a hundred thousand lotuses in full bloom.

There are sentient beings who, when observing the Tathāgata’s palms, see the lines between them forming palaces like those of the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; their palms are level and even, peerless among humans and devas, and from within the palms arise the marks of the thousand-spoked wheels, which radiate mani-lights in the ten directions, beneath which are ten kinds of paintings, each painting as pure and clear as the eyes of the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, before they enter into the palm-marks.

There are sentient beings who, when observing the Tathāgata’s backs of the hands, see the hairs pointing upward and curling, like deep blue lapis lazuli, emitting five-colored lights that enter into the webbed spaces.
There are sentient beings who, when observing the Tathāgata’s hands and feet, see them as soft as celestial *karpāsa* cotton.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s hands, held in the inward-and-outward-clasping gesture;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s chest, marked with the "Virtue" character and ten thousand seals, and possessing the radiance of the *cintāmaṇi*;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s navel, which is like a *vaiḍūrya* jewel.
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the ribs of the Tathāgata, which are equal in size and joined together in a graceful curve;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the various bones and joints of the Tathāgata, which are knotted like coiled dragons and joined with such density that they are seamless;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the hook-and-chain bones of the Tathāgata, which can be extended or contracted at will without obstructing one another.

There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s bone color as fresh white; even crystal or the Snowy Mountains cannot serve as a simile for it, for it is interspersed with red light forming patterns and has a luster like congealed fat.
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of the calves of an eneya deer king;
there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the Tathāgata’s mark of the ankles.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s feet, which possess the mark of being level and even;

there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the exquisite color of the Tathāgata’s feet, which is like the color of Jāmbūnada gold, with body hairs pointing upward and curling, and the webbing between the toes like the patterns of fine gauze, with various colors—dark and bright—within those patterns that cannot be fully named;
and there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s copper-colored nails, at the tips of which are the mouths of five lions.
There are sentient beings who delight in contemplating the conch-shell patterns on the tips of the Tathāgata’s toes, like the seals drawn by the god Viṣṇukarman;

there are sentient beings who delight in contemplating how the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet are flat and full, not admitting even a single hair, with the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles, complete with hubs and rims, the scales arranged in succession, and the mark of a vajra.
The heels also possess the mark of the Brahmā-king’s crown, with the whorls no different [from those on the palms]; such is called the method of "contemplation in accordance with the order.

There are also sentient beings who delight in "contemplation in reverse order": starting from the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet, they contemplate upward from the bottom to the tips of the toes, clearly observing each mark, each secondary characteristic (*anuvyañjana*), and each color, proceeding from the bottom to the top; this is called the method of reverse contemplation.

There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s golden body; because the Buddha was born in Jambudvīpa, he manifests as the supreme color among all colors, yet like the brilliance of a hundred thousand suns upon a mountain of purple gold, it cannot be seen in its entirety.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s colossal body of sixteen feet;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the Tathāgata’s halo extending one fathom.
There are sentient beings who delight in beholding the radiance of the Tathāgata’s entire body;
there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the auspicious signs that appear when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma;
and there are sentient beings who delight in beholding the marks of the Tathāgata’s navel, whether it tends upward or downward.
3. Chapter on Contemplating the Marks (1–4), Part One of Three: Contemplating the Marks, Chapter Three. The Buddha addressed the King, his father:
"What is meant by 'contemplating the crown of the Tathāgata's head'?"

The Tathāgata’s cranial bone is perfectly rounded like a joined scroll; its color is pure white, appearing reddish where the thin skin is seen, or golden-hued like a diamond where the thick skin is seen; the hairline is golden, and the brain is the color of crystal.
There are fourteen channels, fully adorned with various paintings, and likewise fourteen lights; these lights are as distinct and clear as the channels themselves.

From within the cranial channels, various lights swirl and arise, surging upward to strike the skull bone; emerging from the skull bone and reaching the hairline, there are fourteen colors that encircle the mass of hair. Beneath the hair, golden light also arises in manifold rays, entering into the midst of the fourteen colors.
This is called the Tathāgata’s birth within the royal palace with the fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon his crown;
because the five great Brahma-marks manifest upon his summit, neither Māyā nor the Buddha’s maternal aunt could see them.

The five Brahma-marks manifested radiance that reached the Brahma-world, further extending upward through immeasurable worlds to transform into palatial towers—the realm of all Buddhas, which even Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Ground cannot perceive.

"I shall now describe for my father, the King, the birth of the crown-protrusion mark (*uṣṇīṣa*). Those who hear this should contemplate the Buddha’s supreme crown-mark; its radiant light is like the atoms of dust of the great earth throughout the three-thousandfold world system, and cannot be fully described."

If sentient beings of future generations hear these words and contemplate these signs, their minds will be free from regret. It will be as if they were seeing the light of the World-Honored One’s supreme crown-mark; even with eyes closed, they shall see it clearly and distinctly through the power of mental visualization, as if the Buddha were present in the world.

Although one contemplates these signs, they do not become numerous; rather, one gives rise to the perception of one object, and having perceived that one object, one perceives another. Reversing and repeating this process sixteen times in both forward and reverse order, one causes the mental characteristics to become extremely clear and sharp.

Thereafter, one should settle the mind and fix the attention on a single point; in this manner, gradually extend the tongue toward the palate and keep it firmly positioned there for two weeks. Only then can the body and mind attain tranquility and stability.
Furthermore, one should bind the mind and again contemplate the Buddha’s crown; in the method of contemplating the Buddha’s crown, one first enters through the pores.
The Buddha addressed the Father King and commanded Ānanda:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!”

The Tathāgata now has eighty-four thousand hairs upon his head; they all lean toward both sides, growing in a clockwise curl, clearly demarcated and distinctly arranged in four clusters. From each and every pore, five rays of light spiral forth and enter into the previously mentioned fourteen-colored lights.
"Formerly, when I was in the palace, while my wet nurse was washing my hair, Mahāprajāpatī came to where I was and said:
'When Siddhārtha was born, there were many extraordinary wonders.'"
If someone were to ask me,
"How long is your son's hair? how should I answer?
"Now I shall measure my hair to determine its length.
He then commanded me to stretch out his hair, and his mother measured it with a ruler.
It was one zhang, two chi, and five cun long; once released, it curled to the right, forming the pattern of a conch shell.
When he was about to take a consort, he washed his head once more, and his mother again commanded him, saying:
"Previously, when your hair was measured, it was exactly one zhang two chi five cun long; you must measure it now."
He immediately measured it with a ruler; it was one zhang, three chi, and five cun long.
When I left the household life, the devas carried it away, and it was likewise one zhang, three chi, and five cun long.
"Now, does the Father King wish to see the marks of your hair?
The Father King replied,
"Indeed, O World-Honored One!"
"May I behold the hair of the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata extended his hair with his hand from the Nyagrodha Monastery to the palace of his father, the King; it was like deep blue lapis lazuli, encircling the city seven times.

Within the Buddha’s hair, the great assembly all saw various colored lights that cannot be fully described; each and every light shone universally upon all things, appearing the color of deep blue lapis lazuli.
Within the lapis lazuli-colored [hair], there are innumerable emanation Buddhas.

Having manifested this sign, he gathers his hair and rolls back its light; it spirals to the right in graceful curves and returns to rest upon the crown of the Buddha’s head, forming a conch-shell pattern. This is called the Tathāgata’s mark of the true hair.
"If there are bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, and others who wish to contemplate the Buddha’s hair, they should practice this contemplation and not engage in any other."

If one contemplates it otherwise, it is called false contemplation, called madness, called loss of mind, called wrong view, and called a perverted mind; even if such a person were to attain meditative concentration, it would be impossible.
"Thus it was with our father, the King; the reality of the Buddha’s true hair-mark is exactly like this.
Having observed the hair-mark, he next observed the hairline, which was the color of red pearls and hung down in graceful curves."

There were five thousand rays of light, distinct and intermingled, all directed upward and curling around his hair; emerging from the crown of his head, they encircled it five times, like the technique of a celestial painter, perfectly round and as fine as a single thread.

Within the spaces between those strands, various transformation Buddhas arise, with transformation Bodhisattvas serving as their retinue; all the forms and appearances of the eight classes of devas also manifest therein. Their color is like the solar disc and cannot be fully seen; this is called contemplating the hairline of the Buddha.
"To observe in this manner is called right observation; to observe otherwise is called wrong observation.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"This is called the Tathāgata’s true observation of the hairline."
"How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad, level, and upright forehead?
Within this mark of the broad, level, and upright forehead, there are three marks:
the first is what is called the mark of the white hair (ūrṇā-kośa)."
When the Buddha was first born, the King and his consort took the Prince to the seer Asita to have him examine the Prince’s marks.

The seer removed his cotton robe and first saw a white tuft of hair growing between the Prince’s eyebrows; surrounding this white hair were various circular rims that followed its curve. As the physiognomist spread the hair out, he saw it grow long; he then took a measuring scale to measure its length, which was a full five feet, like a tube of lapis lazuli. When released, it curled to the right like a crystal bead, manifesting immeasurable hundreds of thousands of colored lights. This is called the light of the white tuft mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) manifested at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth.
"When he reached the age of eight, his maternal aunt again observed that as Siddhārtha had grown older, the hair between his eyebrows had likewise grown with him.

She then examined it and saw that the white hair was straight, like a tube of white lapis lazuli; from the tip of the hair, light of five colors emerged and returned into the pore. Her affection for her son was boundless, and she said to the people:
'The mark of my son’s hair has reached such a state.'"
When the people saw him, he appeared as before, turning to the right and being exceedingly lovely to behold.
This is called the mark of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa) from the time the Bodhisattva was a youth.
What is called the mark of the white tuft of hair from the time the Bodhisattva took a consort?

Yaśodharā’s father personally dispatched a physiognomist to examine the Prince; seeing that his thirty-two marks were as brilliant as a painting, he was only uncertain regarding the white hair between the eyebrows.
The physiognomist immediately said:

"Prince Dhitīśvara! Your other physical marks are identical to those of a Golden-Wheel-Turning King; only this white hair that radiates manifold lights is beyond my understanding. May I now extend it to examine it?"
The Prince replied, "Do as you wish.

At that time, the physiognomist stretched out his hair with his hand, and from it flowed a stream like the milk of a bull-king, which struck the physiognomist's eyes. His eyes became clear and bright, and within the hair he saw hundreds of thousands of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), complete with the seven treasures and a thousand sons.
The physiognomist was struck with amazement and said: "Prince Dharanindara!

I extended my white hair to observe its length, but I do not know for what reason this substance, like the milk of a bull-king, has come and sprayed into my eyes. Is this a true vision, a dream, or a state of madness?"
Now I have forgotten it all.

All the marks and signs of the Prince have completely vanished; I see only hundreds of thousands of wheel-turning sage kings with their seven treasures, their thousand sons, and their fourfold armies arising from the four directions. My heart is filled with joy, like that of a Brahmin who has attained the bliss of the Brahma world.
Having spoken thus, he released the hair, which curled to the right and returned to its original place.
At that time, the physiognomist named Raivata, having witnessed this event, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the Prince and said:

"The various marks of the Prince cannot be fully seen; yet according to my method of physiognomy, one who possesses even a single mark becomes a king of the four continents and attains sovereign mastery."
"Now the Prince's marks are like those of Maheśvara; his sovereign spiritual powers are beyond record—how can they be known?
The Prince replied, "I do not understand this; you should return home and report it to your King."
At that time, the physiognomist returned to his native country and related the aforementioned matters in detail to the king.

Upon hearing these words, the king mounted a famous elephant and, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of attendants, proceeded to the city of Kapilavastu. Arriving at the palace of King Śuddhodana, he washed the Prince’s hand with water, presented the girl to him, and prostrated before him, saying:
"O Prince of the Earth! Heaven!"
"I pray that you will accept my daughter to serve as your attendant; the physiognomist saw an exceptionally sublime mark of hair upon her, and I now wish to see it—is this permissible?
The Prince replied, "Look at her as you please."

At that time, Yaśodharā’s father stretched out the Prince’s white hair with his hand; seeing that white hair, it was like a crystal pillar with its joints perfectly aligned. Within the spaces between the joints, he clearly saw immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Brahmā kings, Śakras, and various eminent sons of gods together with their palaces, as distinct as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a bright mirror.

Having seen this, he rejoiced and immediately released it; as before, it circled to the right and returned to rest between his eyebrows, its brilliant radiance spreading out in the four directions, entering into the contours of his face in ways that cannot be fully described—this is called the mark of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) of the Bodhisattva at the time of taking a consort.
The Buddha told the King, his father:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if the fourfold assembly wishes to contemplate the white hair-tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) of the Bodhisattva when he was a youth and when he took a consort, they should perform this contemplation."
"Observing in this manner is called right observation; observing otherwise is called wrong observation.
The Buddha told the King:
"What is meant by the white tuft mark (ūrṇā-kośa) when the Tathāgata renounced the household life?"

When I desired to leave the household life, my father the king and my mother dispatched numerous court ladies to constantly guard me; the gates were fitted with bolts and latches that produced a sound upon opening or closing, like the roar of a lion.
He secretly hung bells between the windows, with golden chains interlocking them, so that dragons, ghosts, and yakṣas could find no way to enter.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings spoke from afar through the air, saying:
"Prince of the Earth! "
"The time has arrived; one ought to study the Way.
I now wish to go and make offerings to the Prince, yet I fear that because there is noise within the palace, I shall have no opportunity to enter.
At that time, the Prince extended his hair with his hand as far as the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings; it was like celestial silk, soft and lovely to behold.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings perceived his mind with profound love and reverence; because of this love and reverence, they immediately saw within the hair a manifested Bodhisattva sitting in the full lotus posture, appearing like a crown prince.
Each and every bodhisattva, moreover, has immeasurable great bodhisattvas as their retinue.
When this sign appears, immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others all simultaneously gain entry.
The King commanded Chandaka:
"Go to the rear stable and bring me Kanthaka. Chandaka replied:
"Now, when one lifts their foot upon this ground, it trembles and roars like the sound of a great elephant; how can one proceed?
At that time, the Prince again extended his white hair so that Chandaka might see it; it was like the petals of a lotus flower, each following the other, as white as snow.

Upon seeing this, Chandaka’s mental eye immediately opened; through the gaps between the leaves, he beheld emanated bodhisattvas sitting in the full lotus posture, as numerous as incalculable motes of dust, and the white tufts of hair between the eyebrows of these emanated beings were likewise so.

At that time, Chandaka saw that the ground within the palace was the color of crystal, solid throughout like diamond, such that his footsteps made no sound. He quickly reached the rear stable, saddled the horse with its golden saddle, and led it before the palace. Chandaka addressed the Prince, saying:
"The devas stand in the air with palms joined in reverence, praising in unison the merit of your renunciation; Prince, you should now swiftly mount the horse."

At that time, the Prince again extended his white hair and held it out toward the maidens, causing the hearts and minds of all the attendants to experience joy and bliss, just like a bhikṣu who has attained the third dhyāna.
At that time, this hair curled gracefully to the right and returned to the space between his eyebrows.
The devas again beheld a hundred thousand rays of light from the Prince’s brow, like a river of milk flowing everywhere.
Within the Milk River, there were emanated bodhisattvas riding upon emanated lotus flowers, all together praising the merit of leaving the household life.
From the space between the eyebrows of each of these emanated bodhisattvas, rays of light flowed forth like the Milk River, just as before.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"This is called the various auspicious omens of the white-hair mark at the time of a Bodhisattva’s renunciation.

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly wishes to contemplate the Tathāgata’s white-hair mark from the time of his renunciation, they should perform this contemplation; to contemplate it otherwise is called a false contemplation."
The Buddha said to the King, his father:
"What is meant by the mark of the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa) at the time of practicing asceticism?

After I had departed from the palace city and traveled not far from the city of Gayā, I went to the Aśvattha tree; at that time, hundreds of thousands of devas, including the Devaputra Śāntamati, all thought thus:"
"The Bodhisattva, if he is to sit here, must have a sitting mat; I should now offer him the celestial grass.
He then took the celestial grass, which was pure, soft, and named "Auspicious" (*śrīvatsa*); having received it, the Bodhisattva spread it upon the ground and sat down.

At that time, the devas observed that the physical marks of the Bodhisattva’s body were lovely to behold; they further saw a white tuft of hair, three inches in circumference, curling to the right in graceful spirals with hundreds of thousands of colors, which flowed into all the other marks.
When these devaputras observed the white tuft of hair, each had this thought:
"The Bodhisattva now accepts only my grass and does not accept yours.
At that time, within the white hair, there were ten trillion bodhisattvas sitting cross-legged, each taking his own grass and sitting beneath this tree.
Each of the sons of heaven saw such a mark within the white tuft of hair.
At that time, the son of heaven Kṣema praised him, saying:
"Excellent, O Superior Being!"

Cultivating great compassion, through the power of that compassion one attains the marks of a Great Man; within those marks, there are immeasurable manifestations capable of fulfilling all the virtuous aspirations of the devas, giving rise to the bodhicitta without engendering contention or strife.
When Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath this tree, each offered ambrosia as an offering.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva wished to subdue those six teachers, he did not accept their offerings. The devas caused flax and rice to grow spontaneously on his left and right; yet the Bodhisattva would not eat them, whereupon all the devas said:
"O virtuous son!..."
"Having not eaten for many days, my physical strength is utterly exhausted and my remaining life is but a short time; how then can I accomplish Bodhi?
At that moment, the Bodhisattva entered the *nirodha-samādhi*, a meditative state known as "the stilling of all faculties."
The devas wept and their tears fell like rain, entreating the Bodhisattva to arise and partake of food.
When they made this request, the sound pervaded the trichiliocosm, yet the Bodhisattva remained unaware.
There was a son of heaven named Rucirā.
Seeing the grass growing from the earth piercing through the Bodhisattva’s flesh and rising as high as his elbow, he addressed the devas, saying:
"How marvelous is this man!
"His asceticism is such as this!
Having not eaten for a long time, his cries are no longer heard, and he is unaware that grass has grown over him.

He then extended the white hair with his right hand; the tip of the hair was straight, exactly one zhang, four chi, and five cun in length. It was like a celestial white jewel, hollow both inside and out. When the gods looked within the hair, they saw ten billion rays of light; those lights were so subtle and wondrous that they could not be fully described.
Within that light, emanated bodhisattvas appeared, all practicing asceticism in no way different from this; these bodhisattvas were neither small nor large.

When the devas saw them, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. They then released a white hair that curled to the right, which, together with the radiance, returned to its original place.

At that time, the various devas gazed intently at the white hair, their eyes never wavering for a moment. They saw five tubes emerge from within the white hair, enter through the mouth, and flow with a continuous stream of nectar, drop by drop. This flowed upward from the root of the tongue into the body, making it transparent inside and out like a mountain of lapis lazuli, wherein hundreds of thousands of millions of great bodhisattvas appeared within his own body.
Upon seeing this, the devas joined their palms in joy and said:
"Our previous words were foolish, for we said that this Great Being’s life would not last long.
Now that we behold these signs, he will certainly attain Buddhahood without a doubt; before long, the sun of unsurpassed wisdom shall shine upon the world."
Having spoken these words, they circumambulated [the Buddha] a hundred thousand times and each returned to their own palace; such sounds were heard throughout the six heavens of the desire realm.
The Buddha told the King, his father:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if the fourfold assembly wishes to contemplate the white tuft-mark (ūrṇā-kośa) of the Tathāgata from the time of his ascetic practices, they should perform this contemplation."
"Observing in this manner is called right observation; observing otherwise is called wrong observation.
Thus spoke the Buddha. *The Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, Scroll One.
*The Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Three, Part Two: On Contemplating the Marks.
The Buddha addressed the King, his father:
"What is meant by 'the light from the ūrṇā-kośa when the Bodhisattva subdues Māra'?

King Māra Pāpīyān, observing Jambudvīpa from afar with his divine eye, saw the son of Śākya having renounced his kingdom as if it were spittle, sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment with his flesh and bones withered away, his body emaciated like a long-term patient;
only the golden radiance became even more manifest, his eyes sunken and dark like stars at the bottom of a well, and his joints so pressed together that the patterns of coiled dragons had vanished."

Pāpīyān said joyfully, "Gautama’s body is emaciated and his bones are like withered grass; though he possesses a radiant complexion, his remaining life is but brief. Before he has perfected the Way, you should go and defeat him."
Glaring with eyes wide in rage, he commanded the yakṣas to quickly assemble the host of troops, saying:
"I now intend to descend to Jambudvīpa to go and wage war against Gautama.
At that time, a son of Māra named Satara knelt long and addressed his father:

"When the Prince of King Śuddhodana was born, ten thousand deities attended upon him and his radiance permeated the various heavens. His compassion universally covers all beings; he now sits beneath the Bodhi tree for the sake of all living creatures. Why does the Father King give rise to such evil and rebellious intent?"
The Māra immediately said in anger:
"In your youth you were ignorant, yet you speak of Gautama as having superior virtue and morality.
Gautama’s body is as emaciated as a skeleton; what, after all, is he capable of that you speak of his compassion?"
The son spoke again, saying:
"Gautama’s body is so emaciated because he does not eat; yet observe his radiance, like purple flames streaming forth from Mount Vajra, as he sits serenely for six years with a mind unshaken.
Observe his countenance; it never shows a trace of fear."
"I only pray, Great King!
Please remain in your celestial palace and do not wish to go and attack.
Pāpīyān spoke again:
"You need only remain silent; why must you speak so much?
At that time, a yakṣa lord named Kīṭa went to the place where Māra was, prostrated himself with his head to the ground in salutation to Māra, and addressed him, saying:
"O Heavenly King, what are your commands?"

Pāpīyān replied: "Using my voice, you shall issue a general command to the six heavens, informing the King of Ghosts below along with the eight classes of beings, as well as the wilderness ghosts, the eighteen hells, and the deities of Yama; let them all assemble and go to where Gautama is."

At that time, the various ghosts gathered from the four directions like rising clouds. Some ghosts had heads like oxen with forty ears; within those ears grew iron arrows, from which red flames rose upward to a height of one yojana. They had eighteen horns, the tips of which supported mountains, upon which were dragons swallowing glowing iron balls.

Furthermore, there were various ghosts with heads like those of foxes, possessing ten thousand eyes; their eyelashes were as long and large as bolts of lightning, and upon their necks were mouths that spat forth blazing fire, while the hair on their bodies was like a forest of sword-trees.

Furthermore, there are various ghosts dwelling upside down in mid-air with twelve feet; upon their heels are wheels of a thousand blades, their heads are like Mount Tai, and atop their heads are five hundred sword-trees from which flames erupt.
Furthermore, there were various ghosts crawling belly-first along the ground, carrying Mount Cakravāḍa on their arched backs as they arrived.

There were also various ghosts with one neck and many heads, each mouth possessing a thousand tongues; upon these tongues grew thorny trees, while their bristling hair pointed upward, raining blood from its tips as they spat out thorns and rushed forward, leaping through the air.
The *piśāca* demons let out a great, malevolent roar; their breath surged like clouds and rain as they suddenly arrived with glowing iron balls.
The *kumbhāṇḍa* demons crouched upon earthen mounds, displaying their hideous forms.

The *pūtana* demons were black and emaciated; carrying large cauldrons filled with glowing iron balls upon their heads and grasping sword-wheels in their hands, they rushed forward, treading on dogs with their left feet and wolves with their right.

The various Rākṣasa kings had backs as black as lacquer and chests as white as the moon; their eyes were like blazing fires, and their hair was disheveled and matted like a bundle of thorns. Their canine fangs protruded upward, shaped like sharp swords; the claws on their ten fingers were as keen as the points of needles, and they had ten talons on their feet that extended crosswise like blades. With iron headstalls, they arrived running with great speed.

The Great Generals of the wilderness ghosts and spirits had six heads upon a single neck and six faces upon their chests, with two more faces upon each knee; their entire bodies were covered in bristling hair resembling arrowheads, and they leaped forward to shoot at people. With eyes wide open and glowing crimson, blood flowed down from them as they arrived running swiftly alongside these various ferocious beings.

Furthermore, there were various ghosts whose heads were like those of tigers with twelve eyes, and whose noses were like those of elephants with thirteen nostrils; they carried mountains upon their left shoulders and bore fire upon their right shoulders, clutching sharp swords in their hands and treading upon lions with their feet as they arrived with a roar.

Furthermore, there were various ghosts whose bodies were like clouds; from the heads of these massed clouds, thunderbolts and fire erupted. At the edges of these cloud-masses were hundreds of thousands of millions of dragons; their bodies could not be seen, but only the poison they spat forth was visible. From the ten directions, all manner of evil things gathered like clouds.
The spirit Kumbhāṇḍī, leading her sons, each holding a stone wall ten *li* square, arrived racing together, their jagged cliffs terrifying to behold.

Furthermore, there are various ghosts with their spines curled and tails tucked between their legs; they sniff the ground with their noses, from which flames erupt, and as these flames transform and give rise to more ghosts, they run away with their faces turned toward them.
At that time, the Māra King looked back at the yakṣas and commanded the various spirits:
"Now that the ghost armies have already gathered like clouds, and since the virtuous Gautama might know incantations, we must mobilize the fourfold army."

Using the Māra-kings’ jewels, he conjured four divisions of troops—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—with weapons arrayed like a forest; most terrifying, they descended directly from the sky to the edge of the Bodhi tree.
Māra thought again:
"Perhaps these troops will not be able to subdue Gautama through protracted struggle.

He then removed his jeweled crown and held it out toward the earth; the radiance of the crown traveled directly to the lower realm, arriving above the palace of the transformed beings of King Yama, where he cried out in a loud voice, issuing commands to all the ghosts:

"You jailers and King Yama, take all these—the sword-wheels, swords, halberds, fire-chariots, and glowing coals of the Avīci Hell—and cast them all toward Jambudvīpa, desiring to extinguish Gautama by hurling him into their midst."

“The Avīci Hell is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides. It has sevenfold iron walls and eighteen compartments below; on its four sides are sword-forests, also eighteen rows each. To the east, there are eighteen small hells surrounding it;
to the south, eighteen compartments surround it;
and to the west, eighteen compartments surround it.”
To the north, eighteen tiers surround it.

Beneath the ground, there is naturally a fierce and blazing fire; the iron city and the iron netting are both ablaze, and all the hot flames swirl and circulate, passing downward through the eighteen tiers.

If there are sentient beings who have committed the five heinous crimes, their bodies shall fill the interior [of this hell] and undergo such suffering, without ceasing day or night and without any interval of respite; when the kalpa is about to end, the four gates shall open of their own accord.

The various sinners see the entire forest of swords outside the eastern gate as if it were a grove of cool shade; they run from the bottom tier up to the second tier, from the second tier up to the third tier, and so on until they reach the top, rushing toward the eastern gate.

The rākṣasas and hell-wardens pierce their eyes upward with hot iron forks; the essence flows out onto the ground like molten copper. Immediately they collapse, filling eighteen compartments. Their minds remain in a state of bewildered distress for one small kalpa, after which they rise again and proceed toward the southern gate.

In this manner, the four directions are no different from what was described before; one undergoes suffering day and night for the duration of one great kalpa. When that kalpa ends, one is reborn in other minor hells.

Regarding the shapes and sizes of the remaining various hells, the lightness or heaviness of the retributions received, and all miscellaneous retributions concerning physical appearance—whether beautiful or ugly—all these shall be explained in detail within the *Maitrī-samādhi*.

"At that time, there were eight thousand hell-wardens to the east of the city, and likewise in the other three directions. Each warden’s hair was like a mountain, with razor-wheels, swords, and halberds growing from it;

their ears were like those of donkeys and came in hundreds of thousands of varieties, and from within each ear, smoke and flames rose together. Their lips, mouths, and teeth surpassed those of rākṣasas by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; their horns were like those of oxen, with swords growing from the tips. They appeared differently from the five perspectives; their bodies were crimson-black like dogs afflicted with leprosy, and they possessed four hundred tails."

At the tail-end, there is boiling blood and excrement; iron-beaked insects coil around their bodies. With iron forks in hand and treading upon wheels with their feet, they are pierced through to the very marrow of their hearts by razor-edged wheels that spin as swiftly as the wind. Each uses an iron fork to impale the waist of the sinner and runs straight upward, while the Avīci Hell follows the sinner like a shadow follows its form.
"In an instant, they arrived at the foot of the Bodhi tree and gathered like clouds, intending to commit an evil rebellion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva remained solemn and unmoving, entering the sublime compassion of *adhyāśaya-maitrī*."
The Māra King, boasting and exerting his martial prowess, let out a roar and commanded his hosts:
"You all must swiftly harass and harm Gautama!

Above, he caused thunder, rain, and hot iron balls to shake the heavens; blades, wheels, and weapons were piled upon one another, crisscrossing through the air. The various ghosts on all four sides acted simultaneously, yet the flaming arrows did not come near the Bodhisattva.

At that time, the Bodhisattva slowly raised his right arm and extended the hair-tuft between his eyebrows, pointing it downward toward the Avīci Hell. He caused the various sinners to see a multitude of waters flowing from within the white hair-tuft, pouring down like rain with axles for its torrents upon the great fires. The great fires were momentarily extinguished, leaving only the scent of smoke, which caused those undergoing punishment to attain a slight awakening and to remember of themselves the various sins they had committed throughout hundreds of lifetimes, thousands of lifetimes, and hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes in their past.
The various hell-wardens took up great iron forks and raised them to lift the offenders, yet they could not move them even by exerting all their physical strength.

Suddenly, they saw for themselves that the heads of the great iron forks were like mountains of white silver, with tens of millions of grottoes. Within these, white lions coiled their bodies to form seats, upon which white lotuses sprang forth. Therein sat sublime Bodhisattvas who had entered into supreme benevolent resolve; thus adorned, they were like Mount Sumeru.

He cast the pitchfork down upon the ground, and seven-jeweled lotuses sprang up from beneath its base. A white radiance shone forth, illuminating all the hells and the bodies of the hell-wardens, causing King Yama and his various wardens to appear as mountains of white silver, visible for a brief moment like a flash of lightning.

The various beings undergoing retribution experience a sudden, violent arousal of their six sense faculties; fire blazes at the joints of their limbs and nails grow from their sinews. For a brief moment, they are able to rise and join their palms together with fingers interlaced, directing them toward the ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft of hair between the brows), whereupon their minds immediately open.

Seeing those among the white-haired ones as no different from himself, he sat within a forest of lotuses and sprinkled water upon the crowns of the heads of all the sinners, causing their burning afflictions to find temporary relief and coolness;
they then all simultaneously cried out: "Namo Buddha!"

By these causes and conditions, having completed his retribution for the offense, he was reborn directly among human beings with all his faculties intact. Possessing right view, he left the household life; once ordained, he severed twenty billion deep-seated fetters and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
When Māra saw this sign, he became haggard and distressed, and lay down upon his bed.
Māra had three daughters: the eldest was named Rati, the middle one was named Arati, and the youngest was named Tṛṣṇā.
Then the three daughters of Māra went to their father king; they knelt down with palms joined in salutation to their father and addressed him, saying: "Father King!
For what reason today are you so distressed and haggard?"
His father replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama has made a profound and solemn vow; he now sits beneath the Bodhi tree intending to destroy my people, and for this reason I am grieved!"
The daughter said to her father, "I can go and disturb him; I pray you, Father, do not worry.

She then adorned herself, wearing a crown of various jewels; her beauty and grace were so exceptionally outstanding that they surpassed the Queen of Māra by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

She cast sidelong glances and assumed seductive postures, manifesting all manner of enchanting charms. Her jeweled necklaces shone so brightly that their radiance eclipsed the six heavens. She rode in a carriage made of precious feathers, upon which a jeweled canopy was securely set and celestial flowers hung down. From the tips of the flower stamens emerged various transformed jade maidens, holding musical instruments and performing with drums, lutes, and songs; their voices produced ten thousand varieties of sound, all of which are the delights cherished by worldly people.

Each jade maiden was attended by five hundred women as her retinue; silk canopies, banners, and streamers descended like clouds. From the pores of their bodies, fragrant incense smoke issued forth in hundreds of thousands of colors—dark blue, yellow, and brilliant hues—that dazzled the eyes and brought great delight. They proceeded with slow and composed steps to where the Bodhisattva was, alighted from their carriage, joined their palms, and paid homage to him. After circumambulating him seven times, they addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"When the Prince was born, ten thousand deities served him and the seven treasures arrived. Why do you now renounce the celestial throne to come here beneath this tree?"

"I am a celestial maiden of incomparable and magnificent beauty; my radiant countenance is peerless throughout the six heavens. I now offer this humble body to the Crown Prince to serve at his side and attend to his needs."
"We are skilled at massaging and tending the body; we now wish to attend upon you, so we pray that you grant our humble request.
The Prince has sat beneath the tree until his body grew weary and exhausted; it would be fitting for him to rest and partake of ambrosia."
He then presented a precious vessel filled with the hundred flavors of the heavens. The Prince remained silent, his body and mind unmoving;

he pointed with his white tuft of hair, causing the three celestial maidens to see within their own bodies the sacs of pus, mucus, and saliva, as well as the nine orifices, the tendons and veins, and all their fundamental organs—the large and small intestines, the stomach (the raw receptacle) and the colon (the cooked receptacle). Within these, various worms writhed, coiled, and surged forth in abundance, numbering a full eight thousand families, each family consisting of nine hundred million tiny worms. When these worms played, they would enter the small intestine, each having four mouths with gaping jaws turned upward. When the larger worms played, they entered the large intestine, exiting from it and entering back into the stomach.
When cold diseases arise, the stomach passages become obstructed and the parasites cannot enter; consequently, food is not digested.

Within the spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, heart, gallbladder, throat, the pleural membranes, and the diaphragm, four further types of parasites are produced. Like four snakes joined together, they simultaneously devour the various internal organs from both above and below. When the solid waste is exhausted and only the fluids remain, these enter the eyes as tears, enter the nose as mucus, gather in the mouth as saliva, and flow out from the mouth as drool.

On the thin skin and thick skin, as well as within the sinews, marrow, and all the vessels, worms were born—finer than the finest hair of an autumn down, so numerous that they cannot be fully described.
When the woman saw this, she immediately vomited, and the discharge from her mouth was inexhaustible.

He immediately saw his own body: a snake’s head emerged from the left, a fox’s head from the right, and a dog’s head from the center; atop these heads, nine-colored corpses manifested through transformation, resembling the nine contemplations on the foul.
"The nine contemplations on the signs (*navasaṃjñābhāvanā*) are as follows: First is the sign of recent death (*abhinavamarana-saṃjñā*):

One sees a dead person whose body is upright and who no longer possesses any consciousness; one reflects, 'This body of mine shall likewise become thus, no different from this,' and therefore it is called the sign of recent death."
Second is the sign of the livid corpse (*vinīlaka-nimitta*):

one sees a dead person, from one day up to seven days [after death], with the body appearing bluish, swollen, and blackish-purple; one reflects, "My own cherished body shall likewise become thus, no different from this," and therefore it is called the sign of the livid corpse.
Third is the sign of pus and blood:

one may see a dead person whose body has already decayed and is smeared with flowing blood; it is utterly loathsome and unfit to behold. One reflects, "My own cherished body shall likewise become thus"; hence, it is called the sign of pus and blood.
Fourth is the mark of crimson fluid:

one may see a dead person whose body lies prostrate with yellow fluid flowing from it, resembling crimson juice; thinking, "My own cherished body shall likewise become thus," it is therefore called the mark of crimson fluid.
Fifth is the sign of undigested food:

one may see a dead person being eaten by crows and birds, devoured by insects and wolves, or infested with maggots from flies, such that their flesh is nearly gone or only half the body remains. One reflects, "My own beloved body shall likewise become thus"; therefore, it is called the sign of undigested food.
Sixth is the mark of being bound by sinews like a bundle of firewood:

one may see a dead person whose skin and flesh have completely vanished, leaving only the bones and sinews connected to one another, resembling a bundle of firewood that remains intact and does not fall apart. Thinking, "This body of mine which I cherish shall likewise become thus," it is called the mark of being bound by sinews like a bundle of firewood.
Seventh is the mark of the separation of bones and joints:

one may see a dead person whose sinews have already rotted away and whose bones and joints lie scattered in all directions, no longer in a single place; thinking, "My own cherished body shall likewise become thus," it is therefore called the mark of the separation of bones and joints.
Eighth is the sign of being scorched and loathsome:

one may see a dead person being consumed by a house fire or scorched by a wildfire, shriveled upon the ground, so utterly loathsome that it cannot even be looked upon; thinking, "My own beloved body shall likewise become thus," it is therefore called the sign of being scorched and loathsome.
Ninth is the mark of ancient bones:

one may see dry bones from long ago, whether fifty years, a hundred years, two hundred years, or three hundred years old; the bones have turned white again, and as the sun beats upon them, flames rise up from the bones. After they are consumed by fire, the wind blows them into the earth, where they return to the soil.
This is called a brief explanation of the nine contemplations; this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s initial opening of the gateway to the contemplation of impurity while first beneath the tree.

At that time, the three demonesses saw themselves once again carrying an old woman upon their backs—her hair white and her face wrinkled, her lips and mouth crooked and distorted, her hands and feet twisted and contorted, her complexion dark and parched like a corpse.
Upon her chest she further cradled a dead infant, from whose six orifices various pus flowed; within the pus were worms that closely resembled roundworms.

When the women saw this, they were struck with horror and cried out in alarm; they retreated and departed, looking down at her navel, where six dragons had emerged. The dragons spat forth water and fire, while winds issued from her ears, and her body was as hard as iron.
She saw her own female form as something ugly, loathsome, and impure, exactly as it was.
Upon those loathsome parts there were various small insects; each insect had four heads—two above and two below—and they devoured her body.

From the mouth issue the five poisons; these poisons have five channels that extend upward to the heart and downward to the throat.
