From the six sense organs, various channel-roots arise—ninety-nine in number—which flow directly downward to the crowns of all the insects, mutually infusing them and penetrating to the hearts of all the insects.
These women, having committed various perverse acts throughout countless lifetimes, have obtained such impure and ugly bodies due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma.
Furthermore, there are various worms shaped like armlets that cluster together with many mouths; from these mouths, the five poisons emerge to gnaw upon the female organ.
Because these women committed acts of sexual misconduct in their previous lives, they have obtained foul-smelling bodies as their adornment.

Upon seeing them, [the Bodhisattva’s] heart was filled with extreme anguish, as if arrows had pierced it; when they turned back to leave, they crawled away like the slow steps of a weak camel. As they first lifted their feet, fire flared up from every joint. Their hair was yellow-black like a thicket of thorns, which wrapped around their own bodies as they wailed and sighed before arriving at the presence of the Māra King.
The Māra King’s heart was filled with rage; brandishing his sword and assuming a fierce expression, he was about to advance directly forward when the Māra princes remonstrated, saying:
"Father King, you have brought this calamity upon yourself through no fault of your own. The Bodhisattva’s conduct is pure and as immovable as the earth; how can he be destroyed?"

When this admonition was given, the Bodhisattva again directed the light from his white tuft of hair [at Māra], causing the bodies and minds of Māra’s retinue to become peaceful and blissful, as if they were bhikṣus having entered the third dhyāna.

When the hungry ghosts see the white hair, upon each tip of the hairs there appear hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great bodhisattvas. These bodhisattvas also enter the *samādhi* of supreme intention and compassionate mind; each takes the tip of his left index finger with his right hand, and from the tips of their nails, milk flows forth, sprinkling and extinguishing the fierce fires. Once the fierce fires are extinguished, they immediately attain coolness and clarity; their bodies and minds become naturally satiated, and they leap for joy. They give rise to the *bodhicitta*, and by virtue of this mind, they abandon the suffering of the hungry ghost realm.

These various ghosts see their own bodies as resembling white jade, like mountains of lapis lazuli, like mountains of crystal, like mountains of golden hue, or like mountains of agate; the pores of their bodies resemble strings of pearls, and their eyes are bright and pure like moon-pearls; the smoke and flames from their bodies are like clouds of variegated jewels, and the swords and staves they hold are like towers made of the seven treasures. Within these towers of the seven treasures, layers of fine rugs are spread and crimson pillows are placed; naturally, on their left and right, there appear transformed Brahma kings.
He saw transformed bodhisattvas seated upon flower pedestals, each speaking differently regarding the retribution of the various sinners:
"Because you committed evil deeds in your previous lives, you have obtained such loathsome forms."
When these words were spoken, among those spirits and deities, some gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta);
some planted the causes and conditions for becoming śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
and some were destined to be born in superior realms of humans or devas in future lives.
At that time, the Māra King suddenly returned to his palace, while the white tuft of hair followed him all the way to the Sixth Heaven.
During this interval, countless devaputras and apsaras saw that the interior of the white pore was entirely empty, perfectly round and lovely like the banner of Brahmā.

Within that space, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of jewel lotuses, as numerous as the atoms of dust in a hundred thousand *gaṅgā* rivers. Each and every lotus had a pedestal made of immeasurable and boundless exquisite white substances. Upon each pedestal stood an emanated bodhisattva, emitting the light of the great person’s mark of the white tuft of hair, just as before!

Upon the crowns of all these bodhisattvas are exquisite lotus flowers, golden in color; upon these flowers are the seven Buddhas of the past, who, as these emanated Buddhas, each proclaim their own names, no different from those in the sūtras.

Furthermore, there were certain devas who possessed roots of goodness from past lives; they saw that from a single pore of the manifested Bodhisattva, another Bodhisattva was born, with a manifested Buddha upon the crown of that Bodhisattva’s head, no different from what had appeared before.
At that time, from between the brows of all the manifested Buddhas, flowers emerged, adorned with a hundred jewels, such that nothing in the worlds of devas or humans could compare to their color.
There were manifested light-pavilions, and upon each pavilion was a manifested Buddha, no different from those before.
From the pores of the bodies of all these manifested bodhisattvas, there were manifested all manner of things long desired by sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

Beneath the feet of these manifested persons were manifested light-pavilions that gave rise to celestial palaces, surpassing the palaces of the Māras of the six desire realms and excelling even the stately palaces of Mahābrahmā.
The cranial protuberances (uṣṇīṣa) of all the Brahmās emerge from between the wheels on the soles of the transformed Bodhisattvas.
These white hairs extend upward to the Formless Realm, universally illuminating all the infinite and boundless worlds of the devas, appearing like white jewels, crystal, or bright mirrors.

"When the devas beheld these supreme auspicious signs, they took no pleasure in celestial delights and resolved upon bodhicitta; even the eighty-four thousand celestial maidens of Māra regarded the body of Pāpīyān as resembling a dead dog or withered wood."
Beholding only the light of the Bodhisattva’s white tuft between his brows, his mind was filled with such joy that it could not be compared to anything else; he then grew angry with Pāpīyān and said:
"The deeds you previously committed were intended to destroy others, yet they have only caused you to lose your own army."
When these words were spoken, hundreds of thousands of countless devaputras and devakanyās likewise resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path to Bodhi.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"All such various and supreme signs as these arise solely from the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of the Bodhisattva!"
It does not require the merit of other parts of the body.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the fourfold assembly can for even a moment abandon distraction and fix their minds on the correct contemplation of the Bodhisattva’s white tuft between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) as he subdues Māra, they will extinguish the dark karma and evil obstructions of incalculable kalpas and eliminate the afflictive obstructions of the ten non-virtuous actions. They will be able to see the image of the Buddha clearly and distinctly in this very life; such various realms of contemplative signs cannot be fully described.

"After my parinirvāṇa, those who wish to contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the white hair at the time he subdued Māra should perform this contemplation. To contemplate in this way is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation."

"What are called the marks of a great person when the Tathāgata attains Buddhahood; the mark of an awakened person; the mark of an immovable person; the mark of a liberated person; the mark of a luminous person; the mark of a person whose wisdom is full; the mark of one who is complete in all the pāramitās; and the mark of the ocean of samādhis such as Śūraṅgama?"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva arises from the Samādhi of Supreme Intentional Compassion and enters the Concentration of Extinct Intention;
arising from the Concentration of Extinct Intention, he returns to enter Śūraṅgama;
arising from Śūraṅgama, he enters the Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom.
Arising from the Samādhi of the Torch of Wisdom, he enters the Samādhi of the Characteristics of All Dharmas;
arising from the Samādhi of the Characteristics of All Dharmas, he enters the Samādhi of the Characteristic of Radiance;
arising from the Samādhi of the Characteristic of Radiance, he enters the Samādhi of the Lion’s Roar.
Arising from the Lion’s Roar Samādhi, he enters the Lion’s Leap Samādhi;
arising from the Lion’s Leap Samādhi, he enters the Oceanic Intent Samādhi;
arising from the Oceanic Intent Samādhi, he enters the Universal Wisdom Samādhi.
Arising from the Samādhi of Universal Wisdom, he enters the Samādhi of the Seal-Form of Dhāraṇī;
arising from the Samādhi of the Seal-Form of Dhāraṇī, he enters the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of Physical Forms;
arising from the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of Physical Forms, he enters the Samādhi of the Nature of the Dharma-Dhātu.
Arising from the Samādhi of the Nature of the Dharma-realm, he entered the Lion’s Roar Power King Samādhi;
arising from the Lion’s Roar Power King Samādhi, he entered the Samādhi of Extinction of All Mara-Phenomena;
arising from the Samādhi of Extinction of All Mara-Phenomena, he entered the Samādhi of Emptiness Wisdom.
Arising from the Samādhi of Emptiness-Wisdom, he enters the Samādhi of Understanding the Characteristics of Emptiness;
arising from the Samādhi of Understanding the Characteristics of Emptiness, he enters the Samādhi of Great Emptiness-Wisdom;
arising from the Samādhi of Great Emptiness-Wisdom, he enters the Samādhi of the Physical Body Pervading All Places.
Emerging from the Samādhi of the Body-Form Pervading All Places, he entered the Samādhi of the Quiescent Mental Characteristics;
emerging from the Samādhi of the Quiescent Mental Characteristics, he entered the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samādhi of the Vajra Characteristics;
emerging from the Samādhi of the Vajra Characteristics, he entered the Samādhi of the Vajra Peak.
Arising from the Vajraśekhara Samādhi, he enters the ocean of all samādhis;
arising from the ocean of all samādhis, he enters the samādhi of the ocean of all dhāraṇīs;
arising from the samādhi of the ocean of all dhāraṇīs, he enters the samādhi of the ocean of the spheres of all Buddhas.
Rising from the samādhi of the ocean of the spheres of all Buddhas, he enters the samādhi of the ocean of the liberation and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation of all Buddhas;
rising from the samādhi of the ocean of liberation and the knowledge-and-vision of liberation, he then enters the ocean-gates of immeasurable dust-motes of samādhis;
rising from those gates of the oceans of samādhis, he enters the samādhi of quiescent mind and extinguished mind.
Emerging from the Samādhi of Quiescent and Extinct Intent, he entered the gate of the Great Liberation Samādhi characterized by the Vajra-like Concentration.
At that time, the site of enlightenment was transformed into something resembling vajra; it extended for eighty *li* and was pure white in color, such that its full extent could not be seen.

When this sign appears, the light from the white tuft between the Bodhisattva’s eyebrows is pure, upright, and stands straight toward the east, measuring one zhang and five chi in length, with ten facets clearly manifest.

The five women of the same class as the lady Mṛgā, as well as countless tens of billions of devas, nāgas, and spirits, the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa such as the worthy Maitreya, and immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya numbers of great bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of dust—all of them likewise beheld this sign.

"When this sign appears, by the power of the white hair, jewel flowers will spontaneously manifest beneath the root of the Buddha’s Bodhi tree, forty yojanas in length and breadth, equal in all dimensions; these flowers are golden in color, with pedestals made of vajra."

The light from between the Buddha’s eyebrows illuminated this flower pedestal; that light extended straight down to the adamantine limit (*vajrapratiṣṭhāna*). At the adamantine limit, two adamantine seats spontaneously manifested through transformation, striking against one another with a sound that shook the trichiliocosm and caused this great earth to tremble in six ways.

From the adamantine seat, it pierced upward through the lotus to its root; that lotus root was likewise adamantine. These three kinds of adamantines struck against one another, then passed straight downward to the adamantine limit, revolving ten times. The light from the white tuft of hair encircled [the seat] ten times, causing the adamantine seat to remain firm and immovable.

"The Buddha sat upon this seat and eliminated the three obstructions to achieve the path of Bodhi. The realm of the Buddha’s mind cannot be fully described; were it to be explained in detail, even all sentient beings up to the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage would be unable to know it, nor would it be within their comprehension."

Therefore, within this white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*), it remains hidden and is not spoken of. "By the power of the radiance of such white hair, the Bodhi tree has a stem of vajra and roots also of vajra;

its trunk is formed of the seven treasures, from which light is produced. Each of these lights encircles the Buddha’s body seven times, transforming into jeweled curtains. The leaves of the tree are golden in color, and the flowers are the colors of a hundred jewels. Upon the flowers is light of a hundred thousand jewel colors, for which the precious lights of the devas cannot serve as an analogy. The fruit is the color of white jewels, surpassing even the exquisite white jewels of the Yāma Heaven. The radiance of those fruits transforms into nets of *maṇi* gems that cover the tree; from within the meshes of these nets, threads like white silk hang down in graceful curves, transforming into jeweled bells."
"At each of the four corners of the bell is a great jeweled terrace; these terraces are so lofty and prominent that they surpass immeasurable worlds above.
Beyond these realms, further transformations manifest as various great jeweled terraces, whose sublime height and exquisite brilliance are beyond full description."

For example, suppose one were to combine hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Sumeru mountains; atop their terraces there would be a great precious canopy made entirely of diamond, interspersed with various colors and emitting subtle, wondrous light, which descends and transforms into a ceremonial banner-canopy.

Within the canopies of banners, clouds of precious parasols rained down; from within the clouds of precious parasols, clouds of banners and streamers rained down; from within the clouds of banners and streamers, clouds of music and dance rained down; from within the clouds of music and dance, clouds of precious light rained down; from within the clouds of precious light, clouds of various fragrances rained down; from within the clouds of various fragrances, clouds of lion thrones rained down; from within the clouds of lion thrones, clouds of flower garlands rained down; from within the clouds of flower garlands, clouds of sublime sounds rained down; from within the clouds of sublime sounds, clouds of verse hymns rained down; and from within the clouds of verse hymns, clouds of various precious offerings rained down.
These various kinds of offerings all emerged from the light of the white-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) on the Bodhi tree.

At that time, the light from the white hair descended and illuminated the ground, causing the vajra-ground at the edge of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to transform into seven ponds. These ponds produced water of virtue; the water had seven colors, each color distinct and clear, and from these colors issued ten rays of light that shone upward upon the King of Trees.

The four banks of that pond are composed of various jewels; each bank is formed by the combination of a hundred kinds of jewels, and from each single jewel flow ten billion rays of light. The bottom of the pond is made entirely of diamond-maṇi, serving as its bed of sand.
The various flowers growing in the water have petals of pure gold, and upon each petal, a thousand rays of light transform into circles of radiance.

The pond has seven channels from which the water spontaneously wells up; at the mouths of the ponds grow flowers with petals arranged one after another, and from the filaments of the lotuses flow various waters, as clear and transparent as lapis lazuli beads.
On both sides of the channel, various flowers grow in rows, numbering eighty-four thousand, adorned with many precious gems.
The waters within this channel flow into one another; as the water flows, light follows along with it, reflecting upon the Bodhi tree.

Within the light of this tree, upon each and every leaf, precious lotus flowers arise; these flowers spread throughout all worlds, and atop each flower, a white jeweled terrace is manifested, reaching as far as the infinite worlds of the ten directions. From between the Buddha’s eyebrows, a white tuft of hair emits light, and the precious lotus flowers are perfectly round and equal in size, filling one yojana.
In this manner, proceeding successively upward through immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds as numerous as motes of dust, there were flowers following one another;

upon each flower sat a Buddha, his body golden in color and sixteen feet in height, sitting cross-legged upon a lotus pedestal. His vajra-throne and bodhi-tree were exactly as described above, without any difference, and so it was throughout the ten directions.

From within the white curl between his brows, there further emerged precious lotuses, a hundred billion times more magnificent than the previous precious lotuses. Upon each flower sat a Buddha, identical in every way to Śākyamuni, with no difference at all; on the tip of each stamen was another Buddha-body, likewise sixteen feet tall, entering profound meditative concentration with a mind unmoved.
"In this way, the radiance shone upon immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of worlds in the eastern direction, causing all those worlds to become the color of gold.

When those sentient beings saw the light manifesting from the opening of the transformation Buddha’s pores, they likewise emitted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jewel-radiances; within each and every ray of light, there were again immeasurable billions of transformation Buddhas."

At that time, the devas, nāgas, spirits, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others beheld this radiance, which circled the Buddha a thousand times and illuminated the lands of the ten directions; they saw those lands with their high and low places, large and small, all clearly and distinctly, as if holding a bright mirror and seeing their own reflections.

This great assembly—the eighty trillion followers of Pāpīyān, including the various ghosts, spirits, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others—each saw the white tuft of hair between his brows, straight and fifteen feet long. Its light illuminated the ten directions, so dazzling that it eclipsed the eyes of the multitude like ten billion suns, such that they could not behold it in its entirety.

Within that light, one sees immeasurable and innumerable billions of koṭis of manifested Śākyamunis; the white hair between their eyebrows is exactly fifteen feet long, and from each hair issues forth immeasurable light, and within each ray of light appear immeasurable manifested Buddhas, the white hairs between whose eyebrows are likewise the same!

From within the circular rim of this white tuft of hair, a multitude of rays of light stream forth, ascending to the Buddha’s forehead and manifesting the mark of a broad, level, and upright brow. The hairs upon his forehead all slant upward; their roots at the base are the color of the Brahma-maṇi jewel, pleasing the minds of sentient beings, while the tips of the hairs emit flowing light like molten purple gold. These radiant marks slant upward to enter the hairline, then curl gracefully downward to reach the edge of the earlobe, before dispersing upward into the hair, encircling the conch-like whorls hundreds of thousands of times. Arising from the occipital bone, they resemble the petals of a golden lotus flower opening under the sun; between the petals and within the stamens, various colors appear with distinct clarity, as if painted by Śakra.

Within those colors, there are immeasurable transformation Buddhas, each attended by seven bodhisattvas and various devas who hold precious flowers that are whiter than white; these flowers possess five lights and five distinct colors, following the transformation Buddhas without losing their proper positions—this is called the light of the white tuft between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) emitted when the Tathāgata first attained Buddhahood.

"Because of the light from the white tuft of hair, the light of the neck first arose; when he was born in the royal palace, this light was like the sun, yet it was not clearly seen. As for the halo extending one fathom, I shall explain it separately."
At that time, the eight classes of beings beheld the light from the white tuft of hair, yet what they saw differed: some saw the white hair as being like those of the Buddhas;
some saw the white tuft as being like those of the Bodhisattvas;

and some saw the white hair as being like their own parents or any other object worthy of veneration in all the worlds. They perceived these things clearly at the tip of the hair, and having seen them, they were filled with joy.

There were those who gave rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta, and there were those who gave rise to the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; when these various ghosts saw the white hair, they spontaneously developed hearts of compassion and were free from all malicious intentions.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"Regarding the white hair of the Tathāgata, from the time of his initial birth until his attainment of Buddhahood, every subtle and minute event occurring in the interval can be perceived."

Once he had attained Buddhahood, his white-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) and its radiance, along with all the other marks of perfection, were already extensively explained by the Buddha within the various *sūtras*. As for the ultimate limit of the light from the white-hair mark, only a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) is able to see it. What was previously described as "small" is that which accords with the world, as this matter is easily perceived.
The Buddha addressed the King, his father, and commanded Ānanda:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!

Transmit these words to all disciples of future generations so that they may all come to know: if, after my parinirvāṇa, various bhikṣus should ask about this matter—what practices did this Bhadraśrī (White Tuft) Bodhisattva originally cultivate in the past to attain this?”

You should answer thus: "The Buddha’s white tuft of hair between his brows results from his practice of a non-avaricious mind over immeasurable kalpas. He perceives no prior signs and does not dwell on material wealth; he practices giving with a mind free from attachment. He governs his physical demeanor through the Dharma of body and mind, upholding the prohibitive precepts as if protecting his own two eyes. Yet within his heart, it is vast, empty, and tranquil; he perceives neither the arising of transgressions nor the rules for forfeiture. His mind is as stable as the earth, without any wavering."
Suppose there were a person who, with hundreds of thousands of knives, butchered and mangled his body;
and suppose there were another person who, with various thorns, lashed and whipped his body—the Bodhisattva would not harbor even a single thought of anger.

Furthermore, suppose there were a person whose head possessed a thousand tongues, each uttering a thousand words of various disparaging insults—the Bodhisattva’s countenance would remain unchanged, like a pure lotus flower; his mind would be free from attachment, his body and mind unwearied, and he would feel no sense of exhaustion, as if his head were on fire and he were striving to extinguish it.

As if suffering from a *nalī* ulcer growing upon the pores of his body, he sought a skilled physician with diligent effort day and night. His mind was free from defilement, pure both within and without like a lapis lazuli gem. Restraining his body and withdrawing his mind, he closed his eyes, joined his palms, and sat upright in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). His mind was as profound and unmoving as the ocean, indestructible as a mountain of diamond (*vajra*).

Although he forms such an intention, he does not take birth through dhyāna; his mind is extinguished and his wisdom is stilled, free from all preferences or aversions. He is without vitarka and vicāra, yet it is not that he does not contemplate the Dharma. His mental wisdom is sharp and incisive, encompassing all skillful means; he perceives no phenomenon, whether great or small, as possessing even the most subtle marks. These various and manifold qualities are called the pāramitās.

Furthermore, it is from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, as well as from the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, and all other sublime merits, that this white tuft of hair is obtained.

“After my parinirvāṇa, if any disciples of the Buddha abandon all evils, leave behind the clamor of the world, delight in the dharma of few words, and do not concern themselves with many affairs; if they can, during one of the six periods of day and night, or even a small portion of that period, or for a mere moment within that small portion, clearly contemplate my white ūrṇā-kośa so that the mind is vividly clear, free from delusive thoughts, and remains distinctly settled; if they focus their attention without ceasing to contemplate the white ūrṇā—whether they actually see my marks and signs or not—such persons shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over ninety-six billion *nayuta* of *Ganges-sand* atoms of *kalpas*.

"Furthermore, if there should be a person who, upon merely hearing of the white hair, feels no alarm or doubt, but instead receives it with joy and faith, this person shall likewise eliminate the offenses of birth and death for eighty billion kalpas."

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās commit any of the four root offenses—excluding those equal to the root offenses or the five heinous crimes, as well as the slander of the Vaipulya sūtras—and these individuals wish to repent, they should practice with body and mind undaunted throughout the six periods of day and night.
It is like a person walking through deep grass when fires break out on all four sides; as a fierce wind blows toward him, about to consume his body, the person thinks:
"If this fire burns me, my limbs will be shattered before I have died; how shall I extinguish this fire?"
"If I do not devise a plan, my life will surely not be saved; what wise person, possessing many skillful means, could save my life?
And even if my life were fully preserved, what would I have to begrudge that person?"

Having reflected thus, like a great mountain collapsing, he prostrated himself with his five limbs upon the ground, wailing and shedding tears like rain; joining his palms toward the Buddha, he praised the Tathāgata’s manifold virtues and conduct.

Having offered this praise, one should recite the method of repentance while maintaining focused mindfulness before them. By contemplating the light of the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows for one day up to seven days, the four aforementioned types of offenses may be mitigated; after twenty-one days, the manifestations of the offenses will gradually vanish; and after seventy-seven days, one may then perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), as the details of which are found in other sutras.

If a bhikṣu has committed an offense that is not according to the rules, and he perceives that the light of the white tuft of hair appears dark and obscured, he should enter a stūpa and contemplate the image between the eyebrows for one to three days. With palms joined and weeping, he should contemplate with single-minded concentration. Thereafter, he shall enter the saṃgha and confess his previous offense; this is called the extinction of the offense.
"For the first five types of offenses, one must recite the *Baimaoguang Jing* (Sūtra of the White Tuft Light) for eight hundred days; thereafter, there is a separate *karmavācanā* rite.
The Buddha told the King, his father:

"The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Within each mark, there are eighty-four thousand minor marks and signs. Yet, such marks and signs do not equal even a small fraction of the merit of the white tuft."

Therefore, for the sake of sentient beings of future generations who commit evil, I shall now explain the contemplation method of the Great Wisdom Radiance of the White Tuft Mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) for eliminating evil.
It is impossible that any person of extreme evil with wrong views, upon hearing this contemplation method and its complete characteristics, would give rise to a heart of anger and resentment.

Even if one should give rise to anger, the light of the white tuft of hair will still protect them; merely hearing these words removes the sins of three kalpas, and in a future life, wherever they are born, they shall be born before all Buddhas. Such various hundreds of thousands of billions of kinds of subtle and wondrous realms of light cannot be fully described; yet when one contemplates the white tuft of hair, they will naturally be reborn therein.
One who observes in this manner is said to have right observation; if one observes otherwise, it is called wrong observation.
"What is meant by observing the broad, level, and upright forehead—the mark of the broad, level, and upright forehead?"
The two wheels emit radiance; the perimeter of this wheel of light consists of a thousand spokes, hubs, and rims, formed of maṇi jewels, shaped like the painted image of the deity Viṣṇu-Karma.

From within this painting, exquisite golden light flows forth and enters the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa). It circles the tuft seven times, then ascends into the pores of the forehead and all the various marks up to the hairline. It winds down gracefully to the earlobes, then disperses upward into the hair, circling the hair seven times.

Emerging from the occiput, it encircles the front lotus-mark in seven perfect rounds; the seven lines are distinct, and each line is of seven colors, from which seven flowers arise. Each flower contains one Buddha with seven bodhisattvas as attendants, who respectfully surround them, circling to the right.
Thus, there are three marks of the broad and level forehead:
the mark of the hairline, the mark of all the pores on the head, and the mark within the brain.

Within the brain, there are also fourteen rays of light that manifest throughout the various vessels; they penetrate both the interior and exterior, appearing clearly and lovely. White light surges forth, interspersed with red and purple; these subtle colors emerge from the occipital bone and also circle three times around the front.
Within each and every painted section, there is a Buddha seated, with two bodhisattvas serving as attendants; they appear even more distinct and magnificent, many times superior to before.
"How does one contemplate the mark of the Tathāgata’s eyebrows?"

The two eyebrows on the left and right are shaped like the crescent moon; they grow with curled hairs that are neither too sparse nor too dense, following the curvature of the moon. Their color is a brilliant purple, with hair-tips of deep azure-blue; their exquisite light, like that of lapis lazuli, has no equal. The radiance of the eyebrows flows both ways, dispersing into the various strands of hair; once it enters the hair, it extends upward to the tips of the locks, where the light coils upward like a conch shell, its hue beyond comparison—resembling the colors of a bumblebee, emerald, or a peacock’s plumage.

It was like a mass of ink compared to the light of lapis lazuli; furthermore, it descended from the occiput, spiraling to the right as it wound around the light four times. From each of these lines emerged an emanation Buddha, flanked on both sides by two bodhisattvas and two bhikṣus, all standing upright upon the filaments of lotuses, brilliant and lovely, surpassing the former by several times.

Below the eyebrows, at the three lines, and within the eye sockets, four lights—blue, yellow, red, and white—arise in rotation; they move upward with brilliance, entering and exiting through the brow bones, and emerging from the tips of the eyebrows in the same manner as before.
Emerging from the occiput, the light circled four times, its four colors distinct:

the yellow emanation Buddhas had bodies the color of golden-yellow; the white emanation Buddhas had bodies the color of white silver; the blue emanation Buddhas had bodies the color of refined gold; and the red emanation Buddhas had bodies the color of musāragalva.
Thus, the clockwise spirals became even more distinct and superior, many times greater than before. "How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the eyelashes?

On each of the Tathāgata’s upper and lower eyelashes grow five hundred hairs, soft and lovely like the filaments of an *utpala* flower. From the tips of these hairs, a ray of light flows forth, the color of crystal, which enters into the preceding marks. Within this radiant color, it encircles the head once; from the occipital bone, it arises and surrounds the previous light, purely producing various exquisite blue lotuses. Upon the calyx of each lotus is a blue parasol, held in the hand of a Brahmā King."

When this sign appears, the Buddha’s eyes are blue and white; the white surpasses white jewels by hundreds of billions of times, and the blue excels blue lotuses and dark lapis lazuli by hundreds of billions of times.

The upper and lower eyelids blink together like the eyes of a bull king; from the tips of both corners of the eyes, two rays of light spiral outward. Like blue lotuses, they are extremely subtle; they encircle the hair once and emerge from the occipital bone, illuminating and adorning all the flowers so that they bloom, making their radiance even more manifest. Such supreme marks and immeasurable merits are called the Tathāgata’s eye.
"If there are those who wish to contemplate the Tathāgata’s eye, they should perform this contemplation; those who perform this contemplation will diminish all evils.

Sitting upright with eyes closed, they should correctly contemplate the Buddha’s eye for one day up to seven days. In future lives, they will always be able to see the Buddha and shall never be blind or dark-sighted. Furthermore, they will not be born in borderlands, among those with wrong views, or in places where the Buddha-dharma does not exist; their wisdom-eye will remain ever-open, and they will not give rise to folly."
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"Therefore, a wise person, in order to eliminate the darkness of blindness, should contemplate the Buddha-eye.
The Buddha possesses five eyes; within this method of contemplation, the fleshly eye is explained first."

The clear, pure light manifests as the realization of the eye-mind’s sharpness; the realms of animals cannot be fully described. If one contemplates the Buddha-eye for even a brief moment, or contemplates the image-eye, then throughout five future lifetimes, one’s eyes will remain constantly clear and pure, the faculty of sight will be free from disease, and the sins of birth and death for seven kalpas will be eliminated.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and commanded the fourfold assembly:

"Diligently contemplate the Buddha’s eyes; be careful not to let this practice cease or be abandoned. Those who contemplate the Buddha’s eyes will surely obtain immeasurable, subtle, and wondrous merit."

The hairline and broad forehead, the curls of the hair, the eye sockets, the eyebrows, the eyelashes, and the markings of the eyes—through the radiant light of such manifold marks, if one can behold them even for a moment, the sins of birth and death for sixty kalpas will be eliminated.

In future births, they will surely behold Maitreya; protected by the majestic radiance of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, their minds will be like lotuses, free from attachment, and they shall never fall into the three miserable realms or the eight difficult conditions.

If, while sitting, you do not see [the vision], you should enter a stūpa to contemplate. When entering the stūpa to contemplate, you should likewise form this visualization of various lights. With a sincere mind, join your palms, kneel, and observe with focused attention for one to three days until your mind is no longer distracted. After your life ends, you will be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where you will face-to-face behold the majestic and dignified physical body of Maitreya Bodhisattva. Moved by your response, he will provide guidance; having seen him, your body and mind will rejoice, and you will enter the stage of the True Dharma.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"To contemplate in this manner is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation.
From the *Buddha-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, Scroll Two.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Three: Contemplating the Physical Marks.

The Buddha told the King, his father: "How does one contemplate the ears of the Buddha? The Buddha’s ears hang down evenly on both sides, adorned with the various marks such as the seven whorls of hair and the outer rims. Furthermore, from the time he was born in the royal palace and his ears were first pierced, lotus flowers grew within and without the two ear canals. From within these lotuses and from the seven hairs of the ears, various rays of light flow forth in five hundred branches; each branch has five hundred colors, and from each color emerge five hundred transformation Buddhas, each accompanied by five Bodhisattvas and five bhikṣus as attendants. These rays circle to the right around the light for five turns, shining equally above and below upon the Buddha’s ears. The Buddha’s ears are so lovely that they resemble precious lotus flowers suspended in the sunlight."
"When the Buddha was in the world, the entire great assembly all beheld this sign; this is called the light of the Buddha’s ear-mark.
The Buddha told the King, his father:

"If the fourfold assembly distances themselves from clamor and distraction, and with right mindfulness contemplates the mark of the Buddha’s ears, such persons will have pure auditory faculties free from all defilement and evil wherever they are born. Their ears shall constantly hear the unsurpassed and subtle twelve divisions of the scriptures; having heard them, they will believe and understand, practicing according to the teachings, thereby eliminating the sins of birth and death for eighty kalpas."

If one does not see [the Buddha], then as previously described, one should enter a stupa and contemplate the image with focused attention for one day up to fourteen days; one will likewise obtain the merits as previously explained. Therefore, the wise person should diligently cultivate and accumulate the correct contemplation of the Buddha, ensuring it is not neglected or lost.
Even when suffering from illness and lying on one's side or bed, one should still contemplate the pure ear-lobes of the Buddha.

Observing the image in this manner, with the mind as previously conceived remaining diligent and undaunted, one will, in future births, always find companionship with those who possess dhāraṇīs; hearing the Dharma, they will retain it like beads strung on a thread.
One who observes in this manner is said to have right observation; one who observes otherwise is said to have wrong observation.
"How does one observe the Tathāgata’s mark of square jawbones?

Upon the Tathāgata’s cheeks, within six lines, there are on both the left and right sides equal and perfect wondrous radiance, brilliant and more intense than usual. The color of Jambūnada gold shines everywhere, making the Buddha’s face like pure golden color, as if a hundred thousand suns and moons were gathered together. This is called the Tathāgata’s mark of square jawbones."

"After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, those disciples of the Buddha who bind their mindfulness in contemplation and perform this visualization shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over a hundred kalpas; they will face-to-face behold all Buddhas with perfect clarity and without doubt."
One who observes in this manner is said to have right observation; one who observes otherwise is said to have wrong observation. "How does one observe the Tathāgata’s mark of the lion's yawn?

When the Buddha opens his mouth, it is square and symmetrical like that of a lion king. From the edges of both lips, three rays of light stream forth; these golden rays surpass the previous lights by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. They enter upward into the ears and encircle the various hair-tufts, then emerge from the occipital bone and encircle the frontal halo. Within each of the painted intervals, there are three transformation Buddhas."
Each of these manifested Buddhas has two Brahma kings serving as attendants; this is called the Tathāgata’s mark of the lion’s yawn.

Any of the fourfold assembly who practices this contemplation after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa shall eliminate the sins of birth and death for ten kalpas. In their future lives, their mouths will always possess the fragrance of the utpala lotus, and all who hear what they proclaim will believe and accept it, just as the thirty-two heavens all place their trust in Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
To observe in this manner is called right observation; to observe otherwise is called wrong observation.
"What is meant by observing the Tathāgata’s mark of the nose?

The Tathāgata’s nose is high, long, and straight, positioned at the center of his face. The tip of the Tathāgata’s nose is like the beak of a king of eagles, and light flows from the nostrils, pouring down and up in a continuous stream."

The superior [light] enters the eyes, eyebrows, ūrṇā-kośa, and hairline; thus it enters straight into the crown of the head at the *uṣṇīṣa* bone, like a golden banner. Emerging from the occipital bone, it transforms into various flowers. Upon each flower are celestial musicians holding musical instruments, who enter everywhere among all the emanated Buddhas as attendants, circling the light ten times.

The lower part extends down into the Buddha’s beard, encircling the beard hairs so that flowers bloom at their roots like millet seeds; it flows into the lips and palate, reaching between the teeth to adorn the throat, and descending to the Buddha’s chest, it forms a cloud of light, pure inside and out without any dust or obscuration, like a vessel of lapis lazuli emitting golden flames—this is called the Tathāgata’s mark of the truly pure nose.

"Those disciples of the Buddha who contemplate in this way after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa will eliminate the most grievous evil karma of a thousand kalpas. In their future places of birth, they will smell sublime and wondrous fragrances; their minds will be clear and discerning, remaining unattached to such scents, and they will always take the fragrance of the precepts as their bodily ornament."
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.
"How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mustache?

Each hair-tip of the mustache unfolds three lights—violet, crimson, and red. These radiances extend straight from the edge of the mouth, spiraling up to illuminate the neck and encircling the halo with three distinct lines, which are clearly defined."

Regarding the supreme quality among forms: from within each and every hair-pore, a precious jewel is produced; the radiance of these jewels possesses hundreds of thousands of colors. Beneath the jewels, white flowers grow with their stalks touching one another, filling three circumferences. Thereafter, that light returns and enters back into the beard-hairs. This is called the Tathāgata’s mark of the radiance of the beard-hairs.

"Those who practice this contemplation after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa will eliminate the sins of birth and death for thirty kalpas. In their future lives, wherever they are born, there will be natural light from the pores of their bodies; their minds will take no pleasure in attachment to home, family, or worldly delights, and they will always delight in leaving the household life to cultivate the dhūta practices."
One who observes in this manner is said to have right observation; one who observes otherwise is said to have wrong observation.
"How does one observe the Tathāgata’s mark of lips that are red and beautiful like the *bimba* fruit?"

From the upper and lower lips, as well as the gums and palate, light was emitted in unison; this light was perfectly round, like a string of hundreds of thousands of red pearls, emerging from the Buddha’s mouth and entering his nose;
from the Buddha’s nose it entered the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft;
and from the *ūrṇā* hair-tuft it entered the spaces between his hairs.
[Light] enters and exits from between his hair into the halo, adorning it with various flowers.

From the forty teeth in his mouth, seals produce light; this light is reddish-white, shining brilliantly upon one another, illuminating the forty teeth so that their roots naturally become as white and even as crystal walls, with the upper and lower rows perfectly level and without any irregularity. From the patterns and lines between the teeth, various lights also flow forth, likewise reddish-white in color.
Regarding these various forms: while the Buddha was in the world, they dazzled the human eye; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one should perceive these forms with the mind’s eye.

Those disciples of the Buddha who practice this contemplation shall eliminate the sins of two thousand kalpas of birth and death. In their future lives, their lips and mouths will be exquisite and their teeth neither sparse nor missing; they will attain the highest excellence among all forms. Although they attain such beauty, their minds will not be greedily attached to it. They will constantly see the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, who will preach the Dharma for them so that their minds remain free from doubt.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.
"How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the broad and long tongue?

The Tathāgata’s tongue is obtained as the retribution for the ten pāramitās and the ten wholesome deeds. Beneath the root of that tongue and on both its sides, there are two precious jewels from which drops of nectar flow down onto the root of the tongue. Neither the devas and people of the world nor the bodhisattvas of the ten stages possess such a tongue-mark or such a flavor."
Upon his tongue are five lines like the pattern of a precious seal; as this supreme flavor enters into the seal-pattern, it flows up and down into a lapis lazuli tube.

When the Buddhas smile, they move their tongue-roots, and by the power of this flavor, the tongues emit five lights of distinct five colors, which circle the Buddhas seven times before returning to enter through the crowns of their heads.
When the Buddha extends his tongue, it is like a lotus petal; reaching up to the hairline, it completely covers his face. Beneath the tongue there are also various veins of manifold colors.
Such exquisite flavors flow into these veins, and by the power of those flavors, they transform into various rays of light in fourteen colors.
"The two rays of light shine upward, illuminating immeasurable worlds; between each ray of light is a light-pavilion, its colors so wondrous as to be beyond full description.
Within each light-pavilion are countless grotto-chambers;
within each chamber, immeasurable transformation Buddhas sit cross-legged, surrounded by assemblies of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and all the great multitudes."

Above, in immeasurable worlds, he transforms into a single Buddha; the Buddha’s body is tall and prominent like Mount Sumeru. Thus, these Buddhas are immeasurable in number, and all of them likewise extend their tongues in this same manner!

The two rays of light shone downward as far as the Avīci Hell, causing the Avīci Hell to appear like golden yellow; by the power of the Buddha’s tongue, those suffering beings were granted a brief respite, leading them to lament their own evil deeds committed in previous lives.

Thus, proceeding downward through immeasurable worlds, in each world he manifested jewel-flower trees with leaves like the tongues of Buddhas. From these tongue-features radiated light, and as the lights illuminated one another, they transformed into emanation-Buddhas. The bodies of these emanation-Buddhas were of pure white silver, their physical marks fully perfected.

Each emanation-Buddha extended a broad and long tongue; within the light of these tongues appeared further emanation-Buddhas. Such emanation-Buddhas were immeasurable in number, and the radiance of these emanation-Buddhas formed a single mountain of silver, a mountain of immense height and boundless extent.

Within those mountains, there grow exclusively silver trees with golden blossoms and silver fruits; beneath each tree are white jade lotuses, and upon each flower is a manifested being of white jade. From the navels of these jade beings, six dragons are born through transformation; the mouths of these dragons are black while their bodies are pure white, and the number of these manifested jade beings is immeasurable.

Furthermore, as the light descended even lower, it illuminated immeasurable realms. There, he saw white jade trees emerging from below that reached up to the Sahā world; they grew lush and dense all the way to the summit of the triple world (*tridhātu*). Their branches and twigs were luxuriant, and their leaves possessed colors—ninety-eight in number. Each leaf of every tree completely covered the triple world. Within the spaces between those leaves, there were dragons, elephants, tigers, wolves, lions, venomous insects, malevolent beasts, wildcats, and mice; there was nothing that did not exist there. As for the other realms, those seated there saw them for themselves.

"I saw a light shining toward the east, causing the ground of the eastern region to become entirely golden; mountains, rivers, trees, and all else were consumed by fire, yet the flames and the golden light did not obstruct one another."

At the tips of the golden light rays were various emanation Buddhas, one following another, extending as far as the immeasurable worlds of the eastern direction, like stalks of rice or sesame seeds with no space between them.

Each Buddha has immeasurable bodhisattvas as his attendants, and these bodhisattvas likewise extend their tongues to a length equal to that of the Buddha’s. From such tongues, immeasurable radiance transforms into clouds of light; within these clouds of light, immeasurable transformation-Buddhas, as numerous as motes of dust, sit in the full lotus posture. The number of such radiances is likewise immeasurable.

At that time, at the tips of the flames, there were five yakṣas holding sharp swords; each had four mouths on its head from which it sucked fire as it ran. Such ghosts were immeasurable in number, and it was likewise so in the eastern direction!
"A single light shines upon immeasurable worlds in the southern direction, causing those worlds to take on the color of lapis lazuli; upon the lapis lazuli ground, golden flowers grow;
upon the golden flowers, agate flowers grow;
and upon the agate flowers, musaragalva flowers grow."
From the *śaṅkhaśilā* flowers, *mūṣāra* flowers arise;
from the *mūṣāra* flowers, *musāragalva* flowers arise;
from the *musāragalva* flowers, *pravāḍa* flowers arise.
From the coral flowers, golden essence flowers arise;
from the golden essence flowers, vajra flowers arise;
from the vajra flowers, mani-light flowers arise.
Between each of the petals of the mani-luminous flowers, there were hundreds of millions of jeweled blossoms of immeasurable colors.

Upon each stamen of these flowers sat an immeasurable Śākyamuni Buddha in the full lotus posture, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas; at that time, such flowers also issued forth from the pores of the bodies of all those in the assembly.
Upon each flower, rare and marvelous events appeared, just as described above.
These emanated Buddhas extended their broad and long tongues, manifesting light that was hundreds of thousands of millions of times more magnificent than this [original] mark.
Amidst the various flowers were wondrous jewel thrones, lofty and conspicuous, like the couches of Brahmā;

upon each throne sat a great Bodhisattva, with physical features as dignified and majestic as Maitreya, who also extended his broad and long tongue. The light of these tongues formed nets of *maṇi* jewels, covering all the emanated Buddhas and the great assembly. From within the *maṇi* nets issued forth great jewel-lights, the tips of which were adorned with precious gems.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable and boundless transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), each of whom was attended by countless bhikṣus. At that time, these bhikṣus sat upon golden lotuses, their bodies the color of gold; they entered the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* with peaceful meditation and palms joined. From the pores of their bodies, rays of golden light issued forth, and each of these rays transformed into a transformation Buddha, like a mountain of gold, surrounding the bhikṣus. There were also transformed bhikṣus surrounding the Buddhas, in such vast numbers that they could not be described.
"A single light shines upon the western direction, causing the ground of the western region to become the color of crystal; upon the crystal ground there are clouds of vajra;
within the vajra clouds are clouds of white jewels;
within the white jewel clouds are clouds of red pearls."
Within clouds of red pearls, there were clouds of white pearls;
within clouds of white pearls, there were clouds of purple pearls;
within clouds of purple pearls, there were clouds of green pearls.
Within clouds of green pearls, there were clouds of red pearls;
within clouds of red pearls, there were clouds of Jāmbūnada gold sand;
within clouds of gold sand, there were clouds of diamond-maṇi atoms.
Within the clouds of vajra-maṇi atoms, there are clouds of atoms of every precious color.

Within each of these individual clouds, there are five hundred and sixty million colors, subtle, exquisite, and surpassing the range of the visual faculty; only a mind of profound stillness can be in harmony with them.

Within these various marks, there were furthermore immeasurable atoms of emanated Buddhas; each emanated Buddha had immeasurable atoms of emanated disciples. These atoms were not large, and the Buddhas were not small; they were dignified, sublime, and as exquisite as Śākyamuni, and they likewise extended their tongues.

"A single light shines toward the north, causing the ground of the northern quarter to become the color of musāragalva. Upon that musāragalva ground there are vajra-stūpas; each stūpa is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of wondrous stūpas, their number being immeasurable. Even the smallest of these stūpas is fifty billion nayuta yojanas in height.
Within each stūpa, there are further grottoes as numerous as the atoms of ten billion worlds.

From within each grotto, waters of immeasurable and boundless jewel-hues spontaneously surge forth. Upon these waters, great lotuses appear, radiating light. When this light manifests, its fragrance is so subtle and exquisite that it surpasses the scent of sandalwood from this side of the ocean by hundreds of thousands of millions of times."

This fragrance transforms into subtle and wondrous light; within these lights are emanated buddhas, their bodies of exquisite color, the most supreme among all jewels, with every kind of precious gem emerging from the mark of their tongues.
At that time, each and every cave was filled with immeasurable radiance;
from each ray of light emerged immeasurable transformation Buddhas;

and each transformation Buddha further extended his tongue, emitting immeasurable light that likewise formed fragrant stupas. These extended beyond immeasurable worlds to the north, beyond all reckoning, arising solely from the ocean of the *nien-fo* (Buddha-remembrance) samādhi.

"A single light shines upon the southeastern direction, causing the ground of the southeastern region to become the color of agate. Upon the agate ground there is a mountain of amber; atop the amber mountain grows a forest of seven-jeweled trees. Between these seven-jeweled trees are ten springs, whose waters possess the colors of the ten jewels. The colors of the water emit light that universally illuminates immeasurable worlds in the southeastern direction. Wherever the light shines, there are great jewel mountains, and between each mountain and beneath each tree grow *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers."

Upon the flower pedestal was a manifested Buddha, of pure lapis lazuli color, transparent both within and without beyond description; a light of various jewel colors encircled his body a thousand times, and within each ray of light were immeasurable manifested Buddhas.
Each manifested Buddha was surrounded by a vast assembly, all of whom were of lapis lazuli color;
from the tongue-mark of each manifested Buddha issued forth radiant light that transformed into a mountain of jewels.
Such jewel mountains extend further toward the southeast across immeasurable worlds.

A single light shines upon immeasurable worlds in the southwest, causing the ground of the southwest to become the uniform color of coral; upon this coral ground arise towers of green jade, the lowest of which are fifty billion *yojanas* in height.
The pavilion had one hundred million pillars; each of these pillars possessed ten billion jewel colors, and each jewel emitted countless rays of light.
Each of these rays of light transformed into immeasurable thousands of billions of jewel trees.
Beneath each tree there are six springs; their water enters through the roots of the trees and emerges from the branches, and as it flows forth, it possesses the colors of the six jewels.
Within each body of water grows a lotus flower, and these flowers are brilliant white.

Upon the flower, there was further a white transformation Buddha, whose body was so exceedingly white that it surpassed all others; above this white color were five hundred colors, and a subtle, wondrous radiance surrounded the Buddha’s body.
From each ray of light, countless transformation Buddhas were manifested; each transformation Buddha had countless bodhisattvas, and the pillars of the various pavilions all emitted radiance;
within each ray of light were countless transformation Buddhas.
Blue transformation Buddhas were walking back and forth upon coral ground, while white transformation Buddhas were walking back and forth atop towers of blue jade.

Within the chambers and grottoes of these pavilions, there were likewise countless such transformation Buddhas, who also extended their tongues and emitted great radiance; that light was subtle and wondrous, illuminating immeasurable worlds in the southwest direction without end.

"A single light shines upon the northwest, causing the northwest to become a land of amber. Upon this amber ground, mountains of pearls arise; atop these pearl mountains are coral trees with leaves of white jade, flowers of *maṇi* jewels, fruits of gold, and stamens of refined gold. Beneath each tree there naturally appears a great lion, its body composed of the seven treasures."

From within the eyes of the Lion, a great radiance was emitted, illuminating the agate ground and causing a great lotus flower to arise from it. This flower was perfectly round, immeasurable and boundless; upon each petal was a cloud of light, the clouds being purple in color. Above the clouds were nets of green pearls, and from within the intervals of these pearl nets grew golden lotus flowers. Upon each golden lotus flower sat a manifested Buddha, with a body the color of purple gold, surrounded by the five-colored radiances of blue, yellow, red, and white.
Within each ray of light are innumerable manifested Buddhas;
within each manifested Buddha are immeasurable great assemblies. These manifested Buddhas likewise extend their broad and long tongues in this same manner!
In this way, he universally illumines immeasurable worlds in the northwest; the radiance of his tongue-mark is inexhaustible.
A single light shines upon the northeast, causing the ground of the northeast to become entirely the color of diamond, and upon that diamond ground, flowers formed from the seven treasures arise.

The banners atop the flowers were Jambū-river gold in color; at the tips of these banners were flowers, which possessed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jewel-hues and countless petals. Each flower petal transformed into immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jeweled canopies.

At each corner of every canopy stood a banner made of the seven treasures, and atop each banner was a parasol of the seven treasures, which completely covered all the worlds upon the ground of the northeastern quarter.

There were five banners made entirely of pure gold; each banner was adorned with ten billion immeasurable jeweled bells, which emitted wondrous sounds praising the names of the Buddhas, praising the worship of the Buddhas, praising the mindfulness of the Buddhas, and praising repentance.

After these sounds had issued forth, from beneath the jeweled canopy, a great light surged upward; that light was subtle and wondrous, numbering countless thousands of billions. Within each ray of light were immeasurable transformation Buddhas sitting in the full lotus posture, seated within the jeweled canopy.

Furthermore, there were those who leaped up into the air and remained suspended there: leaping from the east and vanishing in the west, leaping from the west and vanishing in the east; leaping from the south and vanishing in the north, leaping from the north and vanishing in the south; leaping from the edges and vanishing in the center, and leaping from the center and vanishing at the edges.

Sometimes they manifest a great body that fills the void of space; then, from great, it again manifests as small, its body like a mustard seed, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining within the void. Water flows from the upper part of the body while fire issues from the lower part; fire issues from the lower part of the body while water flows from the upper part. They tread upon the earth as if it were water, and walk upon water as if it were solid ground.

Within the water, lotus flowers grew as large as chariot wheels; upon each flower sat a Buddha in the full lotus posture. Such emanation Buddhas were infinite and boundless. Simultaneously, they beheld these Buddhas leaping into the air and performing the eighteen miraculous transformations: atop the fire arose a golden Mount Sumeru, adorned with the stars, the sun, the moon, and the seven treasures, along with various nāgas, yakṣas, and the waters of the great ocean.
In this manner, all that exists to the left and right of these many Mount Sumerus appeared.

These mountains were immeasurable in number, and upon each mountain peak there was a Buddha who likewise extended his tongue; the radiance of these tongues shone everywhere throughout immeasurable worlds in the northeast, beyond all measure.

"A single light shone upward from Jambudvīpa to the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, causing the Four Heavenly Kings to all behold Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One—the sun among men—mounted upon a platform of seven treasures."

Together with the great assembly, he went to that celestial realm; upon seeing him, the devas resolved their minds on Bodhi. Even all the devas up to the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) beheld this sign with perfect clarity and undisturbed minds, causing the Formless devas to cease slandering Nirvāṇa and instead give rise to the thought of Bodhi.

“A single ray of light shone downward upon all the asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, nāgas, rākṣasas, pūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, those ghosts who devour the vital energy of humans, kūṣmāṇḍas, śakunikas, āṭavakas, pretas, those ghosts who eat vomit, those ghosts who eat mucus and saliva, those ghosts who eat pus and blood, those ghosts who eat excrement and urine, the mountain deities, the tree deities, and the water deities.”

In this manner, these several hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities had their bodies temporarily assume the color and form of celestial beings, becoming supple, joyful, and blissful—just as a bhikṣu enters the third dhyāna. Each of these spirits, according to their respective karmic actions, gave rise to the three kinds of bodhicitta.

When the light of the tongue-mark appears before the various hungry ghosts, it is like cold water extinguishing the fire between their joints; once the fire is extinguished, the molten copper falls to the ground and sinks straight into the earth.
At that time, all the hungry ghosts opened their mouths wide and cried out, "Hunger!
Hunger! For ten million years we have never seen water; now that we have encountered this water which removes our heat and brings coolness, by whose power is this?"
A voice from the air said:
"Foolish hungry ghost, there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has extended the radiance of his tongue; its light shines upon you, causing all your agonizing suffering to find complete rest."

Having spoken these words, before each and every ghost, he saw a compassionate mother sitting upon a lotus pedestal. Just as a compassionate mother might embrace an infant and give him milk to drink until the child is fully satiated, so too did she satisfy the ghosts;
once they were fully satiated, they gave rise to the bodhicitta, and once they had given rise to that mind, each compassionate mother transformed into a Buddha.
At that time, each of those Buddhas likewise extended their tongue-marks to rescue the hungry ghosts.

When the Buddha withdrew his tongue-mark, this light of a thousand colors circled the Buddha a thousand times; within the light were a thousand Buddhas who entered through the crown of the Buddha’s head.

Having entered, the Buddha’s body appeared majestic and resplendent; his thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary characteristics were all brilliantly radiant, with light streaming from every part of his body, shimmering and dazzling more intensely than hundreds of thousands of countless billions of suns.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"Such is the appearance of the Tathāgata’s tongue and its merits; such are the matters observed within the realm of the tongue!

After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, those who, with a mind keen on mindfulness of the Buddha, contemplate the Buddha’s tongue, will perceive the realm of their mental eye exactly as previously described."

One who practices this contemplation shall eliminate the karmic offenses of birth and death accumulated over ten billion and eighty-four thousand kalpas; upon casting off this body in another world, they will encounter eight billion buddhas.
In the presence of all Buddhas, they shall likewise see the broad and long tongue-marks of those Buddhas emitting great radiance;
only then shall they receive the prediction of their attainment of the path to Bodhi.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Hold fast to my words and do not let them be forgotten or lost. Tell all the disciples: those who sit upright with body and mind rectified, entering right concentration to contemplate the broad and long tongue, shall be no different from me while I am in the world."

If there are sentient beings who hear this teaching and do not become startled or doubtful, nor give rise to slander; who do not trouble those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, but instead encourage and inspire those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and who make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise them.

Although such persons do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, by virtue of their wholesome minds, they eliminate the most grave evil karma accumulated over a hundred kalpas. In their future place of birth, they shall encounter Maitreya and continue on until they meet Loushi Buddha; at the abodes of these thousand Buddhas, they will hear the Dharma and receive transformation, constantly attaining this Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"To observe in this manner is called right observation; to observe otherwise is called wrong observation.
How does one observe the Tathāgata’s mark of the neck, the mark of the fullness of the *khaṇḍaka* bone, the mark of the *śrīvatsa* on the chest, and the mark of the *svastika* seal?"
Between these various syllables, radiant halos emerge; his neck is full and rounded like a tube of lapis lazuli, from which hang exquisite golden banners;
upon his throat, there is a clearly defined mark shaped exactly like the letter *i*.
From each and every dot, two rays of light stream forth; each ray circles the preceding circular halo, completing seven full revolutions with every detail clearly delineated.
Between each of these lines is a wondrous lotus flower, and upon each lotus flower are seven transformation Buddhas.
Each transformation Buddha has seven bodhisattvas serving as attendants.
Each and every bodhisattva held a wish-fulfilling jewel in both hands; the golden light of those jewels was fully endowed with all colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and the hue of mani-gems.

Thus, among the various surrounding rays depicted within the painting, these are known as: the mark of the circular halo emerging from the Buddha’s neck; the *śrīvatsa* symbol on his chest; the mark of the full vessel within the seal of the ten thousand characters (*daśasahasra-lakṣaṇa-mudrā*); and the pearl-like mark beneath his armpits.
Within each of these marks, every superior characteristic possesses five hundred multicolored rays of light that shine forth together, illuminating one another without mutual interference;
each colored ray encircles the light of the neck for five hundred revolutions;
and within each painted mark, there are five hundred transformation Buddhas.
Each of these manifested Buddhas was attended by five hundred bodhisattvas as their retinue, while five hundred bhikṣus stood at their left and right, holding white whisks.

Among all the lights—the light of the manifested Buddhas, the light of the manifested bodhisattvas, and the light of the manifested bhikṣus—all were clearly revealed: Mount Sumeru, the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, the celestial mansions of the various devas, the sun, moon, and stars, the palaces of the nāgas, the palaces of the spirits, and the palaces of the asuras; the deities of the ten jewel mountains, the water deities of the four oceans, and the gandharvas of the aquatic realms.

All those things revered by the various brahmins, the ninety-five kinds of supernatural arts of the rishis, and the ancestral lineages and karmic conditions experienced by one's parents—all such deities were fully manifested within the Buddha’s light.
Furthermore, there were ten billion immeasurable spirits and deities whose reflections appeared within the halo, preaching the matter of filial support to the people of Jambudvīpa.
When these manifested apparitions saw the multitude, they each spoke of themselves, saying:
"I am your father; I am your mother. Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, your name was so-and-so, and my name was so-and-so."

"In this way, these many immeasurable multitudes are all matters revered by sentient beings; within the Buddha’s radiant halo, they are clearly visible as if in a painting or as one sees one's own face in a mirror—these various marks are called the 'radiant halo' (prabhā-maṇḍala)."

It encircles the Buddha’s neck, measuring one fathom above and one fathom below; it is likewise one fathom on the left and one fathom on the right, totaling eight feet in height. From within this circular halo, emanated Buddhas flow forth.

All things that sentient beings long to behold appear within it, clearly and distinctly. Upon the circular halo there is a brilliant golden luster, as magnificent and lovely as a mani jewel; amidst the radiance of the mani jewels, flowering trees manifest through transformation. These trees are golden, such that even hundreds of thousands of millions of Jambūnada golds cannot compare to them. Beneath each tree is a precious lotus flower, and upon each flower is a transformed Buddha of true golden hue. Like a lapis lazuli canopy covering the Buddhas, their golden countenances are revealed with perfect clarity. Such manifested images are infinite in number.
"When the Buddha was in the world, as the World-Honored One traveled, this light illuminated the ground: for one yojana ahead, it was pure golden-yellow;
for one yojana behind, it was pure golden-yellow;
and for one yojana to the left, it was pure golden-yellow."
To the right, for one yojana, it is pure golden color.
If anyone walks near the Buddha to his left or right, their foul odors and impurities all disappear; from afar, people see them as being the same golden color.
As the Buddha sat beneath the tree, this radiance blazed brilliantly, like a profusion of golden flowers scattered among the branches of the Jeta Grove.
Those who gazed intently at the light upon the Buddha’s neck saw him before them;
those who looked from behind saw the Buddha behind them.
Looking from the left, one sees the Buddha on the left;
looking from the right, one sees the Buddha on the right.
People coming from the eight directions see the light radiating from his neck from afar, and each says:
“The śramaṇa Gautama is traveling with sovereign ease amidst the Golden Mountains and has come to my place.
Thus do the various people each have their different perceptions; this is called the "light from the neck."

When this light was seen, ten thousand *koṭis* of rays emerged from the *uṣṇīṣa* on the Buddha’s crown; these rays followed one another in succession, reaching even to the infinite worlds above. Neither the gods, nor the people of the world, nor the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages could see the hair upon his head, which spiraled to the right in exquisite conch-like curls. Its color surpassed that of bees, emeralds, or peacock feathers; a thousand brilliant rays blazed forth. When these rays arose, all the wondrous marks within the Buddha’s cranial bone and head were fully revealed. His countenance was perfectly complete, its radiance lovely and sublime; even the exquisite flowers obtained as retribution by humans, devas, and pure lands cannot serve as a comparison.
The radiance from the Buddha’s face became even more brilliant;
the light from the Buddha’s neck, chest, and arms became several times more radiant than before;
and light issued from the Buddha’s knees—this light was white and divided into four branches, which ascended along his body, transformed into white flowers, and entered beneath the light of his neck.

From the navel, five rays of light emerge; each ray has two branches, and each branch possesses five colors that enter into the ribs. They are like tubes of white jade filled with water of various colors, which naturally wells up from behind both shoulders. Like the flames of golden *maṇi* jewels, they stand in close proximity to one another. Within the light of these *maṇi* jewels are wondrous lotus flowers; upon each lotus flower are seven transformation Buddhas, appearing as if painted or stamped. They rotate along with the Buddha’s body without obstructing one another, their limbs like those of a deer king, their bones linked like hooks, and their joints bound like coiled dragons.

In this manner, various golden rays issued from the middle; each of these rays entered one joint and exited another, merging together to form a single great radiance like a golden maṇi. It rested behind the Buddha’s elbow and extended its brilliance up to the crown-light. His copper-colored nails and the webbing between his toes each possessed their own light, which was brilliant and shimmering like lapis lazuli and crystal, endowed with the colors of the seven jewels. From the Buddha’s insteps, it corresponded in measure to his body like a maṇi jewel, and like the previous light, it ascended upward to the halo.

"From the wheel-mark on his foot and from his long heel, a flower blossoms upon each; these flowers are exquisite and subtle, like the *utpala* lotuses in a pure land. Emerging from the Buddha’s heels, they surround his radiance in ten complete circles, with each flower following the next in succession."
Within each flower are five transformation Buddhas;
each transformation Buddha has fifty bodhisattvas as attendants.

From the crowns of each bodhisattva’s head, light from *maṇi* jewels emerges. When this sign appears, from every single pore of the Buddha’s body, eighty-four thousand subtle, minute rays of light spiral forth, adorning the bodily radiance so that it is exceedingly lovely. These various colors are called "constant light," "light that accords with the mind," "light that follows whatever sentient beings wish to see," and "light bestowed upon sentient beings as their eyes."

This light extends one fathom and its manifestations are manifold; when Ghoṣila contemplates the Buddha’s light, it appears small, whereas when the great bodhisattvas from other directions contemplate the Buddha, this light appears large, as described in the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (or *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*).
The Buddha addressed the King, his father, and commanded Ānanda:
"I shall now manifest for you my complete physical form and its radiance.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha rose from his seat and said to Ānanda:
“You bhikṣus and you sons of the Śākyas!

All of you, rise and join your palms toward the Buddha; gaze intently at the Tathāgata, from the light of his crown down to the light of his feet, and from the uṣṇīṣa on his crown down to the level, full marks beneath his feet.”
He further instructed the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, from the mark of the level and full soles of the feet, extending upward to the uṣṇīṣa, you should also contemplate the light of the Tathāgata’s body and the light of his neck."
He further commanded:
