"From each and every pore of the Buddha's body down to the very end of a single limb, contemplate each detail until it is perfectly clear, just as a person holding a mirror gazes at their own facial reflection."
"If one gives rise to a defiled, evil, or unwholesome mind,
or if one violates the prohibitions of the Buddha's precepts, they will see the image as purely black, like a person made of charcoal.
Among the assembly of Śākyas, five hundred Śākyas saw the physical body of the Buddha as being like a person made of charcoal.
Among the assembly of bhikṣus, there were one thousand who saw the Buddha’s physical body as being like a person smeared with red earth;
among the assembly of upāsakas, there were sixteen who saw the Buddha’s physical body as being like the leg of a black elephant;
and among the assembly of upāsikās, there were twenty-four who saw the color of the Buddha’s body as being like a mass of ink.
Thus, the four assemblies each had different perceptions.
Among the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, there was a bhikṣuṇī who saw the Buddha’s physical body as the color of white silver;

among the assembly of upāsikās, there was an upāsikā who saw the Buddha’s physical body as the color of indigo-dyed blue. In this way, what the four assemblies perceived of the Buddha’s physical body differed from one another.
At that time, when the fourfold assembly heard these words of the Buddha, they wept with tears falling like rain and, joining their palms, addressed the Buddha:
"We can no longer behold your wondrous form.
Five hundred sons of the Śākya clan tore out their own hair and threw themselves to the ground; blood flowed from their nostrils.
“The Buddha was born into our family.

When the Buddha was first born, everyone saw him as pure golden color, yet we alone always see the Buddha’s body as being like a person of charcoal, or like emaciated brahmins. What karmic transgressions have we committed in our past lives?”
"I only pray that the Buddha-sun will explain this for me.
Having spoken these words, he plucked out his own hair and wailed as before, prostrating himself on the ground again and again.
At that time, the Compassionate Father, emitting a Brahma-like voice, comforted the Śākyas and the fourfold assembly:
"O sons of noble family!
The Tathāgata, the Sun of the Buddha, has appeared in the world precisely to eliminate your transgressions. Arise, for the Buddha himself knows the proper time and shall speak for your sake."
At that time, the great assembly rose from the ground, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
Five hundred sons of the Śākyas went to where Ānanda was, paid their respects to him, and said:
"Venerable One!..."

Both you and I were born into the Śākya clan; yet you alone are intelligent and possess the power of total retention (*dhāraṇī*) for the Buddha’s words, like water poured from one vessel into another. Because of my past transgressions, I do not even see the Buddha’s body, let alone hear his Dharma.
Having spoken these words, he wept before Ānanda.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Śākya sons and commanded the great assembly with a Brahma-voice:
"O brothers, do not wail any longer. In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world to teach and transform sentient beings."

After he had completed his work of saving sentient beings and entered parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was an elder named Candrasūryaśrī (Moon-Sun Virtue). He had five hundred sons who were intelligent and possessed great wisdom; they were extensively learned in all worldly arts and sciences, and there was nothing among the stars, constellations, or calendrical calculations that they did not master.

The father, the elder, had faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma; he constantly taught his sons the practice of contemplating the Buddha-mind and also spoke of the profound twelve links of dependent origination.
Having heard this, the sons were filled with doubt and did not believe it, saying:
"Our father is old and senile, having been deceived and deluded by those śramaṇas. None of our books contain such meanings; where has our father sought and found this?"
At that time, because the elder father took pity on his sons, he concealed the Buddha-dharma and did not proclaim it for them.

Then, all the sons simultaneously fell gravely ill; the father, observing that the lives of his sons could not be sustained for long, went to where his sons were. Before each of his children, he wept with tears, joined his palms, and said:
"You all held wrong views and did not believe in the True Dharma. Now the sword of impermanence cuts through your bodies; your minds are distressed and agitated—upon whom can you rely?"
"There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin; you may invoke his name.
Having heard this, the sons, out of respect for their father, invoked him, saying: "Namo Buddhāya."
The father spoke again, saying:
"You may recite the Dharma; you may recite the Sangha.
Before he had even finished the third recitation, his son passed away.

Because he had praised the Buddha, he was reborn in the heavens among the Four Great Kings. When his heavenly lifespan ended, he fell into the great hells due to his previous karma of wrong views. While suffering there in hell, the rakshasa wardens pierced and destroyed his eyes with hot iron forks.

While undergoing this suffering, he recalled the instructions given to him by his father, the elder. Because of his mindfulness of the Buddha, he emerged from hell and was reborn among humans, though in a state of poverty and low station. When Śikhin Buddha appeared, he encountered him; however, he heard the Buddha’s name but did not behold his form.
When Viśvabhū Buddha appeared, he likewise heard the Buddha’s name;
when Krakucchanda Buddha appeared, he also heard his name.
When Kanakamuni Buddha appeared, I also heard his name;
when Kāśyapa Buddha appeared, I also heard his name.

By virtue of the causal conditions of hearing the names of these six Buddhas, I have been born together with you; though born in this place, my physical form is now so exceedingly dignified and majestic!

You see my body as that of a frail Brahmin, yet my body is golden, such that even the color of Jāmbūnada gold cannot compare to it; you see my complexion as being like that of a person made of charcoal.
The Buddha addressed the Śākyas:
"You should now recite the names of the past Buddhas and pay homage to them;
furthermore, recite your father’s name and pay homage to the past Buddhas."
They shall also invoke my name and pay homage to me; they shall likewise pay homage to the future Buddha named Maitreya.

I shall declare the sins of your wrong views from past lives. Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world and the great assembly of śramaṇas is gathered like clouds, you must confess and repent before this multitude of venerable monks. In accordance with the Buddha’s words, you must repent for all your transgressions, prostrating yourself with your five limbs touching the ground like the collapsing of Mount Tai within the Sangha of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha.
Having repented before the Buddha, his mind’s eye was opened, and he beheld the Buddha’s physical body as majestic and subtle as Mount Sumeru, its radiance illuminating the great ocean.
Having seen the Buddha, his heart was filled with great joy, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I now behold the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; his body is the color of gold, and each mark and characteristic emits immeasurable light.
Having spoken these words, he immediately attained the Way and became a Srotāpanna.
They addressed their father, the king, saying:
"We now wish to leave the household life and study the Path within the Buddha-dharma.
The father, the king, replied:
“Did you personally inform the Buddha, and did the Buddha grant you permission?
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"I wish to leave the household life.
The Buddha said to the son of the Śākyas, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!"

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and he immediately became a śramaṇa; the garments he wore were transformed into dharma robes. With palms joined, he paid homage to the Buddha and cried out, "Namo Buddha! Before his head had even been raised, he became an arhat, fully endowed with the three insights and the six supernormal powers.
The Buddha said to the King, his father:
"Great King, do you now see these Śākya sons repenting to eliminate their offenses and becoming arhats?
The King replied to the Buddha:
“Yes, indeed, I have seen them! The Buddha told the King, his father:

“In previous lives, these bhikṣus slandered the True Dharma of the Buddha out of an evil mind; however, because they merely uttered ‘Namo Buddha’ for the sake of their father, they were able to hear the names of the Buddhas in every birth. Thus, having encountered my appearance in this present life, they have seen the physical body of the Buddha and the assembly of monks, and they have heard the Buddha’s teaching on repenting all transgressions. Because of this repentance, all obstacles have been eliminated; because the obstacles have been eliminated, they have become Arhats.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if gods and people of the world invoke my name or invoke 'Namo to all Buddhas,' the merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless; how much more so for those who maintain focused mindfulness of all Buddhas—how could their various obstacles not be extinguished?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The reason you see the Buddha’s physical body as being like red earth is that in a previous life, during the final dharma period of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, you left the home life to study the Way. Having left the home life, you gave rise to impure thoughts toward your preceptor;
however, that preceptor had attained the path of an Arhat and, knowing his disciple's mind, said to him:"
"Son of the Dharma!
Do not give rise to thoughts of doubt toward your preceptor or the community of monks; if you give rise to such doubts, there will be no possibility of ever attaining the pure precepts."
When the bhikṣus heard what their preceptor said, resentment arose in their hearts.
At that time, the preceptor, perceiving his disciples' thoughts, gradually restrained himself and did not speak further to them.
At that time, the thousand disciples, each according to the length of their lifespan, were about to pass away, yet their preceptor still remained and had not entered parinirvāṇa.
Then the preceptor went to where his disciples were and spoke these words: "O bhikṣus!..."
"When you first received the Dharma, you doubted your teacher and doubted the precepts; you have consumed the offerings of the faithful in vain. Upon whom can you now rely?
Hearing this, the people were struck with terror and their hair stood on end.
They said, "Preceptor!..."
"Please preach the Dharma for me.
The Upādhyāya replied, "Your current situation is urgent;
it is not appropriate for me to instruct you in repentance elsewhere. You should now simply invoke the ten titles of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and so forth."
At that time, the bhikṣus followed their preceptors’ words and all together exclaimed, “Namo to all Buddhas.

Having thus paid homage to the Buddhas, they immediately passed away; because of their wholesome state of mind, they were reborn in the heavens. They ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven where they enjoyed natural splendors, and upon the completion of their celestial lifespan, they descended to the human world. However, due to the sins of their previous lives (having consumed the faithful offerings of others in vain), they fell among the hungry ghosts, where molten copper was poured down their throats for a long duration of eighty-four thousand years.

When their retribution as hungry ghosts is exhausted, they are born among animals; when their retribution as animals is exhausted, they return to birth among humans, where poverty and lowly status serve as their adornment. Having been born among humans, they hear the names of the Buddhas;

because of the power of their renunciation in previous lives, faith arises within them, and through their former latent consciousness, they cry out "Namo Buddha. By virtue of the merit and conditions of uttering the Buddha’s name, they encounter the era of a Buddha for eight thousand lifetimes; yet, though their eyes do not behold the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas, how much less could they hear the Dharma?
"Thus, even until today, having encountered my era, you see my body appearing like red earth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In previous lives, regarding matters that were beyond doubt, you arbitrarily gave rise to views of doubt; regarding matters that were trustworthy, you arbitrarily gave rise to lack of faith."

Because of these offenses, you do not see the Buddhas nor hear the True Dharma; whereas I am now manifest in a royal palace, my complexion being truly sublime—the most excellent among all complexions—yet you see me as if I were covered in red earth.
When the bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, they each repented and reproached themselves. Baring their right shoulders and joining their palms toward the Buddha, they spoke thus:

"In immeasurable kalpas of our past lives, we held wrong views and doubted our teachers, and we accepted offerings from the faithful in vain. Because of these causes and conditions, we fell into the hells; though we have now emerged, for immeasurable lifetimes we did not see the Buddhas but only heard their names. Now we see the World-Honored One’s body, the color of red earth, exactly five feet in height."

At that time, the World-Honored One drew back his saṃkakṣikā to reveal the syllable *bhadra* upon his chest; having caused the bhikṣus to recite the syllable *bhadra*, they came to know the adornment of the Buddha’s merit and wisdom, and through the seal of ten thousand syllables, he expounded the eighty-four thousand meritorious practices of the Buddha.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu praised the Buddha, saying:
"The World-Honored One is most extraordinary; he expounds immeasurable meanings from a single character 'chest' (xiōng), let alone all the merits possessed by the Buddha's mind."

Having spoken these words, he repented before the Buddha, prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground like the collapsing of Mount Tai. Wailing piteously and shedding tears like rain, he wept before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One comforted him with gentle words, causing the hearts of all the bhikṣus to rejoice.
Having thus rejoiced, just as when the wind blows heavy clouds apart in all directions, the golden countenance with its thirty-two marks was revealed and seen with brilliant clarity.
Having seen the Buddha, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The Buddha told the King, his father:

"These one thousand bhikṣus have sought the Dharma with earnest diligence, their minds never wearying; in a future age, after kalpas beyond counting, they shall attain Buddhahood, each named Namu Guangzhao Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."

When he attains Buddhahood, the ground shall be of pure golden color, adorned with rows of trees made of the seven treasures and exquisite jeweled pavilions. The sentient beings of that land will all be those who practice shame and remorse, being exclusively Bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the supreme mind.
"In this way, a thousand Buddhas appeared in succession, just as the thousand Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa will successively attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"These bhikṣus, by doubting their teacher and doubting the Saṃgha, have incurred a grave and heavy offense."

As previously stated, the karmic fruit obtained by reciting "Namo Buddha" is such that one receives a prediction of enlightenment in my own world in the present life; how much more so for those who contemplate the Buddha with right mindfulness!
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw that the Buddha was silver-colored, they rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, paid homage to the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!”

The Tathāgata now speaks of his own physical form to eliminate the immeasurable heavy sins of all sentient beings. For what reason have we, from birth and since leaving the household life until this very day, seen the Buddha’s body as silver-colored, with silver flowers and silver light, such that all his ornaments are entirely made of silver?
"Why is it that we do not see the Tathāgata’s golden light so brilliantly radiant, nor do we see the merit and retribution of the Buddha’s thirty-two marks?
At that time, when the Tathāgata heard the words of the bhikṣuṇīs, he immediately smiled; a golden light issued from his face and circled his silver body ten full times.
When this light appeared, the bhikṣuṇīs beheld the Buddha’s body, golden-hued like purple-gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks, its radiance shining forth beyond description.

Having seen this, they gazed upon the mark of the white tuft between his brows, curling gracefully to the right; having seen it, they were filled with joy and immediately attained the path of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
The bhikṣuṇīs recollected their past lives: in the past, during immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, also named Śākyamuni.

After that Buddha had passed into extinction, there were disciples who left the household life to study the Way. Among them was one monk who traveled about to teach and transform others; he saw five hundred young girls in the mountains and marshes, enjoying themselves in merriment.
At that time, the bhikṣu, maintaining his dignified deportment, walked slowly and composedly to where the women were. He spread out a *niṣīdana* on the ground and sat down.
When the women saw him, they each rejoiced and said:

"This secluded place is frequented by seers and immortals; yet suddenly this eminent gentleman, a bhikṣu, has come here and sits. This must surely not be an ordinary person; we ought to make offerings to him."
Each removed a silver ring and scattered it over the bhikṣu, saying:

"This bhikṣu is diligent and his virtuous conduct is perfectly complete; he will surely attain Buddhahood in the future. We pray that when we behold him, it shall be as these rings we have scattered."

“Because you were greedily attached to the color of silver treasure, life after life you have always dwelt among the White Silver Mountains, receiving the bodies of precious daughters of the Silver Mountain deities;
because you offered silver rings to the śramaṇas as a mark of respect, you have now encountered my world, been purified through bathing, and become arhats.”
The bhikṣu at that time was none other than myself! The women of that time were you!
Because you made offerings to śramaṇas and paid homage to the Buddhas in previous lives, from that time onward you have always encountered the Buddhas.
The Buddha told the King, his father:

"A Buddha is a treasure among men, bringing manifold benefits and blessings. If one merely hears his name, pays homage, and makes offerings, one shall obtain a great and weighty reward; how much more so for one who fixes their mindfulness upon the Buddha and contemplates his true countenance!"

Among the assembly of upāsakas, those who saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, resembling the leg of a black elephant, immediately rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"I was born in this country; the prince of our nation has left the household life and attained Buddhahood. When the seer Asita beheld the thirty-two marks, he told me:
'There is no doubt that Prince Dīpaṃkara will become a Buddha.'"

"Upon hearing these words, I took refuge in the Buddha; from that time forth, I have constantly followed behind the Buddha, receiving the three refuges, upholding the eight precepts of the fast, and receiving the dharma of the five precepts."
"Yet such is my transgression that I hear only the Buddha's voice but do not see the Buddha's form; whenever I see the Buddha, it is like the foot of a black elephant. How extreme is this cruelty!
Having spoken these words, she raised her hands to beat her breast, wailed aloud, and fell prostrate upon the ground.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with a voice like that of Brahmā, as a compassionate father comforts his son, addressed the upāsakas, saying:
"Sons of the Dharma, sit down again; the Buddha shall eliminate your doubts and regrets for you, and extinguish all obstacles."
Having spoken these words, he addressed the upāsakas:
"In the past, during immeasurable kalpas, you were each a king in Jambudvīpa, ruling over various kingdoms with complete sovereignty."

There are certain śramaṇas who, for the sake of gain and offerings, provide you with false teachings that do not accord with the Buddha’s instruction; they proclaim what is Dharma as non-Dharma and what is non-Dharma as Dharma, and you all place your trust in them.

Because this person followed these various evil teachings, after his life ended he fell into the Avīci Hell; because you have followed the instructions of evil friends, after your lives end you too shall fall into the Black Darkness Hell.

Due to the power of the wholesome mind from hearing the Dharma in the past, you have now encountered my world and received the five precepts; you should now, before the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, confess with a sincere heart the false views and the teachings of your evil friends.
Upon hearing these words of the Buddha, the upāsakas cried out, "Namo buddhāya! Namo dharmāya! Namo saṃghāya! and, confessing their various transgressions, they repented with all sincerity.

At that time, the Buddha immediately emitted light from the mark of a great man between his eyebrows, which illuminated the minds and hearts of all people so that they attained understanding; simultaneously, they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Once these upāsakas had attained the Way, they beheld the Buddha’s physical body—dignified, sublime, and peerless in the world—and sought the Buddha’s permission to leave the household life, eventually becoming arhats.

Among the assembly of upāsikās, those who perceived the Buddha’s physical body as being like a mass of ink immediately rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and wept with falling tears, wailing in such grief that they could not speak; raising their hands to strike their heads, they fell to the ground, breathless.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having witnessed this event, comforted the women with a Brahma-like voice and said to them:
"O women! For what reason are you so sorrowful as to reach such a state?"
At that time, when the women heard the voice of the Buddha, their faculties were opened; they immediately rose, joined their palms, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Buddha-sun has appeared in the world and shines universally upon all; all people see him as the full moon, yet I alone do not see him."
When the Buddha preached the Dharma, all people heard the eightfold qualities of his voice, yet I alone did not hear them, like one born deaf.

When the Venerable Śāriputra conferred the precepts upon me, I then heard him speak of the five precepts; however, whenever I attended the Buddha’s assemblies, I saw the World-Honored Buddha as if he were a mass of ink.
"Only I pray, World-Honored One!
Out of great compassion, please remove my transgressions and allow me to behold you.
At that time, the World-Honored One...

He sat back down upon the lion throne and extended his legs, manifesting the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel to show the women; the women saw only various wondrous lotuses emerging from the wheel-mark, and upon each flower was a transformed Buddha resembling a figure made of ink.
Again, joining his palms and bowing in prostration toward the Buddha, he addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Although I have been a disciple of the Buddha for a long time, it is only today that I have seen these wondrous lotus flowers; seeing all the manifested Buddhas, they appear to me as if painted with ink."
"What grave offense did you commit in a previous life that your vision has become so dim?
The Buddha told the women:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect upon this well!"
The Tathāgata shall now analyze this for you.
In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Ekaratnacchatradīparāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

After that Buddha had passed into extinction, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were bhikṣus who entered villages to beg for food; with their alms bowls and staffs in hand, they maintained their dignified deportment without transgression, even as they arrived at the house of a courtesan.
Then the courtesans took the bhikṣu’s bowl, filled it with rice, and said to him playfully:

"O son of the Śākyas! Your complexion is loathsome, like a mass of ink; the clothes you wear are like those of a beggar. Your repulsiveness is peerless in all the world; since you claim to be free from desire, who would ever think of you?"
When the bhikṣu heard these words, he cast his alms-bowl into the air and soared away.
Upon seeing this, the women were filled with shame and remorse, and they confessed their transgressions, saying:
"We have now offered food to the śramaṇa; we pray that in a future life our bodies may attain mastery just as this śramaṇa does."
The Buddha told the women:
"Those women who at that time provided food to the arhats are none other than yourselves!
Because you gave food to the bhikṣus with a virtuous mind, for two thousand kalpas you have never suffered from hunger or thirst."
Because he previously reviled me with foul language regarding matters of lust, he fell into the Black Darkness Hell for sixty minor kalpas;

yet because his initial vow and virtuous mind were not extinguished, he has now encountered my era and been able to receive the five precepts. This is due to his having made offerings to an Arhat; thus, he beheld Śāriputra but did not see my own body.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, a great lotus flower immediately emerged from his navel. This great lotus flower transformed into a radiant platform, within which were hundreds of thousands of countless śrāvaka bhikṣus, such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, who, within the Buddha’s radiant platform, exercised mastery over their supernormal powers and performed the eighteen transformations.

Upon seeing this, the women were filled with joy; immediately, by means of the fire of wisdom, they incinerated twenty billion knots of affliction until they were completely consumed, and they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Once the upāsikās had attained the Way, they beheld the Buddha’s physical body as majestic, dignified, and subtle; yet they alone did not see the light of the Buddha’s *ūrṇā-kośa*.
The Buddha said to the King, his father:
"Because of their frivolous speech and harsh words, even though they have attained the Way, what they perceive remains unclear."

"Therefore, all you people should diligently guard your speech, concentrate your minds, and rectify your intentions to practice the Buddha-visualization samādhi; by seeing the Buddha, you shall obtain immeasurable merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One—

Wishing to cause the great assembly to see the Buddha’s physical body with perfect clarity, the Buddha immediately transformed the vihāra into a mountain of white jade; its height and majesty, as well as its dimensions, were like those of Mount Sumeru, and it contained hundreds of thousands of grottoes. Within these many grottoes, various images appeared as reflections, indistinguishable from the Buddha himself.

At that time, there was a great lotus flower upon the ground before the Buddha; the flower had a thousand petals, each petal possessed a thousand rays of light, and from each ray emanated a thousand transformed Buddhas, each with a thousand disciples serving as attendants.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, if any of the Buddha’s disciples can sever and abandon all worldly affairs, cast off all evils, and focus their mindfulness on contemplating the Buddha’s constant radiance, even though the Buddha is no longer present, they may still be said to see the Buddha."
By virtue of seeing the Buddha, all evils are eliminated, and according to their aspirations, they shall attain the path to the three kinds of bodhi in future lives.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Observation such as this is called right observation; any other observation is called wrong observation.
*The Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha*, Scroll Three.
The Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Three: Contemplation of the Marks, Part Four.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of emitting his constant radiance?

For the sake of ordinary persons in future ages, the Tathāgata shall now manifest a limited light; those ordinary persons should practice this contemplation, for contemplating it in this way will be no different from seeing the Buddha’s radiant marks today."
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from the uṣṇīṣa; this light was of a thousand colors, and each color branched out into eighty-four thousand rays.
Within each ray, there were eighty-four thousand wondrous transformation Buddhas.

The bodies of these emanation Buddhas are infinite in size; from the crowns of their heads, they likewise emit this light, with each ray following the next, extending upward through immeasurable worlds.
In the realm above, transformed bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms of clouds, descended from the sky to surround the Buddhas.

When this light appeared, the Buddhas of worlds as numerous as atoms in the ten directions all beheld it; this light shone directly upon the crowns of the Buddhas' heads, and the Buddhas emitted light, which in turn illuminated the crown of Śākyamuni’s head.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If sentient beings wish to contemplate the light of the *uṣṇīṣa* of Śākyamuni Buddha, they should perform this contemplation. Those who perform this contemplation, even if their minds are not sharp, shall see it in a dream; though this is merely a mental visualization, it can eliminate immeasurable hundreds of thousands of layers of heavy sins."

One who contemplates in this manner will, in their present body, surely behold the great bodhisattvas; because they behold the bodhisattvas, they hear their preaching of the Dharma; because they hear the preaching of the Dharma, they attain a dhāraṇī, which is named "Whirling Recollection and Retention."
"One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.
The Buddha told the King, his father:
"What is meant by contemplating the light between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows?"
"The Tathāgata now, for the sake of all sentient beings in future generations, shall briefly manifest the light of the white tuft between his brows.

As he spoke these words, the Buddha immediately emitted from the space between his eyebrows the light of the Great Man’s white tuft. This light divided into eighty-four thousand rays and displayed eighty-four thousand colors, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.
Each ray of light transforms into a golden mountain;
each golden mountain contains immeasurable grottoes;
within each grotto is a manifested Buddha, sitting cross-legged in profound meditative concentration, with hundreds of thousands of great assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas as his retinue.

At that time, within the Buddha’s cave there were various transformation Buddhas, all of whom emitted the light from the mark of the great man—the white tuft between the eyebrows—which likewise illuminated immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, making them all golden in color.
Upon the golden ground were golden lotuses, and upon each golden lotus sat an emanation Buddha, all of whom shared the same name, Śākyamuni.

From the space between the eyebrows of these Buddhas, this light was likewise emitted; it illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, appearing like hundreds of thousands of billions of Sumeru Kings merged into a single mass.

Upon all the Mount Sumerus, various Buddhas appeared; the bodies of these Buddhas were tall and prominent, exactly equal in height to the mountains. From the radiance between the eyebrows of these emanated Buddhas, light circled those emanated Buddhas seven times and then returned to enter the space between the eyebrows of Śākyamuni.

When this light enters, within each and every pore of the Buddha’s body there appears a transformed image; within the pores of each of these transformed images, eighty-four thousand wondrous images are further manifested. These are all things rarely seen by any sentient being in the trichiliocosm, and are called one of the radiant marks among the eighty secondary characteristics of the Tathāgata.
Thus, these eighty minor marks of excellence and their radiance cannot be fully described.

When the Tathāgata briefly manifested the light from his white ūrṇā-hair, eight thousand people among the multitude led by the Father King attained the pure Dharma-eye, far removed from dust and free from defilement.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The light from the Tathāgata’s ūrṇā-kośa has already been extensively explained by the Buddha within various sūtras. Such a wondrous light is seen only by Buddhas; even Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage do not see it clearly."
Therefore, only a small portion of this is explained here; it is for the sake of ordinary persons that this small portion is taught.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation, whereas one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.

This light eliminates transgressions as previously described; those who behold the light attain clear understanding in their minds and see ten billion Buddhas, while those who see the white hair perceive them through the power of their mental visualization.
"How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of a broad and level forehead, the three circles on his face, and the mark of the hairline?
From each of these various marks, golden light issues forth; this golden light transforms into golden couches.

Upon each couch are a thousand bodhisattvas, beginning with Krakucchanda and extending down to Ruci. These thousand bodhisattvas all emit radiance as they sit upon the golden couches. In this manner, there are ten billion koṭis of bodhisattvas and ten billion koṭis of golden couches."
Upon each of those golden beds there was a precious canopy, and each precious canopy emitted a thousand rays of light;

each ray of light formed a thousand jeweled banners, and atop each banner were ten million jeweled canopies. Beneath these various jeweled canopies were many jeweled pennants, and within those jeweled pennants were immeasurable transformation Buddhas.
All these emanated Buddhas preached suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
When this verse was spoken, all the emanated Buddhas likewise spoke it.
Śākyamuni Buddha, his body sixteen feet tall, stood before the practitioner, raised his right hand, and spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!"
"You are now able to perceive the marks and signs of the Buddhas; in our past lives, when we practiced the bodhisattva path, we were no different from you.
You are now able to perceive the realm of the Buddhas; yet this realm is merely produced by the deluded conceptualizations of your own mind."

Having spoken these words, he immediately vanished and did not appear again; yet the various lights upon his forehead became even more manifest, and from them flowed out hundreds of thousands of billions of rays. Each individual ray of light illuminated the faces of the bodhisattvas upon the jeweled bed, and the faces of those bodhisattvas likewise emitted light that illuminated Śākyamuni. When this sign appeared, the practitioner’s true contemplation of the Buddha’s face was clear and free of doubt.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, those disciples of the Buddha who are able to contemplate in this way and truly see the face of the Buddha will be no different from my remaining in the world."

One who practices this contemplation eliminates the sins of birth and death for one hundred million kalpas; in their future lives, they will behold all Buddhas face-to-face, be born into the families of the Buddhas, and have the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as their retinue.
One who observes in this manner is said to have right observation; one who observes otherwise is said to have wrong observation.
"How does one observe the Tathāgata’s nose emitting light?
The light emitted from the nose divides into four branches, which enter upward into the Buddha’s eyes, eyebrows, and eyelashes."

A great radiance issued forth; its light was dense and majestic like the forms of dragons and elephants, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions and entering the eyes of all Buddhas. When this sign appeared, the ten directions were filled with brilliant light.
At that time, the practitioner sees the earth and the void throughout the worlds of the ten directions filled with Buddhas.
From the eyes, eyebrows, eyelashes, and nostrils of each and every Buddha, great light is emitted, just as before!

The two lights from the Buddha-eye shine forth with brilliance that pervasively illuminates and enters the eyes of all Buddhas. In the midst of space, they transform into a pavilion of light; atop this pavilion of light is a cloud of pure radiance, blue and white, beyond compare in this world. Within the blue light are blue-colored transformation Buddhas;
within the white light are white-colored transformation Buddhas.

This blue-and-white Buddha is clearly distinguished on his left and right; clouds of light in the colors of a hundred jewels form his canopy, like a person with supernormal powers soaring through the midst of the clouds. The pores of his body are like flowering trees;
each flowering tree reaches as far as the Brahma-world, and within the petals of the various flowers dwell hundreds of billions of śrāvaka bhikṣus.
Each bhikṣu wears a thousand-layered robe (*nāṃgala-kaṣāya*), and these thousands of layers possess a thousand different colors.
Within each and every form, there were hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas, all of pure golden hue.
These bhikṣus leaped into the clouds and followed behind the Buddha, like great dragon-elephants with their young offspring following in their wake.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the Buddha’s disciples can contemplate the light of the Buddha’s eyes with a correct mind, they shall have their heavy obstacles removed in this present life; in future lives, they will always be able to behold the Buddha and never be separated from the sun-like presence of the Buddha, and even while dwelling in the mother’s womb, they will constantly enter samādhi."

While in the mother’s womb, they see the Buddhas of the ten directions all emitting rays of light that shine upon their bodies; even while within the shell of the womb, they constantly receive the sublime Dharma—how much more so once they have emerged from it!
One who contemplates in this way is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.

"The nose emits two rays of light, which universally illuminate the worlds of the ten directions. Each individual ray transforms into a great body of water, and these waters abide in space and flow into the various rays. When these waters enter, all the lights become even more brilliant. Between each of the rays, crystal mountains emerge, and between the crystal mountains, seven-jeweled flowers grow. From the centers of these flowers, masses of water surge forth; the water is golden in color, like golden banners, and within those golden banners are hundreds of thousands of millions of immeasurable transformation Buddhas."

Each of these manifested Buddhas stood sixteen feet tall; from every pore of their bodies issued eighty-four thousand exquisite jewel-colored rays, and from within each of those jewel colors, further light was emitted, its subtle radiance possessing colors as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, any of the Buddha’s disciples who practices this contemplation will eliminate the most grievous evil karma of a thousand kalpas. In their future rebirths, their minds will have no attachments; they will not dwell in a womb but will always be born by transformation. Having been so born, they will possess a full radiance of body and will never be separated from the Buddhas.”
"One who observes in this way is said to have right observation; one who observes otherwise is said to have wrong observation.
How does one observe the radiance from the Tathāgata’s face?
That light is white, like a mountain of jewels, pure both inside and out; within that mountain of jewels are immeasurable transformation Buddhas with the color of refined, pure gold."
At that time, light issued from the faces of all the manifested Buddhas; this light, of five colors, illuminated the ten directions and entered the faces of all the Buddhas.

When this sign appeared, whether the practitioner was walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they constantly heard the Tathāgata preach the four foundations of mindfulness (the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena), as well as the objects of meditation, which were made to be heard by the practitioner.
Having heard this, he retained it in memory and closed his eyes to contemplate it; by the power of this light, he immediately attained the Dharma of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions and Śākyamuni, each extending their right hand from within samādhi, stroked the practitioner’s crown and spoke these words:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!”
"You are able to truly practice the meditative concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Such contemplation as this is called right contemplation; any other contemplation is called wrong contemplation.
"How does one contemplate the ears of the Tathāgata?"

From his ears issued five rays of light, each ray possessing a thousand colors; from each color emanated a thousand transformation Buddhas, and each Buddha emitted a thousand rays of light. These lights shone everywhere throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, transforming into a single flower. This flower was of such immense scale that its measure could not be known; none were able to know it except by the power of a Buddha’s mind.

Within these lotus flowers, hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of immeasurable Buddha-fields all appear; hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of great Bodhisattvas sit upon a single lotus filament, yet the filaments are not large and the Bodhisattvas are not small, nor do they obstruct one another.
In this way, the Bodhisattva’s ears hang down universally like golden lotuses suspended in sunlight, and from within the ears, five rays of light spiral forth.
When this sign appears, the hairs on the Buddha’s ears are like the tree of Śakra, which all beings delight to behold.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those disciples of the Buddha who practice this contemplation will constantly hear the myriad subtle dharmas preached by ten billion thousand buddhas and various bodhisattvas, without their faculty of hearing being impaired."
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.
"How does one contemplate the mark of the Tathāgata’s neck?
From the mark of his neck issue two rays of light, these rays being of ten thousand colors, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions."

There are sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured who, upon encountering this radiance, awaken to the twelve links of dependent origination and become pratyekabuddhas; this light then shines upon the necks of all these pratyekabuddhas.

When this sign appears, the practitioner sees all the pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions everywhere. They cast their alms bowls into the air and perform the eighteen transformations. Beneath the feet of each pratyekabuddha there are characters, and these characters expound the twelve links of dependent origination (ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair). Each character emits a light, and each light has twelve sounds.
In a single voice he speaks of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self;
in a single voice he expounds the twelve links of dependent origination.
Thus, within the light beneath the feet of each pratyekabuddha, these characters appear, revolving forward and backward twelve times in total; these are called the very root of birth and death.
After this light has illuminated all the pratyekabuddhas, it returns and enters the neck of the Buddha.

One who performs this visualization will not be reborn among humans, but will instead be born in Tuṣita Heaven, where they will encounter a bodhisattva in their last birth before buddhahood who will preach the sublime Dharma to them. Having heard the Dharma, their body and mind will be filled with joy, and they will study the practice of dependent origination as practiced by the bodhisattvas.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.
"How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the fullness of the collarbone?"

The radiance of his full marks shines universally throughout the ten directions, appearing the color of amber; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they will spontaneously give rise to the aspiration for the path of the śrāvaka.
When these śrāvakas saw this light divided into ten branches, with a thousand colors in each branch and ten thousand rays of light, they saw emanated buddhas within the light;
each emanated buddha had four bhikṣus as attendants, and each bhikṣu preached suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.

He analyzed the Four Noble Truths, explained the meaning of the eight stages of personhood, described the characteristics of the four fruits of the path, and taught the three samādhis, thereby causing those sentient beings to seek the way of renunciation within this Dharma; not long after their renunciation, they became arhats.

In this manner, the light shone universally upon the crowns of the heads of all the Arhats in the ten directions. When it illuminated their crowns, it was as if someone were holding a vessel and pouring medicinal elixir into the crown of the head; its appearance and color were like clarified butter (sarpis), and having entered through the crown, it penetrated through both the exterior and interior.

At that time, the practitioner’s body and mind become peaceful and secure; the mind is tranquil and free from unwholesome signs. One no longer perceives the characteristics of the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) or fetters (*saṃyojana*), and thus, with sudden clarity, one becomes an Arhat.
This light further transformed into immeasurable golden parasols, each of which contained hundreds of thousands of seven Buddhas.
Each of these seven Buddhas had four bhikṣus serving as attendants.

Each bhikṣu entered the four great meditative absorptions (*mahā-dhyāna*), and within those absorptions, they manifested the appearances of all their latent afflictions (*anuśaya*). From them, eighty thousand families of worms writhed forth, with all species of small insects following along after them.

When this sign appears, the fire element arises first; that which arises as the fire element is initially like a mustard seed, emerging from the pores and gradually growing until it pervasively burns all bodies, so that the bodies become like masses of fire.

Various insects cry out and roar like the sound of a lion; when this sound emerges, the practitioner’s mind becomes terrified and bewildered, and he falls to the ground. Upon emerging from meditative absorption, he sees his own body as if scorched by a wild fire passing beside trees.

When this sign appears, he should again arouse his mind to form the perception of a single medicine. First, he should form the perception of the body; once the perception of the body is established, he should open the crown of his head to make it empty, forming the perception of being Brahmā, the perception of being Śakra, and the perception of various devas holding jeweled vases and pouring the medicine over him.

When the medicine enters the crown of the head, it pervades the four limbs and all the channels; one perceives the channels and the body as being like tubes of lapis lazuli, seeing only the various worms like withered, dead flowers.
"At that time, the various channels further flow into one another until there is only water; wherever the water reaches, the fire is extinguished accordingly.

At this moment, as the practitioner practices, water gushes forth from every joint like a person shooting arrows upward. The water reaches the limit of the Brahma-world, with wave upon wave following one another up to the Brahma Heaven. One sees the water within the body as vast as the four great oceans. One sees only the heads of the various worms withered and crushed, their hands broken and feet twisted. Only the fire produced in the mind divides into ten branches; though the fire enters the mass of water, they do not extinguish one another. The light of the water surges upward, and the light of the fire follows it. Both the lights of water and fire emerge from the heart, interlacing with one another, reaching upward to the summit of the triple world and downward to the Avīci Hell, extending to the very limits of the world-system. Throughout the east, west, south, and north, the fire likewise rushes along."

"At that time, from the tip of the heart, a single black hair naturally arises. From the tip of that hair, a great black wind issues forth; this wind appears in four colors according to the faculties of the mind, resembling a whirlwind (vairambha-vāyu), with a form like smoke or flame. This wind blows everywhere upon all waters, causing the waters to ripple and their foam to gather into masses. Fire also enters therein, and by the power of the fire, the foam becomes as hard as ice."

Furthermore, a wind arises that blows away ninety-eight kinds of dust, filth, and foul, impure things, placing them upon the ice; because the power of the ice is weak, it dissolves immediately wherever the impurities touch and decay.

When this ice melts, eight men take up blades and hack away chunks of ice, each taking his portion and departing; they are covered in dust and dirt, their hearts faint with distress, and they lie prostrate. Wind, fire, and water converge in one place; because the power of the fire is great, it burns and destroys all things. Four venomous snakes, holding a single precious jewel in their mouths, emerge from the flames and fly off into the void.

There are six great dragons who encounter four small *chi* serpents and swallow them as they flee; trees grow from the crests of these dragons' heads, reaching as far as the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There was a small herb as fine as an autumn hair, its color a pure golden hue. It grew from the tree's stubble down into the roots, and from the roots it grew up into the trunk;

from the trunk it grew out, spreading into the branches and leaves. Its flowers were white, yet also red and crimson; its fruit, as it neared ripeness, displayed four colors, until by the middle of the eighth month it became purely golden in color. This radiance illuminated all the śrāvakas, manifesting immeasurable hundreds of thousands of transformed realms.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.
"If a bhikṣu enters this samādhi, his body is like a plantain tree, lacking any solidity or substance."

Upon emerging from meditative absorption, the limbs and joints of the body will all become painful and numb; if one does not take medicine, one may go mad and die, so one should administer various medicines according to the occasion to regulate the condition.

"One who practices this contemplation shall eliminate the offenses of birth and death accumulated over incalculable kalpas; like a great torrent of water, they shall before long attain the path of Arhatship.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You must uphold these words of the Buddha as true and not forget them; you should proclaim them extensively for the sake of all bhikṣus."
When these words were spoken, five hundred bhikṣus attained the four great dhyānas, and simultaneously all attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
"How does one contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the *śrīvatsa* on his chest and the mark of the *svastika*?"

From beneath their armpits, maṇi-jewels emitted radiance; within that red and purple light were golden flowers. As these flowers blossomed, they transformed into countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of innumerable flowers. Upon each flower sat immeasurable Buddhas, and each of these emanated Buddhas possessed a thousand rays of light. Each ray of light manifested an emanated Buddha, and the light of each emanated Buddha was five-colored.

If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, the insane shall regain their sanity, the distracted shall attain concentration, the sick shall be healed, the impoverished shall spontaneously obtain treasures, the blind shall see, the deaf shall hear, the mute shall be able to speak, and those who are hunchbacked, lame, or afflicted with scabies and leprosy shall all be cured; it then enters universally into the crowns of the heads of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
Having entered, there are hundreds of thousands of rays of light within the chests of all the Buddhas, arising from the *svastika* mark;
within each ray of light, hundreds of thousands of verses are sung, expounding the *dānapāramitā*.
Thus, these myriad lights expound the six *pāramitās* through immeasurable verses; as the practitioner sits upright, they hear all immeasurable Buddhas preaching this Dharma.
Each transformation Buddha dispatches a transformation person, dignified and exquisite in appearance like Maitreya, who consoles the practitioner and says:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

Because you have focused your mindfulness, you see the light of all Buddhas; within that light of all Buddhas, they preach signless giving, preach signless precepts, preach signless patience, preach signless diligence, preach signless concentration, and preach signless wisdom.

When you hear this Dharma, be careful not to be startled or terrified. The Buddhas of the past, having focused their mindfulness and contemplation, also heard this Dharma and understood these characteristics.

Having understood these characteristics, they did not fear birth and death; even when dwelling in the great Avīci hell amidst fierce flames, they could not be burned. Though they remained in hell, it was as if they were wandering through a celestial palace. For this reason, the *svastika* is called the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*).

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have studied and attained this seal throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; because they have attained this seal, they do not fear birth and death, nor are they defiled by the five desires.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, any of the Buddha’s disciples who behold the light of the mark on the Buddha’s chest shall have the sins of birth and death for twelve hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas eliminated. If they cannot see the mark on the chest clearly, they should enter a stūpa to observe it.”
One who observes in this way is said to have right observation; one who observes otherwise is said to have wrong observation.
"How does one observe the Tathāgata’s arms, which are smooth, slender, and rounded like the trunk of an elephant king?"

The ten fingers of his hands were joined in the *añjali* gesture, marked with the pattern of a thousand spokes; from each finger, hundreds of thousands of rays of light were emitted, and each ray divided into a thousand branches, all of which were purely red in color.

In this way, these myriad rays of light universally illumined immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions. Having illuminated the worlds, they transformed into golden water. Within this golden water was a wondrous liquid, the color of crystal; those hungry ghosts who saw it were relieved of their heat and became cool and refreshed;
those animals who saw it recognized their own past lives;
and when mad elephants saw it, they became lion kings.
The lions see him as a garuḍa; the nāgas see him as a king of the garuḍas.

Each of these animals perceives him as their own object of veneration, and with hearts filled with fear, they join their palms in reverence. Because of this reverence, at the end of their lives, they are reborn in the heavens.
Those who see him perceive him as if he were Brahmādeva, or like the sun, moon, and stars; having seen him, they rejoice, and at the end of their lives, they are reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

When the practitioner sees him, his mind and eyes are immediately opened. At that time, transformation Buddhas fill the worlds of the ten directions; from the hands of each transformation Buddha, light rays issue forth and enter the practitioner’s eyes. Whether with eyes closed or open, he constantly beholds the Buddhas. He then observes his own physical form as being like impurity within a wondrous precious vase.

One who perceives in this way, though not yet having attained supernatural powers, will travel everywhere throughout the ten directions to attend upon all Buddhas; seeing each and every Buddha emit light from their hands shall likewise be so!
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.
"How does one contemplate the mark of the Tathāgata’s navel?
Within the Tathāgata’s navel there are ten trillion jewel flowers, and each jewel flower has ten trillion nayutas of petals."
Each leaf has ten trillion nayutas of colors; each color has ten trillion nayutas of rays of light.

When these signs appear, the entire great assembly perceives the mental characteristics of the Buddha. The Tathāgata’s mind is like a red lotus flower, with golden flowers shining upon it and interlaced with wondrous purple-gold light. A wondrous lapis lazuli tube hangs from the Buddha’s chest, and within the Buddha’s body they see ten trillion transformation Buddhas. These transformation Buddhas roam within the Buddha’s heart. From the Buddha’s navel issues forth light, which is as dense and vast as Mount Sumeru. Amidst the various mountains, there are immeasurable jewel mountains, each like Mount Sumeru.
Upon each of these various flowers there is a manifested Buddha, majestic and radiant, as beautiful to behold as Mount Sumeru.

Their light is of a thousand kinds and ten thousand colors, divided into ten billion branches; ten billion branches illuminate the regions below, and ten billion branches illuminate the regions above.
Billions upon billions of rays illuminate the eastern direction;
billions upon billions of rays illuminate the southern direction;
billions upon billions of rays illuminate the western direction.
Billions upon billions of rays illuminate the northern direction;
billions upon billions of rays illuminate the southeastern direction;
billions upon billions of rays illuminate the southwestern direction.
Billions upon billions of rays of light illuminate the northwest;
billions upon billions of rays of light illuminate the northeast.

In this manner, each of the ten directions contains various flowers; even the smallest flower is as large as ten billion Mount Sumerus. Upon each Mount Sumeru are ten billion myriad great bodhisattvas, and even the smallest among them is as large as a Mount Sumeru.

From the navels of each of the manifested bodhisattvas, a great lotus flower emerged; these lotus flowers completely covered the trichiliocosm. Between each flower there was golden light, and this light was like Jāmbūnada gold.
From each golden ray of light, Śākyamuni Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust were manifested.
Within the navel of each Śākyamuni, the radiance was likewise so.

Thus these various rays of light merged to form a platform of light. Upon this platform of light there were also immeasurable great transformation Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms and sands of the Ganges River. These Buddhas stood one after another, each emitting light from their navels; the light was so intensely brilliant that it shone directly upward into immeasurable worlds, passing even beyond them.
The number of such world-systems is equal to the infinite atoms within a trichiliocosm; in each of these worlds, there are buddha-caves made of billions of jewels, such as lapis lazuli and crystal.
Within each of these caves, there are ten billion immeasurable Buddhas, and from the navel of each Buddha, a great lotus flower emerges, no different from those previously described.

These rays of light illuminate all Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; having encountered these lights, those Bodhisattvas immediately enter the subtle and wondrous Śūraṅgama gate and further attain the adamantine-like samādhi.

All the devas who encountered this light deeply conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment; their mental eyes opened and became clear as they beheld the marks of the Buddhas.

After this radiance had illuminated the Bodhisattvas, it caused every pore of the Bodhisattvas' bodies to emit clouds of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) offerings and various ritual implements. Even the smallest of these canopies covered Jambudvīpa. Such a multitude of diverse jewel-adorned offerings cannot be fully described; all these offerings arise from the ocean of Śūraṅgama.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If good sons or good daughters contemplate in this way, form such recollections, or see these matters in their dreams, they will, in every place where they are born, constantly encounter Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī!”
These are sons of the Dharma-king who, for the sake of all practitioners, constantly expound the Buddha-dharma of the three periods—past, future, and present—even within their dreams;

they preach the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* and the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, and also teach the *Buddhānusmṛti Samādhi* as a jeweled necklace, retaining them in memory upon awakening without any loss or forgetfulness.
In this person's present life, the goddess Guṇakārandavatī shall serve as their attendant, and they shall be cleared of the offenses of birth and death for ten trillion kalpas.
One who contemplates in this way is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.

"Billions of rays of light illuminate the lower regions, causing the ground below to become the color of the waters of Jambudvīpa. Within these waters are jewel towers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; beneath each jewel tower is a precious city like a *gandharva* city. Upon these jewel towers stand great jewel trees, from whose branches and leaves all fire breaks out. The flames of this fire burn both upward and downward, consuming these masses of water and transforming them into lapis lazuli."

Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, various trees grow; each tree has four dragons, and upon the heads of these dragons are wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*). The radiance of these jewels shines universally upon the bodies of the dragons, causing both the dragons and the trees to become purely golden in color.

That dragon manifested its power, and from all the pores of its body, golden light issued forth. This light shone directly downward upon immeasurable worlds, and passing even further below, it illuminated yet more immeasurable worlds, causing the ground of those lower regions to become entirely golden in color.

Upon the golden ground were vajra-flowers, and atop each vajra-flower sat a golden celestial maiden. Each celestial maiden was accompanied by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens, and all these celestial maidens praised the ocean-like samādhi of the compassionate mind.
Emerging from below and extending upward as far as the city of Kapilavastu, their voices, like thunder, extolled the mind of loving-kindness.

As these words were spoken, from the tips of the nāgas' hairs there issued forth clouds of various jewels; within each cloud were Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and within each field were transformation Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust.
Each of these transformation Buddhas emitted this radiance.

When this light appeared, in the world-systems below, ten million golden mountains arose; from within their crags, ten billion jewel caves surged upward like clouds. Within these many caves dwelt exclusively white-hued Buddhas, with white and wondrous Bodhisattvas and assemblies of Śrāvakas serving as attendants. To the left and right of these Buddhas was the precious radiance of refined gold, appearing like a mountain peak where various jewels are interspersed and reflected.
There was a wondrous jewel canopy like Mount Sumeru, composed of immeasurable jewels; between each jewel were ten billion rays of light, swirling and revolving.
Within these myriad lights were ten billion lion thrones;
upon each lion throne sat a great assembly of ten billion nayutas of bodhisattvas in the full lotus posture.

At that time, from the pores of that Bodhisattva’s body, there issued forth incalculable rays of light. Within each ray of light was a manifested Buddha, whose body was as tall and rounded as Mount Sumeru. These manifested Buddhas, using hundreds of thousands of verses, praised and expounded how non-killing has compassion as its root; how compassion is the wondrous medicine that removes the afflictions of birth and death; and how compassion is the pure eye that guides all devas and humans. After these manifested Buddhas had finished praising compassion, each performed a transformation, becoming a mountain of lapis lazuli.

Within that mountain, there were ten billion bodhisattvas; each bodhisattva had ten thousand Brahma kings as attendants. Arriving before the practitioner within the Jewel Mountain, they all spoke these teachings with one voice and in unison, saying:
"O son of good family!..."

In your ocean of mindfulness of the Buddhas, you should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; for it is through loving-kindness that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attain the great compassion of a Buddha. You should now practice the precept of non-killing and cultivate great compassion.

At that time, there were also devas, nāgas, and all beings of the eight classes who, upon encountering this light or hearing these words, would certainly be reborn in the Brahma world after the end of their lives.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Hold these words and be careful not to forget them; inform all the bhikṣus and have them carry out this practice.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, among the Buddha’s disciples, those who hear these words and contemplate this Dharma—those with right mindfulness, those with right reception, those unmoved in samādhi, those whose minds do not slacken or retreat, and those who have set forth in the Mahāyāna—you should know that such persons will constantly see this radiance in their dreams. They will also hear transformation Buddhas preaching the Dharma of the compassionate mind; upon waking, they will remember and uphold it, deeply understanding its meaning. By contemplating its significance, they shall immediately attain the concentration of loving-kindness (maitrī-samādhi)."
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those disciples of the Buddha who contemplate this Dharma and uphold this Dharma should know that their minds will be as pure as the minds of all Buddhas. They shall eliminate the offenses of birth and death accumulated over billions of kalpas, and they will always be born in the Brahma-world where they encounter the Buddhas and request them to turn the wheel of the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, they will resolve for Bodhicitta and will certainly attain the Way of Buddhahood in future ages.

"Billions upon billions of lights shine toward the east, reaching as far as the immeasurable worlds of the eastern quarter, causing the ground of the east to become white like the Snowy Mountains. Upon these mountains appear clouds of white jewels; these white jewel-clouds are shaped like jeweled terraces, adorned with ten billion nets of various jewels and jeweled bells. Within the intervals of these nets of bells are one hundred million white rays of light. These white rays transform into golden terraces, and upon each golden terrace stand four transformation Buddhas. Each transformation Buddha has four hundred million bodhisattvas serving as attendants. These Buddhas and bodhisattvas all preach the Dharma of loving-kindness and praise non-killing with a total of one thousand billion verses."
"One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.

"Billions upon billions of lights shine toward the south, causing the ground of the southern region to become entirely red. These red lights extend even to immeasurable worlds in the south, transforming into white clouds; the red and white are clearly distinguished."

"Billions upon billions of lights shone toward the western direction, reaching as far as the immeasurable worlds of the west. Those lights were of various colors, like the moon or the stars. These precious jewels emit the light of lapis lazuli; within this lapis lazuli light are images of true gold. "Billions of rays of light illuminate the northern direction, reaching as far as the immeasurable worlds of the north, causing the ground of the north to become the color of coral, interspersed with agate, ruby, pearl, agate, and crystal;

Upon the lion’s back was a parasol made of the seven treasures; this parasol was lofty and sublime like Mount Sumeru, with a shaft of lapis lazuli and adorned with various precious flowers. their hair was the color of dark-blue lapis lazuli; their bodies were the color of ten billion jewels; their arms were the color of red pearls; their nails were the color of true gold; the marks on their palms were the color of white lotuses; their calves were like those of a deer king and the color of the Udumbara flower; and the soles of their feet were the color of Vaiḍūrya mani-jewels.
From beneath his feet, light of five colors radiated upward to the hairline; from every pore of his body issued transformed lights, and within each single pore were one hundred million bodhisattvas.

At the navel of each bodhisattva was a great lotus flower, as tall and vast as Mount Sumeru and composed of a hundred jewels. Upon each flower sat a Buddha, equal in height and breadth to the flower itself, who likewise emitted light from his navel.
When this sign appears, the lion made of various jewels leaps and bounds as if startled; on each hair of the lion’s mane, at the tip of every single hair, there are ten billion Buddha-fields.

Thus, the multicolored radiance of this assembly of bodhisattvas merged to form a single mountain. This mountain rose high and magnificent like a pedestal of pure gold. Within each field were hundreds of thousands of stupas; even the smallest of these stupas extended from Jambudvīpa up to the Brahma-world, adorned with countless exquisite images made of every kind of jewel.
These jeweled stupas and the manifested bodhisattvas all together praise the two dharmas of joy and relinquishment.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they shall attain great wisdom like that of Śāriputra and possess total retention (*dhāraṇī*) without loss, just like Ānanda.

Those who practice this, even if they do not sit in meditation, will constantly see various forms in their dreams, just as described above.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: "One who upholds these words upholds the Buddha-mind; one who performs this contemplation is able to contemplate the Buddha-mind. All Buddhas and Tathāgatas take great compassion as their mind; they take precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation as their body; and they adorn themselves with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness."
"One who contemplates in this manner is said to be contemplating the Buddha’s mind.

"Billions upon billions of lights illuminate the southeastern direction, extending even to the immeasurable worlds of the southeast, transforming them into golden wheels; each and every golden wheel is followed by the seven treasures.

Within each ray of light is a great lotus flower; these flowers join together, and from within the joined flowers emerges the great radiance of the sun.

The Buddha told Ānanda:

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those disciples of the Buddha who recollect this, contemplate this, and observe this Dharma shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over twenty trillion kalpas, and shall always be reborn in the heavens to hear the teachings of the ten wholesome paths.

"Billions of lights illuminate the southwest direction, reaching as far as the infinite worlds of the southwest. Having reached those realms, the lights fall like rain, resembling multicolored jewels; from within each jewel emerge ten billion rays of light.

In each and every grotto on Mount Sumeru there are immeasurable chambers;

each transformation Buddha has immeasurable bodhisattvas as his retinue, and these myriad transformation Buddhas and transformation bodhisattvas likewise all praise and expound the ten wholesome dharmas.

"Billions upon billions of lights shone toward the northwest, reaching even unto immeasurable worlds in the northwest; those lights were the color of jade, with crystal, red, and purple hues reflecting and adorning one another."

"World-Honored One!

The physical form and color of the Tathāgata are seen by all; yet, within the Buddha’s mind, what realm exists? What characteristics are present? What practices does he cultivate? What is it that the Buddha’s mind contemplates? And what is the nature of the radiance of the Buddha’s mind?
At that time, the Tathāgata smiled, and the light from his tongue-appearance, as described above, circled the Buddha seven times and entered through the crown of his head.

It is like a cave of lapis lazuli containing an image of pure gold. Therein one sees the Tathāgata’s heart like a red lotus flower, adorned with golden petals; the red flower and its golden light are neither open nor closed, perfectly round like a heart. Within each of its eighty-four thousand veins, every single vein is like a line drawn by a celestial artist;
within each drawing are eighty-four thousand rays of light; and within each ray of light are eighty-four thousand varieties of color.
Within each and every form are transformation Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of immeasurable dust;
each transformation Buddha sits upon a vajra pedestal, and those vajra pedestals emit golden light, the number of which is so infinite it cannot be fully described.
Within each ray of light there are likewise transformation Buddhas, their number being as previously stated.
All these emanation Buddhas extend their broad and long tongues upward to the hairline;
from each Buddha’s tongue issue one hundred million rays of light, which gather together to form ten thousand segments.

Upon each ray of light are ten billion emanation Buddhas, sitting cross-legged and entering the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body. Thus, the subtle and wondrous physical bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions enter this ocean of samādhi.

When the Buddha entered this samādhi, the city of Kapilavastu, the Nyagrodha Monastery, and all of Jambudvīpa appeared like a great precious flower. Upon the calyx of this flower stood a crystal banner, and at the tip of the crystal banner was a crystal mirror, within which were manifested the pure lands of immeasurable Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the great assembly beheld the various Buddhas: some saw the Buddha’s body equal in measure to space and pure golden-yellow in color;
some saw the Buddha’s body like Mount Sumeru, composed of the four jewels;
and some saw the Buddha’s body of lapis lazuli color, ten zhang in height.
Some see the Buddha’s body as the color of white silver, a hundred thousand zhang in height;
others see Śākyamuni’s body as sixteen feet tall, or seven feet tall.
Some see it as three feet;
some see it reaching as far as the Brahma-world;
some see it as seven inches, seeing it enter the bowl-stand; various ghosts and spirits see it like a mote of dust, like a mustard seed, or like a grain of golden millet.
