Chapter Four: Contemplating the Buddha’s Mind (5). Chapter Four: Contemplating the Buddha’s Mind.

At that time, the Buddha’s mind was like a red lotus flower. Between the petals of the lotus were eighty-four thousand rays of white light. These lights shone universally upon sentient beings in the five realms of existence. When these lights emerged, all sentient beings undergoing suffering appeared before him.

What is called suffering refers to: the Avīci Hell; the eighteen minor hells; the eighteen cold hells; the eighteen dark hells; the eighteen minor hot hells; the eighteen hells of sword-wheels; the eighteen hells of blade-wheels; the eighteen hells of flaming chariots; the eighteen hells of boiling excrement; the eighteen hells of cauldrons of boiling water; the eighteen hells of the River of Ashes; five hundred billion hells of sword-forests; five hundred billion hells of thorn-forests; five hundred billion hells of copper pillars; five hundred billion hells of iron mechanisms; five hundred billion hells of iron nets; the eighteen iron cave hells; the eighteen iron ball hells; the eighteen sharp stone hells; and the eighteen copper-drinking hells.
Regarding these and many other such hells,
the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Why is it called the Avīci Hell?"
The syllable *a* means "non-existence," and *ni* means "to obstruct";
the syllable *a* means "non-existence," and *bi* means "to rescue";
the syllable *a* means "uninterrupted," and *ni* means "immovable."
"Ā" signifies extreme heat; "ni" signifies extreme affliction.
"Ā" signifies lack of leisure; "ni" signifies non-abiding. This lack of leisure and non-abiding is called the Avīci Hell.
"Ā" signifies great fire; "ni" signifies fierce heat. When fierce fire enters the heart, it is called the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The Avīci Hell is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides. It has seven layers of iron walls and seven tiers of iron nets. Below are eighteen compartments, surrounded on all sides by seven layers of forests of blades. Within these seven layers of walls there is further a forest of swords, with eighteen compartments below, each compartment consisting of eighty-four thousand layers.”

At its four corners there are four great copper dogs; their bodies are forty yojanas in breadth and length, their eyes flash like lightning, their fangs are like sword-trees, their teeth are like mountains of knives, and their tongues are like iron thorns. From every hair on their bodies issues fierce fire, and the smoke is so foul that no worldly stench can serve as a comparison for its malodorousness.

There are eighteen hell-wardens with the heads of rākṣasas and the mouths of yakṣas, possessing sixty-four eyes. From their eyes, iron pellets scatter and fly forth like chariots for ten li. Their dog-like fangs protrude upward to a height of four yojanas; from the tips of these fangs, streams of fire flow out, burning the iron chariots before them, causing each rim of every iron wheel to transform into one hundred million fires. Blades, edges, swords, and halberds all emerge from this fire.
Thus the flowing fire burns the city of Avīci, making the city of Avīci as red as molten copper.
Upon the heads of the hell-wardens are eight ox-heads; each ox-head has eighteen horns.

From the tip of every horn issues a mass of fire, which further transforms into eighteen rims. These flaming rims then change into wheels of fiery blades, the size of chariot wheels; these wheels follow one after another amidst the flames, filling the entire city of Avīci.

Copper dogs with gaping mouths and tongues lolling out lie upon the ground; their tongues are like iron thorns, and when they extend, they transform into immeasurable tongues that fill the Avīci Hell.
Within the sevenfold city walls stand seven iron banners; from the tops of these banners, fire leaps up like boiling springs, and its molten iron flows and splashes, filling the Avīci City.
At the threshold of each of the four gates of Avīci, there are eighty cauldrons from which boiling copper surges forth, flowing out through the gates and filling the city of Avīci.

Between each pair of cauldrons dwell eighty-four thousand iron pythons and great serpents, which vomit poison and fire, their bodies filling the interior of the city. These snakes roar like the thunder of heaven, raining down great iron balls that fill the city of Avīci.
In this city, there are eighty trillion forms of suffering; among all sufferings, the most agonizing are gathered here in this city.

There are five hundred billion worms, each with eighty-four thousand beaks. From the tips of these beaks, fire flows down like rain, filling the city of Avīci. When these worms descend, the fierce fires of Avīci blaze with great intensity; their crimson flames illuminate eighty-four thousand yojanas, surging upward from the ground of Avīci hell past the Great Ocean and Mount Vaḍavāmukha. Drops of water from the Great Ocean, as large as axle-trees, become great iron spikes that fill the city of Avīci.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are sentient beings who kill their fathers, harm their mothers, or revile and insult their six kin, when such offenders reach the end of their lives, copper dogs open their mouths and transform into eighteen chariots; they appear like golden chariots with jeweled canopies above them, and all the flames transform into jade maidens. When the offender sees these from afar, joy arises in his heart, and he thinks:
'I wish to go within! I wish to go within! "
As the wind-swords began to dismember him, he cried out in the intensity of his cold:
"I would rather sit upon a chariot with a fine fire, even if the fire were to explode by itself!

Having formed this thought, his life immediately ended. In the blink of an eye, he was already seated in a golden chariot. Looking back, he saw the jade maidens all grasping iron axes to hack and sever his body; beneath his body, fire erupted like a whirling wheel of fire. In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he fell directly into the Avīci Great Hell.

From the upper gridiron, which revolves like a whirling fire-wheel, down to the lower gridiron, the body is entirely within the grids. Copper dogs howl loudly as they gnaw on bones and suck at marrow. The hell-wardens, who are rākṣasas, seize great iron forks and impale the heads of the offenders, forcing them to stand up. Flames fill their entire bodies throughout the city of Avīci. Iron nets rain down blades that enter through the pores of the skin.

The transformed King Yama issues a loud proclamation: "You foolish ones, breeders of hell! When you were in the world, you were unfilial toward your parents, perverse, arrogant, and unprincipled. You are now born in this place called the Avīci Hell. You knew no gratitude and had no sense of shame; do you find any pleasure in undergoing such suffering?"
Having spoken these words, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.

At that time, the hell-wardens again drove the sinners from the lower grating to the upper grating, passing through eighty-four thousand gratings; they were driven across the body until reaching the edge of the iron net. It takes one day and night to complete this circuit. One day and night in the Avīci Hell is equivalent to sixty minor kalpas by the reckoning of days, months, and years in this Jambudvīpa. Such is the span of their life, which lasts for one great kalpa.

A person who has committed the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), being devoid of shame and remorse, commits these five transgressions. Because of these five heinous crimes, at the time of death, eighteen "wind-blades" (vātāsi)—like iron chariots—cut and dismember their body. Due to the pressure of this heat, they speak thus:
"Would it not be pleasant to find beautiful flowers and a cool great tree, to sport beneath it?"

When he formed this thought, the eighty-four thousand forests of evil swords in the Avīci Hell were transformed into jewel-trees with luxuriant flowers and fruits standing in rows before him; the great hot flames were transformed into lotuses beneath those trees. Having seen this, the sinner thought:
"The wish I have made has now borne fruit."

When these words were spoken, he was instantly carried upon a lotus flower, swifter than a torrential rain. Having sat there for a brief moment, iron-beaked insects rose from the flaming flowers, piercing his bones and entering his marrow; they penetrated his heart and pierced his brain as they climbed up the tree. All the sword-branches sliced his flesh and bored through his bones, while immeasurable blades and staves descended from above. The chariot-fires, glowing coals, and eighteen types of agonizing torments all came at once to greet him.

When this sign appears, one sinks into the earth and rises up from the lower stratum; the body is like a blooming flower, filling the entire lower stratum. Rising from the lower stratum, the flames blaze fiercely until they reach the upper stratum; having reached the upper stratum, the body fills its entirety. Due to the intensity of the heat and distress, one opens the eyes wide and sticks out the tongue.

Due to this person's transgressions, ten trillion molten coppers and hundreds of thousands of razor-wheels descend from the sky, entering through the head and exiting through the feet; all these sufferings exceed those previously described by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
One who commits the five heinous crimes shall suffer retribution for a full five kalpas.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who violate the four grave prohibitions, consuming the offerings of the faithful in vain; they slander the Dharma with false views and fail to recognize cause and effect. They sever their study of Prajñāpāramitā and disparage the Buddhas of the ten directions; they steal the property of the Saṃgha and engage in lewdness and wantonness without moral restraint. They coerce and abduct bhikṣuṇīs of pure precepts, and though they are sisters or close relatives, they feel no shame or remorse. They bring disgrace upon those dear to them and commit a multitude of evil deeds.

When this person’s retribution for their sins approaches the end of life, the "wind-swords" dismember their body; they lie prostrate and restless as if being whipped and beaten. Their mind becomes wild and distracted, giving rise to frantic and deluded thoughts; they see their own house, men, women, and children—all of whom appear as impure things—with foul-smelling excrement and urine overflowing outside.
At that time, the sinner spoke these words:
"Why is it that there are no fine cities or beautiful mountains and forests here for me to enjoy myself, but instead must I dwell amidst such impure things?"

Having spoken these words, the rakshasa hell-wardens took up great iron forks and lifted up the Avīci Hell and the various forests of blades, transforming them into jeweled trees and cool ponds; the flames were transformed into golden-leaved lotuses, and the iron-beaked insects became wild ducks and geese; the cries of pain from the hells resounded like the melody of singing.
Upon hearing this, the sinner thought, "I shall dwell within such a favorable place.

As soon as he had this thought, he sat upon a lotus flower of fire. Iron-beaked insects emerged from the pores of his body and devoured his flesh; hundreds of thousands of iron wheels entered through the crown of his head; iron forks as numerous as the sands of the Ganges plucked out his eyes; and the copper dogs of hell transformed into ten billion iron dogs, vying with one another to tear apart his body and devour his heart.
In an instant, his body was like a severed flower, filling eighteen compartments;

each petal of the flower had eighty-four thousand [parts], and upon each petal-head were the hands, feet, and limbs of his body, situated within each compartment. The hell was not large and this body was not small, yet they filled such a great hell as this. When these sinners fall into this hell, they undergo eighty-four thousand great kalpas, at which point this niraya is extinguished.
"Furthermore, they enter the eighteen compartments in the eastern direction and suffer as before.

In the southern direction of this Avīci Hell there are also eighteen compartments; in the western direction there are also eighteen compartments; and in the northern direction there are also eighteen compartments."

Those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, commit the five heinous crimes, destroy the Saṃgha, defile bhikṣuṇīs, and sever all roots of goodness—such sinners, possessing these manifold offenses, will have their bodies fill the Avīci Hell, with their four limbs further filling the eighteen compartments within it.
In this Avīci Hell, only those beings born into such a realm are burned. When the kalpa is about to end, the eastern gate opens.

Outside the eastern gate, clear springs, flowing water, flowering fruit trees, and groves all appear together. Seeing this from beneath the lower grating, the fire in their eyes momentarily subsides. Rising from the lower grating, they crawl on their bellies, scramble upward, and reach the upper grating; there they grasp at the blades of the wheel, while at that moment, hot iron balls rain down from the void of space.

He ran toward the eastern gate; having reached the threshold, the rākṣasa jailers seized iron forks with their hands and pierced his eyes from behind, while iron dogs bit into his heart until he fainted and died. Having died, he was born again.
He saw the southern gate open, no different than before; likewise, the western and northern gates were all the same!

During this interval, which lasted for half an eon, he died in the Avīci Hell and was reborn in the Cold Ice Hell; dying in the Cold Ice Hell, he was reborn in the Dark Abyss. For eighty million years his eyes could see nothing, and he took the body of a great beast, crawling on his belly.

Their faculties are darkened and obstructed, with no understanding or knowledge; they are dragged and torn apart and devoured by hundreds of thousands of foxes and wolves. After their lives end, they are born among animals, assuming the forms of birds and beasts for five million lifetimes. When they return to birth as humans, they are deaf, blind, mute, afflicted with scabies and abscesses, and impoverished and lowly. All manner of misfortunes serve as their adornment; having endured these base forms for five hundred successive lifetimes, they subsequently return to birth within the realm of hungry ghosts.
"In the realm of hungry ghosts, they encountered great Bodhisattvas who were spiritual friends, who rebuked them, saying:

'In immeasurable lifetimes of your past existence, you committed rootless offenses, slandering and refusing to believe; thus you fell into the Avīci Hell and underwent various sufferings that cannot be fully described. You should now give rise to a heart of compassion.'"
When the hungry ghosts heard these words, they cried out, "Namo Buddhāya! Through the power of the Buddha's grace,
they immediately passed away and were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

Having been born in that heaven, they repent their transgressions, reproach themselves, and resolve to attain bodhicitta. The light of the Buddhas' minds does not abandon such as these; it embraces them and treats them with compassion as if they were Rāhula, instructing them to avoid hell as one cherishes one's own eyes.
The Buddha told the Great King:

"If you wish to know the extent of the light of the Buddha’s mind that shines forth, it constantly illuminates such sentient beings who suffer incessantly and have no refuge. The objects of the Buddha’s mind are always these most wicked sentient beings; because he adorns himself with the power of the Buddha-mind, after kalpas beyond calculation, he causes those sinful persons to give rise to the bodhicitta."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What are called the eighteen cold hells?
As for the cold hells:"
In the eight directions are ice mountains, each with eighteen ridges;
furthermore, there are eighteen smaller ice mountains, the color of crystal.

Between these ice mountains, cold ice fills the spaces like common lotuses, eighteen yojanas high, with an ice-wheel atop each, twelve yojanas in length and breadth, falling from the sky like hailstones from heaven.
In this world, there are those who naturally lack a compassionate heart; they plunder without principle, rob and steal, and freeze or kill sentient beings.
When such a person is about to die as retribution for their sins, all the "sword-winds" transform into blazing hot fire.
The sinner thinks to himself: "Why am I not lying upon ice now?"

While they were thus oppressed by fire and entertaining these thoughts, the rakṣasa hell-wardens, grasping wheels of ice and soaring through the void like white cranes, arrived before them. Upon seeing them, the sinners’ heat was dispelled and they felt cool; their hearts were filled with longing, and when their breath ceased and their lives ended, they were reborn upon the Ice Mountains.

Once born there, eighteen ice-mountains are like fans being fanned; all manner of cold ice enters through his pores, filling each of the eighteen compartments until every single one is full. His body splits, cracks, and tears apart like red lotuses, as ice-wheels above and below completely cover him. The ice-mountains from the eight directions converge simultaneously, leaving no other word to utter, save for the cry: "A-ra-la."
At that time, the sinner thinks to himself:
"When shall I escape this cold ice and be born amidst the hot fires?
Then, from the sky above, there are iron birds with mouths and beaks spitting fire that descend from the air, splitting open the head and pecking at the brain; the sinner dies instantly.
After their lives have ended, the hell-wardens again strike the ground with iron forks and call out, "Live!
Live! At the sound of these words, they immediately revive.
Having emerged, he thought:
"My body is now ablaze with fierce, raging fire; I pray that I may obtain ice to extinguish this fire.
The hell-wardens then met him with a wheel of ice and placed him within the prison, such that there was not one of the eighteen compartments through which he did not pass.
The lifespan in this Cold Hell is equivalent to eighty million years by the reckoning of days and months in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

Once their retribution is exhausted, they are reborn among humans of low status, impoverished and wretched; for five hundred lifetimes they serve as slaves, their clothing failing to cover their bodies and their food failing to fill their mouths. Only when this retribution is exhausted do they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is called the Black Darkness Hell?
As for the Black Darkness Hell:"
There are eighteen layers of black mountains, eighteen layers of black nets, eighteen layers of iron beds, and eighteen layers of iron curtains.
Each mountain is eighty-four thousand yojanas high;
each curtain is likewise eighty-four thousand yojanas thick.
Between each of these layers are eighteen tiers of Black Iron Ring Mountains, standing in rows like a forest that casts deep shadows over these mountains.

Within this world, there are naturally some deluded sentient beings who steal the lamp-light of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they steal from their parents, teachers, preceptors, and elders; they slander those who preach the Dharma, and likewise disparage worldly masters of debate and the like. They show no regard for the distinction between the honorable and the lowly, and possess no sense of shame or remorse.
Because of these sins, when his life was about to end, there were flashes of lightning in his eyes that flickered incessantly, and he immediately thought:
"What sin do I have that I constantly see this fire?"
He immediately closed both eyes, unwilling to behold even the light of the sun and moon.
As his life was about to end, the rakshasa wardens of hell raised a great iron bed and spread a vast iron parasol; like a great mass of clouds, they arrived through the air.
At that time, an incorporeal voice arose from the air, saying:
"Do you wish to go to this place of darkness?
Upon hearing the voice, the offender immediately conceived the desire to go to that location.

When their breath ceases and their lives end, they sit upon iron beds; like a king of geese soaring and then falling, they descend into a place of pitch-black darkness. Once they have entered therein, blades in the form of wheels slice and hack their bodies from above and below. Great iron crows with long and sharp beaks and talons fly down from the mountains to peck and claw at the sinners. In their desperate agony, they run swiftly seeking light but find none; beneath their feet, caltrops pierce their bones and penetrate their marrow.
Thus they remain in a state of terror for five hundred billion years, which is equivalent to the number of days, months, and years in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings.

That person’s head strikes against the various mountains of darkness; their brains flow out and their eyes bulge from their sockets. The hell-wardens, who are rākṣasas, use iron forks to push them back and restore them into their eye sockets. Only when their retribution is exhausted do they emerge as impoverished people, with squinting eyes, blind and sightless, or driven away by those afflicted with leprosy.
"Such retribution for their sins shall last for five hundred lifetimes; after this period has passed, they will encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What are called the eighteen minor hot hells?"
As for the eighteen minor hot hells, like the Avīci Hell, they likewise have sevenfold walls and sevenfold iron nets, adorned with immeasurable evils.

There have been sentient beings who, disobeying their teacher’s instructions, gave rise to malicious and rebellious thoughts; they failed to recognize the kindness of their upbringing, stole from their teacher, harmed their teacher, defiled their teacher’s pure food, sat upon their teacher’s seat, and seized their teacher’s alms bowl to hide filth within it—thus committing these five kinds of evil deeds.
What are the five? They are:
reviling the teacher, slandering the teacher, striking the teacher, killing the teacher, and administering various poisons for the teacher to drink.

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas commit such unlawful acts as harming or slandering the teacher, these evil persons are devoid of shame and remorse; they strip images, destroy stūpas, plunder the property of the Dharma-treasure, and kill uncles, parents, brothers, and sisters.

When such a sinner’s life is about to end, eighteen hell-wardens of the Avīci Hell each take up an iron fork and lift a cauldron-hell; these many hells are like a great jeweled canopy, raining down fine rain with droplets like flowers.
The heat and affliction of this person’s karmic retribution have entered his heart; like one who has been scorched by fire and then sees a cool rain, he immediately thinks:
"Would it not be joyful for me to sit beneath the sheltering canopy, with the cool rain sprinkling upon me?"

Having spoken these words, his breath ceased and his life ended. In the time it takes to throw a ball, he was immediately seated upon a great bed of swords; ten billion sword blades, each emitting fire, pierced and burned his body. A precious canopy in the air transformed into a wheel of fire that descended from above, splitting his crown straight through. His body shattered into thousands of pieces as copper pellets rained down from above, entering through his pores. The rakshasa jailers pierced the sinner’s eyes with great iron forks, or shot him in the heart with iron arrows, causing him to faint and die.
In an instant, he returns to life and sits upon the sword-bed; then, a whirlwind of fierce winds blows him down into hell.
Once he has entered the prison, King Yama, together with his palace, appears in mid-air and declares:
"O seed of hell!"
"You have committed many evils; you killed your teacher and slandered your teacher. The place where you are now born is named Tongue-Extraction Avīci. You shall remain in this hell for three kalpas.
Having spoken these words, he vanished and was no longer seen. The suffering in this hell is as described above.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is meant by the eighteen Sword-Wheel Hells?
As for the Sword-Wheel Hells:"

On all four sides are mountains of blades; amidst these mountains, blades are piled up like bricks. In the void above, there are eight hundred million billion immense great wheels of blades, descending one after another like drops of rain.

There are sentient beings who delight in causing suffering and killing other beings; at the time of their death, they suffer from the ailment of upward-reversing qi (upward-moving wind), their minds become oppressed and congested, and their hearts become as hard as stone. They then make this vow:
"Would it not be a joy to obtain a sharp blade and cut away these various afflictions?"
At that time, the hell-warden took a wheel of blades upon his head, concealing it so it was not visible, and approached the place of the offenders with humble speech and deferential words:
"I have a sharp blade capable of excising grievous illness."
The sinner, filled with joy, thought to himself:
"Only this is pleasurable.
His breath ceased and his life ended, and he was reborn upon the Wheel of Blades, falling among the mountains of blades like a drunken elephant in its run.
At that time, the four mountains close together simultaneously, and the four kinds of mountain-blades cut and slice their bodies; unable to sustain themselves, they faint and die.

The rākṣasa jailers drive and crowd the offenders, forcing them to climb the mountain of blades; before they reach the summit, the blades wound their feet and continue up to their hearts, yet they crawl upward out of fear of the jailers.

Upon reaching the summit of the mountain, the hell-wardens seize all the trees of blades with their hands and strike down the offenders; before they have died, iron dogs gnaw at their hearts through hundreds of forms of agonizing torment. Iron insects devour their flesh until it is entirely gone, whereupon they are immediately revived. Their feet are bound to iron wheels that descend from the sky, such that in a single day and night they undergo sixty billion births and sixty billion deaths.

Thus, there are eighteen such types in total; due to this person's transgressions, the suffering becomes even more severe. When the lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings—eighty million years—is exhausted, they are reborn in the world and fall among the animals, where for five hundred lifetimes their bodies serve as food for the mouths of others, and for another five hundred lifetimes they assume lowly and base forms. Only thereafter do they encounter a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is called the Sword-Wheel Hell?
As for the Sword-Wheel Hell:..."
It is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal, and filled with sword-trees (*asi-vṛkṣa*). The number of these trees is like that of rice, hemp, bamboo, or reeds;
each sword-tree is forty yojanas high, with eighty-four thousand sword-wheels as its leaves, eighty-four thousand sword-wheels as its flowers, and eighty-four thousand sword-wheels as its fruits.
Eighty-four thousand branches are made of boiling copper.

There are naturally some deluded beings in the world who take pleasure in killing without satiety; when such sinners approach the end of their lives, they encounter a great fever and immediately think to themselves:
"Why is my body now sometimes hot and sometimes cold, and why is my entire frame as rigid and hard as an iron anvil?"
He immediately made this vow:
"To obtain the Vajra-sword and cut away this affliction would be an unspeakable joy.
At that moment, the hell-warden transformed his own body into the form of the person's parents, relatives, or friends, stood before them, and said:
“I possess a secret dharma which I shall bestow upon you, just as you have desired.
Upon hearing this, the sinner’s heart was filled with intense longing and he yearned to obtain it with great urgency.

His breath ceased and his life ended; like a galloping horse, he was reborn amidst sword-flowers, where immeasurable blades sliced his bones and pierced his flesh until they were crushed to the size of beans.

Furthermore, there are iron birds that descend from the trees to pluck out their eyes and peck at their ears; there are great rākṣasas who seize iron axes in their hands to split open their heads and extract their brains, while iron dogs come to lick them.
After dying, they are proclaimed to have returned to life and are driven to climb trees; before reaching the treetops, their bodies shatter like dust. In a single day, they pass through many trees;
in a single night, they likewise pass through many trees.
In one day and one night, they kill themselves as many times as there are grains of dust, beyond all calculation.
For committing the crime of murder, one undergoes such calamity as follows: for eighty trillion years, one is born among the animals, constantly bearing heavy burdens and being flayed upon death.

After five hundred lifetimes, one returns to birth among humans, remaining impoverished, short-lived, frequently ill, and emaciated. Only after this period does one encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) and give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is called the Hell of the Fire Chariots?
As for the Hell of the Fire Chariots:"
Each individual copper cauldron is forty yojanas in length and breadth, filled with blazing fire; beneath it are twelve wheels, and above it are ninety-four fire-wheels.

There have been sentient beings who were disciples of the Buddha, as well as those who served the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist practitioners, including both monastics and laypeople, who deceived others, lived by wrong livelihoods, were sycophantic and crooked, and committed evil deeds.
When such a sinner is about to die, the wind-element first agitates him and his body becomes as cold as ice. He then thinks:
"When shall I obtain a great mass of fierce fire, so that by sitting within it, I may forever eliminate this cold ailment?"

Having formed this thought, the hell-warden rākṣasa transformed himself into a fire chariot like a golden lotus; atop it, he appeared in the form of a young boy, holding a white fly-whisk in his hand, and approached while dancing and singing.
Upon seeing it, the sinner conceived a sense of attachment, thinking:

"The radiance and color of these golden flowers are so brilliant that they illuminate me and warm me; they will surely dispel my cold. If I could sit upon them, the pleasure would be beyond description."

Having spoken these words, his breath ceased and he passed away. He was placed upon a fire-chariot, the joints of his limbs ablaze, and fell into a mass of flames where his body was scorched and scattered.

The hell-warden cried out, "Live!", and at that sound he returned to life. The fire-chariot crushed his body eighteen times until it was shattered like dust; then, the heavens rained boiling copper, drenching his entire body, yet he immediately returned to life once more.

Thus they travel back and forth, ascending as far as the surface of the boiling water and descending into the cauldrons; crushed by the fiery chariots, they die ninety billion times and are reborn ninety billion times in a single day and night.

When this person’s retribution for their transgressions was exhausted, they were born into a poor and lowly family as a servant, bound to others and lacking autonomy. Only after repaying their debts and receiving sustenance did they attain liberation; then, by virtue of the wholesome mind and merit from their previous renunciation, they encountered a spiritual friend who preached the Dharma for them. Their minds opened and their understanding was realized, and they became Arhats.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What is called the Hell of Boiling Excrement?
As for the Hell of Boiling Excrement:”
There are eighteen iron cities, eighty *yojanas* in extent; each iron city contains eighteen compartments.
Within each compartment, all four walls are lined with ten billion sword-trees (*asi-vṛkṣa*), and the ground is like the edge of a blade, three feet thick.
Upon these edges are hundreds of thousands of *kaṇṭaka* thorns beyond measure. Between each thorn and sword-tree, there arise countless iron insects.
Each iron insect has hundreds of thousands of heads;

each head has hundreds of thousands of beaks, and from the mouths of all these beaks issue hundreds of thousands of intestinal worms that vomit hot excrement, boiling like molten copper and filling the interior of the iron city, above which are iron nets and iron crows.

In this world, there are sentient beings who violate the eight precepts of the fast, defile the precepts of śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, defile the precepts of śikṣamāṇās, defile their own pure precepts, defile the precepts of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and defile the precepts of upāsakas and upāsikās.

All bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās—these seven assemblies and all others—who defile the pure food of the Saṃgha, defile the food of their parents, steal and eat before [others], or handle it with impure hands; and those who, by relying on their status as administrators of the Saṃgha, defile the pure food of the Saṃgha; and the disciples of the fourfold assembly who sit upon the bedding belonging to the Saṃgha with impure bodies; who commit sthūlātyaya offenses and do not repent for a long time; and who consume the food of the Saṃgha in vain while sitting among the monastic community to participate in the Poṣadha ceremony.

When these many, immeasurable, unwholesome sinners who have committed evil deeds approach the end of their lives, their entire bodies emit a fragrance like that of musk pods, which is so unbearable that they immediately think:
"Where might there be a place where I shall not hear this scent? This fragrance is like a mad wind blowing and熏 (xūn) my heart."

Having formed this thought, the rakṣasa hell-warden transforms his own body into something like a painted jar filled with excrement and filth; he goes to where the offenders are and touches them with his hand, causing those offenders to give rise to feelings of attachment.

When their breath ceases and life ends, they are blown like the wind and fall into boiling excrement. Having fallen therein, they are mangled and devoured by swarms of insects; as they run hither and thither, their bones are pared away to the very marrow. Driven by hunger and thirst, they drink the hot, boiling excrement. Worms and pustule-insects gnaw at the roots of their tongues. Day and night, they undergo ninety billion births and ninety billion deaths. Only when their retribution is exhausted are they born into a poor and lowly family, bound to others and lacking self-mastery.

Even when born into this world, he constantly encounters wicked kings and rulers of false views; various evils oppress his body, and he wears goiters, swellings, and malignant sores as his clothing. Nevertheless, due to the wholesome causes and conditions of having heard the Dharma in past lives, he meets a spiritual friend, leaves the household life to study the Path, and becomes an Arhat, endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is meant by the eighteen cauldron-hells?

As for the cauldron-hells, there are eighteen cauldrons; each cauldron is forty yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal. Within them are seven layers of iron nets filled with boiling cauldrons, and five hundred rākṣasas beat great stones of burning charcoal to heat those copper cauldrons."

These stones emit flames that blaze and overlap one another; for sixty days the fire cannot be extinguished. While twelve myriad years pass in Jambudvīpa, the boiling cauldron surges upward like stars, transforming into wheels of fire that return into the cauldron.

There are sentient beings who, violating the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, slaughter living beings for sacrificial offerings; for the sake of eating their flesh, they burn mountains and wilds, harming sentient beings, and they scald living beings alive before burning them with fire.
When such a sinner is about to die, his body and mind become distressed; he loses control over his excrement and urine, and his body becomes either as hot as boiling water or as cold as ice.
He then thinks: "Would it not be pleasant to obtain great warm water to bathe in?"

The hell-warden rākṣasa transforms himself into a servant and, carrying a basin of boiling water in his hands, approaches the place where the offenders are. The offenders feel great joy and delight in this basin; their breath ceases and their lives end, and they are reborn within the cauldron of boiling water. They are quickly dissolved and rotted away until only their bones remain. An iron fork scoops them out, and iron dogs swallow them, vomiting them onto the ground; immediately thereafter, they return to life.

The hell-wardens drive and crowd them back into the cauldrons; out of fear of the cauldron’s heat, they climb the sword-trees, their flesh and bones severed and broken as they fall into the boiling broth.

Because of the sin of killing, in a single day and night, they die as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and are reborn as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. Only when their retribution is exhausted are they born among animals, passing through every short-lived state such as that of pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs.
Having experienced such a body for eighty million years, after his life ends he is reborn among humans and undergoes two kinds of retribution:
first, being frequently ill; second, having a short lifespan.

"Having short lives and many illnesses as their kinsmen, after passing through kalpas beyond calculation, they will encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), receive and uphold the five precepts, and practice the six pāramitās.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is called the Hell of the Ash River?"

As for the Hell of the Ash River, it is two hundred yojanas in length and twelve yojanas in width; beneath its surface are sharp blades, and upon its banks are sword-trees, while it is filled with fierce flames twelve zhang thick.
Furthermore, there is molten ash spread over the fire, forty *zhang* thick.
In this world, there are naturally those shameless sentient beings who steal from their parents, steal from their teachers and elders, and steal from their virtuous friends, brothers, and sisters.

Such deluded people lack a sense of shame and remorse; they do not recognize the kindness of those who have nurtured them and their hearts show no gratitude or reciprocity. Greedy for profit and desiring gain, they remain ignorant of calamities and fail to follow the instructions of their teachers.

When this person’s retribution for their sins is about to end and their life is drawing to a close, their breath fills their heart and belly so that their gasping becomes intermittent; they then think:
"My heart is like mud and my chest is filled with air; would it not be a joy to have even a tiny spark of fire burn my body!"

The hell-warden rākṣasa, responding to this thought, arrived immediately and transformed himself into the man’s wife. Holding a brazier in his hands with a thin layer of ash covering it, he went to where the sinner was.
At that moment, the sinner felt great joy; because of this joy, his breath ceased and his life ended, and he was reborn in the River of Ashes.

Among the various sword-trees there is a rākṣasa who, grasping a sharp sword in his hand, comes intending to inflict harm. This person, terrified, flees toward the River of Ash; with every step he raises and lowers his foot, blades wound his feet. Swords rain down from the sword-trees and enter through his pores; the rākṣasa impales his heart with a fork and pulls it out. He falls to the ground and faints in death, yet immediately returns to life.

Due to the karmic causes and conditions of their theft from teachers, elders, and parents, these people undergo five hundred billion births and five hundred billion deaths within a single day and night. Driven by hunger and thirst, they open their mouths seeking food; however, sword-trees and raining blades enter through their tongues, splitting their bellies and tearing open their chests, causing them to die in a state of suffocation.

Because they previously heard the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, after their offenses have been exhausted, they will be born among humans in a state of poverty and low station; yet, perceiving the world as impermanent, they will leave the household life to study the Path, becoming Pratyekabuddhas when no Buddha exists in the world, or Arhats when a Buddha does exist in the world.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What is called the Sword Forest Hell?
As for the Sword Forest Hell:”
Eight thousand yojanas deep, the area is filled with sword-trees (*asipattravana*), which have glowing iron balls for their fruit; these sword-trees are twenty-four yojanas high.

There are sentient beings therein who were unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, who committed evil verbal karma, and who, lacking a heart of compassion, inflicted harm upon others with knives and staves.
When this person’s retribution for their sins approaches at the time of death, their mind clings everywhere like lacquer;

they immediately think: "My mind is bound and attached, unable to let go of whatever it encounters. I am addicted to wine and lustful of beauty; though my body has met with affliction, my mind still does not cease. I must obtain a sharp blade to cut through this craving."
The hell-warden rākṣasa arrived immediately upon hearing these words and transformed himself into an attendant; holding up a bright mirror, he showed it to the sinner and said:
"Your mind is full of attachments; you should look into this mirror."
When he looked into this mirror, he saw the image of a sharp sword within it, and he immediately thought:
"My body is now so emaciated that I cannot endure sexual desire; would it not be a source of great joy for me to obtain this sharp sword and sever my own heart?"

While forming this thought, his breath ceased and his life ended; he received the body of a hungry ghost and was suddenly born through transformation amidst the sword-trees. Once born, iron balls entered through the crown of his head and emerged from his mouth; his intestines and stomach were scorched and rotted away as he collapsed to the ground.
The hell-wardens further strike and drive them with iron forks to climb trees; once they have climbed a tree, iron-beaked insects devour them, and out of terror, they leap again to climb other trees.

In this manner, they passed through the Forest of Swords in succession, undergoing eighty thousand births and eighty thousand deaths each day and night. Once their retribution was exhausted, they were born into an age of famine and an eon of pestilence; they became lowly and base among men, their breath was perpetually foul, and they were loathsome to behold. Only after passing through eons beyond calculation did they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and resolve to attain Bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is meant by the Five Hundred Million Spiked Forest Hell?
As for the Spiked Forest Hell:"
The [hell] is filled with iron thorns eight thousand *yojanas* deep; at the tip of each thorn are twelve swords, and upon the trees there are also great, glowing-hot iron tongs.

There are naturally foolish sentient beings in the world who engage in harsh speech, double-tongued speech, frivolous speech, and unrighteous speech; they are wanton and unrestrained, falsely speaking of right and wrong, criticizing the scriptures, and slandering those who discourse on the meaning of the Dharma.
When his life was about to end as a result of such karmic retribution, his throat became parched and his tongue dried up, whereupon he thought:
"If only I could obtain a sharp thorn to pierce my neck and draw blood, so that the various fluids might flow through my veins—would that not be a joy!"

While he was thinking this, the rakṣasa wardens transformed themselves into his parents; they held moon-jewels in their hands, from which thorns grew at the tips, which they held to his mouth as if water were about to drip from them. The sinner rejoiced, thinking:
"That which I have desired has now borne fruit."
Having formed this thought, his breath ceased and his life ended; in the time it takes for a great flash of lightning, he was reborn amidst a forest of thorns.

Once reborn there, the rākṣasa wardens of hell seized him with iron tongs and pulled out his tongue. Eighty iron oxen with great iron plows furrowed and tore his tongue apart. From the trees of the thorn forest, winds blew them toward him to strike his body. Day and night, he was born six hundred times and died six hundred times.
After this period has passed, they may be reborn among humans, yet their lips will be thick, their faces wrinkled, and their speech stammering and indistinct.
Such sinners will have sores breaking out upon their bodies from which pus and blood flow profusely, and for five hundred lifetimes they will be loathed and avoided by all people.

"After this period has passed, although they may have something to say, people will not believe or accept it; yet, upon meeting a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will resolve their minds toward Bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is meant by the 'Hell of Five Hundred Million Copper Pillars'?"
As for the Copper Pillar Hell:

there is a copper pillar shaped like a great mountain, six hundred yojanas in height. Beneath it is a fierce fire; upon the fire is an iron bed with blades as wheels, and between these blade-wheels are iron-beaked insects and iron crows nearby.

In this world, there are naturally foolish sentient beings who, with abundant greed and delusion, become defiled by impure attachment; they commit acts of sexual misconduct, engaging in unwholesome deeds at improper places and improper times.

Suppose there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, brahmins, or other practitioners of the holy life who, at an improper time or in an improper place, commit impure acts, or even engage in all manner of perverse conduct and perform unwholesome deeds.

When such a sinner approaches the end of life, his entire body violently convulses and trembles uncontrollably, like a drawn crossbow that one cannot manage to hold steady. He then forms this thought:
"If only I could find a large, solid pillar of copper or iron to bind this body so that it does not shake."
The hell-warden rākṣasa arrived at that very moment, having transformed himself into a servant holding an iron staff; he went to the place where the offender was and said: "O Elder!"
"Your body is now strong while all other things are weak; you may grasp this staff. His heart was immediately filled with joy, and his breath ceased as he passed away.

In the mere time it takes to play with a staff, he was reborn atop a pillar of copper. A fierce, blazing flame scorched his body; in his terror, he looked down and saw a beautiful woman upon an iron bed. Just as a woman might feel desire for a handsome man, he sought to throw himself from the copper pillar to the ground. But the copper pillar pierced his body and an iron chain encircled his neck. Iron-beaked insects devoured his flesh as he fell onto the iron bed. Simultaneously, fires erupted from the six sense organs of both the man and the woman. Iron-beaked insects entered through their eyes and emerged from their sexual organs.

If one defiles the precepts, there are another nine hundred million kinds of tiny insects; like the *śvitraka* (itching) worm, they have twelve beaks, and fire issues from the tips of these beaks as they gnaw and devour the body.

As retribution for this sexual misconduct, one undergoes nine hundred billion births and nine hundred billion deaths in a single day and night. Only when the karmic penalty is exhausted is one born among pigeons, remaining in the body of a pigeon for five hundred lifetimes;

then one is born among dragons for another five hundred lifetimes; thereafter, one is born among humans, remaining in the bodies of those without genitals, those with dual genitals, those with indeterminate genitals, or eunuchs for five hundred lifetimes.
Even if they should obtain human birth, their wives will not be chaste and virtuous, their children will not be affectionate and filial, and their servants will not be obedient.
Only after this period has passed will they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and resolve to attain bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is meant by the five hundred koṭis of Iron-Machine Hells?
As for the Iron-Machine Hells:"

There is an iron bed, four hundred yojanas in length and breadth, upon which various spears are fixed; between every pair of spears there are ten trillion iron bows, and each bowhead has ten billion sharp blades.

In this world, there are naturally some deluded sentient beings who, for the sake of greed and desire, are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, and disobedient to wholesome teachings; they kill sentient beings and consume the food of various wicked people.
When the life of this person, as a retribution for their sins, is about to end, their body trembles and fluids spontaneously flow from all six apertures.
This sinner perceives his own bed as if it were made of *tūla* cotton and immediately thinks:
"When shall I find a firm and cool place to settle my body and lie down to sleep? Would that not be a source of joy?"

While he was thinking this, the rākṣasa wardens lifted the bed with a forked pole and brought it, spread with a large cotton mattress, to the place of the offender. Upon seeing it, the offender felt joy in his heart; as he wished to lie down upon the mattress, his breath ceased and his life ended, and he was reborn upon the iron machine.

Ten trillion iron-studded gates move from below; as the iron gates rise and fall, immeasurable iron crossbows are all drawn simultaneously, and each iron arrow pierces the hearts of the offenders. In one day and one night, they undergo six hundred billion births and six hundred billion deaths.

After such a sinner has finished undergoing these punishments, they will be reborn among animals for five hundred lifetimes; returning once more to the human realm, they will be poor, lowly, and enslaved by others, frequently falling into prison and constantly subjected to flogging.
"After this period has passed, they will encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) and give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is called the Iron Net Hell?"
As for the Iron Net Hell:
there are eighty-nine layers of iron nets, and within each net there are ten billion iron needles;
each iron needle is fitted with five barbs.

In this world, there are naturally those sentient beings who are false and deluded, whose minds are perverse, crooked, and seductive, using charms to deceive others; harboring treacherous intent, they harbor evil thoughts day and night, accomplishing such evil conceptions in every single moment.
When this person’s retribution for their sins approaches the end of life, their body becomes itchy, and they immediately think:
"Would it not be pleasant to obtain a bundle of needles to prick the scabies-infesting insects?"
While he was thinking this, the rakṣasa hell-warden transformed himself into a skilled physician and, holding a sharp needle in his hand, cried out, "I shall treat your illness!
The sinner’s heart rejoiced;
his breath ceased and his life ended, and he was reborn amidst an iron net. As his body passed beneath it, the many hooks all moved, and immeasurable needles shot into his pores.

Thus they wind back and forth amidst the iron nets, dying for a moment and being reborn the next; only when their retribution is exhausted are they born in a remote land where the Buddha-dharma does not exist, and there they do not even hear the words of worldly goodness, let alone the True Dharma.

"Although born among humans, they are subsumed within the three evil realms; even after passing through eons beyond calculation, they may encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), yet though they hear the Dharma, their minds do not understand it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What is meant by the Iron Cave Hell?"

As for the Iron Cave Hell: it is the supreme state of suffering within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). There is an iron mountain, twenty-five *yojanas* in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides. Upon this mountain are five hundred trillion great, glowing iron balls; each iron ball is perfectly round, measuring thirteen *yojanas* in diameter. Between the mountain peaks, there are further hundreds of thousands of swords and blades.
At that time, the eastern side of that mountain opened wide, revealing a small hole as large as the mouth of a Magadhan *droṇa* measure, from which only black smoke issued.

There were naturally some deluded beings in the world whose minds were bound by stinginess and greed like adamant; they delighted only in seeking and grasping without ever knowing satisfaction. They gave nothing to their parents or wives and children; they regarded their teachers and instructors as dung and filth; and they did not bestow food or clothing upon their servants, slaves, or kinsmen.

Thus, such a miserly person does not contemplate impermanence and guards his wealth as dearly as his own eyes. When the life of this person, burdened by the retribution of his sins, is about to end, his sensory faculties are blocked and his mouth is clenched so he cannot speak; within his heart he silently thinks:
"After my death, these wicked people will consume my wealth as if eating iron pellets, and they will occupy my house as if dwelling in a dark room."

Having formed this thought, the rakṣasa jailer transforms himself into a miserly man; through his illusory power, he collects the person's wealth and brings it to the sinner, where he burns it with fire.
The sinner’s heart is filled with joy, yet his breath ceases and his life ends; he is reborn upon a mountain of fire, like molten copper cast into an iron cave.

Once they have entered the cave, sword-insects and knife-insects devour their bodies, and smoke blinds their eyes so that they cannot see the flames. In a state of frantic terror, they run hither and thither; iron balls strike their heads from above and below, entering through the crown of the head and exiting through the feet. They die in one instant and are reborn in the next. When their retribution is exhausted, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); their bodies are tens of *yojana*s in height, with throats like needle-tubes and bellies like great mountains. Seeking food to the east and west, molten copper is poured down their throats. Only after eight thousand years does their suffering end, and they are born among the "spittle-eaters," the "pus-eaters," and the "blood-eaters. When that retribution is exhausted, they are born as latrine deities, pigs, or dogs. When that retribution is exhausted, they are born into poverty and lowliness in places lacking food and clothing, where they encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and resolve to attain *bodhicitta*.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What is called the Iron Ball Hell? As for the Iron Ball Hell:”

The iron city, eighty *yojanas* in circumference, is divided into eighty-eight compartments; within each compartment are five mountains of knives that cover the top, while beneath them are eighteen great and wicked iron snakes, all of which protrude their tongues—tongues from which issue iron swords with flames blazing at their tips.

In this world, there are naturally some deluded sentient beings who disparage and insult the practice of giving, claiming that gifts yield no reward, and they urge others to hoard and accumulate wealth.
Such deluded people speak before kings, ministers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all the masses, asserting that giving has neither cause nor karmic fruit.

When such a sinner approaches the end of life, his neck stiffens, his pulses contract, and he turns away unable to speak; he takes no pleasure in seeing people and lies with his gaze cast downward, thinking only in his heart:
"I have accumulated wealth and treasures that I would have found indescribable joy to possess together with me."
The hell-warden rākṣasa transformed himself into the man’s wife; taking a glowing iron ball and transforming it into a precious vessel, he stood before the person and said:
"I shall die with you; we shall remain entwined and never part."

His breath ceased and his life ended, and he was reborn within an Iron City. He ran back and forth from east to west as iron snakes emitted venom to coil around his body; fire blazed from the joints of their heads, and he immediately thought:
"May the gods love me and send down sweet rain."

As soon as they think of it, great hot iron balls rain down from above; entering through the crown of the head, they emerge from the soles of the feet. Only when their retribution is exhausted do they become poor, solitary, and mute persons. The duration of these years is as described in the "Iron Cave" [sūtra]; there, they encounter a virtuous friend and give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What is called the Hell of Pointed Rocks?
As for the Hell of Pointed Rocks:”
There are twenty-five rocky mountains, and each rocky mountain has eight icy ponds;
in each icy pond dwell five venomous dragons.

Among the beings of this world, there are those who are naturally foolish—monks, nuns, male novices, female novices, probationary nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as the ninety-five kinds of Brahmins—who proclaim what is not the Dharma to be the Dharma, and what is the Dharma to be not the Dharma; or who violate minor precepts and fail to repent for a long time, their hearts lacking shame and remorse like that of a monkey.

When this person’s life is about to end as a retribution for their sins, their heart sinks, their breath becomes full, and their abdomen swells like a drum; food and drink become choked and vomited up, and even water or thin gruel cannot pass down.
They then think to themselves: "Would it not be a relief to obtain a sharp stone to block my throat?"

While he was thinking this, the hell-warden rākṣasa transformed himself into a skilled physician; by means of his magical power, he seized a stone point and fashioned it into a large medicinal pill, placed it in his mouth, and said:
"Close your mouth."
With a heart full of joy, his breath ceased and his life ended, and he was reborn amidst the stone mountains. Countless sharp stones entered through his back and emerged from his chest.

The hell-wardens then used iron forks to pry open his mouth and thrust stones inside; in a single day and night, he died sixty billion times and was reborn sixty billion times. This is the retribution for his birth, and when his life there ends, he falls into the Black Rope Hell.

As for the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra-naraka*): there are eight hundred iron chains and eight hundred iron mountains. Great iron pillars are erected with chains fastened to both ends. The rākṣasa hell-wardens drive and crowd the sinners, forcing them to carry these iron mountains and run upon iron ropes. Unable to endure the burden, they fall to the ground and drop into cauldrons of boiling liquid. The rākṣasas drive them back up; driven by desperate thirst, they drink iron and swallow stones as they run. In one day and one night, they undergo this suffering a total of one hundred thousand times.

When his retribution for past offenses was exhausted, he was reborn in this world as a servant. Encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), who expounded the true Dharma to him, he was like fine white cotton that easily takes on color; he attained arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What are called the eighteen Copper-Drinking Hells?
As for the Copper-Drinking Hells:”
There were twelve hundred chariots of various colors made of copper, and upon each copper chariot were six thousand copper balls.

There are sentient beings who are stingy, greedy, envious, and hold wrong views; they speak evil words and do not give to their parents, wives, children, or kinsmen, nor to anyone else. Their hearts are filled with stinginess and envy; when they see others obtain profit, it pierces their hearts like an arrow.
When such a sinner is about to die, he becomes emaciated by many illnesses and speaks deliriously in a daze, saying of his own accord:
"I wish to have fruit to eat.

When he says these words, the rākṣasa wardens transform a copper chariot and load it full of fruit, bringing it to the place where the sinner is. Upon receiving it, the sinner feels joy in his heart and thinks to himself:
"Having obtained these delicious fruits, I eat them without knowing satiety; this greatly accords with my wishes.
Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, his breath ceased and his life ended.

Before long, he was reborn atop a copper chariot, and shortly thereafter, he was reborn amidst the Copper Mountains. As the copper chariot crushed his neck, the hell-wardens, rākṣasas, seized him with tongs and forced his mouth open to pour molten copper into it. Having drunk the molten copper, he fell to the ground in a state of delirium and cried out:
"Cold! Cold! they cry.

Immediately, the hell-wardens pry open their mouths and place copper and iron balls inside; as they swallow eighteen such balls, fire blazes up at every joint. They run hither and thither for an entire day before finally their lives come to an end.
The hell-wardens cry out:
"In your previous lives, you were sycophantic, held false views, and were stingy, greedy, and envious; by these causes and conditions, you receive this retribution of iron balls.

Or perhaps you once left the household life but violated even minor precepts, failing to repent for a long time while consuming the offerings of the faithful; by these causes and conditions, you must eat these iron balls."

For this person’s retribution for their sins, they shall not recognize water or grain for hundreds of millions of years. Once their punishment is completed, they will return to birth among humans; for five hundred lifetimes, their speech will be stammering and indistinct, such that they cannot express themselves clearly. Due to the influence of past habits, after eating they will consume charcoal and eat clods of earth. Only after passing through this period will they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and give rise to the bodhicitta.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Scroll Five.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Scroll Six.
