Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the sentient being?
Is emptiness the sentient being?
Is it that what is not empty is a sentient being?
Is it such a sentient being?
Or is it not such a sentient being?
Is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) the sentient being?
Is that which is not the reality-limit the sentient being?
Is conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) the sentient being?
Is unconditioned emptiness a sentient being?

When analyzing and discerning in this way, one does not see a sentient being, does not apprehend a sentient being, and has no notion of a sentient being; with a mind that is unattached and free from seeking, one who understands such pure dharmas as these is said to practice equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are sentient beings who joyfully contemplate the Buddha lying down, this is truly contemplating the pure concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).

If there are sentient beings who hear the Dharma of the Buddha’s reclining, and if the bhikṣus follow the Buddha’s words by lying on their right sides without violating their dignified deportment, you should know that such persons are clothed in the raiment of shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*) and apply the medicine of patience (*kṣānti*). Such bhikṣus, while practicing dhyāna in the present life, shall see the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Great Dharma for them."

Because they neither practice seated meditation nor violate the precepts, they shall behold the Buddhas of the ten directions in future ages. The Buddhas of the ten directions will expound the Great Dharma for them; hearing this Dharma, they will awaken with ease, and in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, they shall immediately attain the path of Arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
The Tathāgata’s reclining benefits sentient beings; because it benefits them, it is called loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
These four dharmas are the mother that gives birth to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Having spoken these words, the Buddha emitted light from his entire body amidst the assembly: eighty-four thousand rays from the front, eighty-four thousand from the left, eighty-four thousand from the right, eighty-four thousand from the back, and eighty-four thousand from the crown of his head.
From each and every one of these pores, a single hair grows in a clockwise curl;

at the tip of each hair, there are lotus flowers as numerous as the atoms in ten million billion worlds. Upon each lotus flower are immeasurable and incalculable transformation Buddhas made of atoms, their bodies tall, radiant, and adorned like thousands of millions of billions of Sumeru mountains.
Within the navel of each Buddha, there are five hundred trillion lions.
From each lion’s mouth issued five hundred trillion offerings;
each offering consisted of five hundred trillion clouds of flowers made of the seven treasures;
and within each cloud of precious flowers were five hundred trillion clouds of verses, their sounds following one another like drops of rain.

At that time, the Tathāgata further manifested the eighty minor marks; golden light issued from the ūrṇā-kośa, and each ray of light shone universally throughout the ten directions, transforming into various Buddhas.
O World-Honored Ones!

Among these, there are countless who walk, countless who stand, countless who sit, and countless who lie down; all these emanated Buddhas preach great compassion, preach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist toward awakening, preach the six pāramitās, and preach the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
When this sign appeared, one hundred million Śākyas attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) with minds free from attachment;

the Buddha bestowed upon them the prophecy: "In a future age, after incalculable eons have passed, you shall become Buddhas, named Samadhi-vijaya-dhvaja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."
In succession, there will be one hundred million who attain Buddhahood.
When those Buddhas appear, the Sahā world will be pure and adorned, exactly like the world-system of the Buddha Light in the world called Holy Victory Banner, without any difference.

When these bodhisattvas attain the Buddha-way, their lands will be free from even the names of those who violate the precepts, have distracted minds, or are unwholesome; they will consist purely of bodhisattvas, and although śrāvakas may be present, they shall not slander the Mahāyāna.

At that time, when the Śākya sons heard the Buddha’s prophecy, their hearts were filled with great joy. Each of them removed their necklaces and scattered them over the Buddha. These necklaces remained suspended above the Buddha, transforming into flowering trees;

each tree had flowers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and upon each flower was a jeweled pavilion as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, within each of which were transformation Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Each of these manifested Buddhas expounded the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*.

Furthermore, there were manifested Buddhas who taught the *śrāvakas* the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*): the radiance of the flowing bones and the flowing bones of the radiance; the perception of the purity of the mind and the perception of the impurity of the mind;
the perception of the arising of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the perception of the extinction of fetters.

The perception of severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the perception of killing the roots of the fetters—such perceptions, numbering nine hundred *koṭis* of *rajas*, are as described in the *Ānāpāna-smṛti*; this is called the Dharma of the Śrāvakas.
The Dharma of a bodhisattva consists of only four practices. What are these four?
First, to confess and repent of one's transgressions during the six periods of the day and night.
Second, they constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha and do not deceive sentient beings.
Third, they cultivate the six points of harmonious respect and harbor no anger or arrogance.
Fourth, they practice the six recollections as if their heads were on fire.
The Buddha told the King, his father:

"Such names as these are called the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddhas in Future Ages; they are also called the Differentiation of the Buddha’s Body, the Knowledge of the Buddha’s Physical Marks, the Recollection of the Buddha Samādhi, and the Radiance of All Buddhas Covering and Protecting Sentient Beings."
When these words were spoken, ten billion beings among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the eight classes of spirits resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and made this vow:
"May we always enter samādhi in future lives and behold the Buddha’s form-body no differently than it is now."
At that time, Brahmā Śikhin, Śakra Devendra, and countless sons of gods prostrated before the Buddha,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One!

We have now been able to behold the Tathāgata, the most supreme of all forms; we pray that in future ages, sentient beings living in an age of turbidity and evil may fix their mindfulness upon him and contemplate the Buddha’s physical body.
This vow shall not be in vain; what I have now spoken and what I have perceived are true and not false. May we and the assembly of devas become like the body of the Buddha.

When he spoke these words, he saw a million rays of light emerge from within his own heart; each ray of light transformed into immeasurable hundreds of thousands of manifested Buddhas. He saw his own body become the color of pure gold, no different from Nanda and the others.
At that time, the Brahmā devas addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Tathāgata, the Hero of the World, has appeared in the world; he will surely benefit all sentient beings. Since his great vows of old have now been fulfilled, and because his words ‘I shall not abandon sentient beings’ are not false, I personally perceive the realm of my mental conceptions, and future sentient beings shall likewise conceive of the true body of the Buddha in this way!”
The Buddha told Brahmā:

"What you have said is true and not false. If future sentient beings merely give rise to such a thought, they will obtain immeasurable merit and be endowed with the marks of a great being; how much more so for those who contemplate it with focused recollection?"
When the Buddha had spoken these words, King Śuddhodana, the Śākya sons, the bhikṣuṇīs, and the upāsikās all rose simultaneously, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew.

At that time, the father-king returned to the palace and described the Buddha’s marks and signs to his court ladies. Upon hearing of the Buddha’s white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*), the twelve hundred and fifty ladies felt great joy in their hearts and were thereby cleared of the sins of hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of births and deaths.
A voice from the sky addressed the women, saying:
"Hearing of the Buddha’s marks which eliminate all faults and transgressions, you should resolve to attain unsurpassed *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Having heard these words, they immediately beheld immeasurable Buddhas in the sky; having seen those Buddhas, they all simultaneously attained the meditative concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
Then the bhikṣus rose from their seats, paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Ānanda bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“The Buddha has spoken of thirty-two marks, yet there remains one mark; why does the Tathāgata not explain it explicitly?
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the bhikṣus, “Each of you, return to your seats.”

At that time, the World-Honored One himself manifested five hundred billion jewel mountains on his left and right; upon each jewel mountain sat four Buddhas, and these four World-Honored Buddhas praised the mindfulness of the Buddha.

The Buddha immediately smiled; from his mouth issued light of five colors, and from his tongue, fourteen rays of light. These radiances transformed into a Buddha, from whose navel flowed five kinds of water, each of a different color. Within each color were nine hundred million bodhisattvas.
Upon the crown of every bodhisattva was a Brahma-maṇi light, within which were transformation Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
From the navel of each of these transformation Buddhas, water likewise flowed forth in the same manner!
In this manner, all these waters flow into the Buddha’s navel, and all these manifested Buddhas and manifested Bodhisattvas likewise enter the Buddha’s navel.
At that time, the Buddha’s body is pure both internally and externally, surpassing even the most exquisite and wondrous *vaiḍūrya* gem;
within the Buddha’s body there is a lion throne, and each lion throne is like Mount Sumeru.
Upon each seat sat a Tathāgata, with ninety billion bodhisattvas serving as attendants; atop the heads of these bodhisattvas, the Buddhas appeared like Mount Sumeru.

In this way, water issued from the navels of the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions and all entered together into the navel of Śākyamuni Buddha. At that time, the various Buddhas did not become larger than Śākyamuni, nor did Śākyamuni become smaller than the various Buddhas; Śākyamuni Buddha was neither large nor small, yet within his body and heart were infinite Buddhas.
Each and every Buddha did not obstruct one another, and from every pore of their bodies they preached the mindfulness of the Buddhas.
At that time, each of the transformed Buddhas extended his right hand and stroked Ānanda’s head, saying:

“You must now skillfully uphold this Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha; do not allow it to be forgotten, but maintain single-minded mindfulness to open the eye of light for sentient beings of the future.”
When these words were spoken, the images of the seven Buddhas of the past appeared standing in the air; each extended his right hand, stroked Ānanda’s head, and entrusted him with this matter.
At that time, there were countless rays of light in the void; within each ray of light were countless transformation Buddhas, who with one voice and in unison entrusted this Dharma to him.
The Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Seven.
The Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of Central India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
7. The Seventh Chapter: Contemplating the Horse-King Treasury (8). The Seventh Chapter: Contemplating the Horse-King Treasury.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"How should future sentient beings contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the sheathed male organ?
As for this mark of the sheathed male organ:
when I was living at home, Yaśodharā and five hundred female attendants all had this thought:"
"The Prince’s birth into this world was filled with many wonders; yet there is one matter regarding him that leaves me in doubt.
Among the assembly of court ladies, there was a woman named Śyāmāvatī who addressed the Queen, saying:
"The Prince is a divine being."
The *Vidyā-sūtra* states:
"If there is a divine person whose fundamental nature is pure, because of their practice of the Brahma-faring, their physical organ is level and full.

The Prince now appears to be one who practices the Brahma-faring; having taken a consort many years ago and been served by his various court ladies for years, we have not seen his physical organ, much less engaged in worldly affairs.
Again, there was a woman named Viśuddhamati who said: "O Mistress!
I have served the Prince for eighteen years, yet I have never seen him suffer from the ailment of needing to relieve himself, much less indulge in any sensual desires."
At that time, the women each spoke differently, all claiming that the Prince was a eunuch.
While the Prince was sleeping during the day, they all heard the women wishing to see the mark of his hidden male organ.

At that time, by the power of his vow, the Prince responded to the women; he turned his body slowly and gracefully, revealing his inner garments and hair. Seeing his golden body with its radiant brilliance, they momentarily parted their knees and beheld his holy form as level as the full moon, with golden light like the orb of the sun.
The women were filled with joy and said, "Such a divine person is truly worthy of veneration and affection; yet for us, all hope for worldly union has been severed!
Having spoken these words, they wept bitterly, their tears falling like rain.

At that time, from the private parts of the Prince, white lotuses emerged, red and white in color; one above and two below, three flowers were linked together. When the women saw this, they said to one another:
"This divine person possesses the mark of the lotus; how could his mind have any defiled attachment?"
Having spoken these words, he was choked and unable to speak further.
At that moment, from within the flower, there suddenly appeared a male organ in the shape of a youth.
When the women saw this, they said to one another, "The Prince has now manifested a marvelous thing; suddenly a male organ has appeared, gradually taking on the form of an adult man."
When the women saw this fulfillment, their hearts were filled with such joy that they could not contain it.

At the time this sign appeared, Rāhula’s mother saw his organ of masculinity manifest as a succession of flowers like celestial *karpāsa* cloth; upon each flower there were countless great-bodied Bodhisattvas holding white flowers and surrounding the organ. Having appeared, they vanished again just as the sun had before.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s mark of the sheathed organ like that of a horse.
Now that the Tathāgata has attained the path of Bodhi, he is a Great Man endowed with a male body; furthermore, he shall manifest his masculine characteristics for you.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Before you went forth from the household life, King Mathurā had a wet-nurse named Dhūmrapa who nursed that king for fifteen years."
When the prince had grown up, he knelt with palms joined and requested a boon from the king, saying:
"Great King, although I am lowly and humble, I have nurtured Your Majesty with diligent toil for many years. I humbly beseech Your Majesty to grant me one wish!"
The king asked,
"What does the wet nurse wish to seek?
The wet nurse then replied:
"Within the royal palace, she was like Śrī-devī; nothing was lacking, yet she was missing one thing: namely, the desire of a woman for a beloved husband.
The king said to the wet-nurse, "You should be united with a high minister as his lawful consort."
The wet nurse did not wish to go and said to the Great King:

"A person of noble rank has many duties, which are not what I delight in. I pray that you command all the men within the kingdom, from those aged fifteen upwards to those under thirty, to all follow me."
"If anyone is able to come, I shall give that person one gold coin;
to those of ugly appearance, I shall give a silver coin.
At that time, the king, in order to repay the kindness of his wet nurse, built a tall tower and issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom, commanding all men:
"May all those as I have wished for assemble here.

As the years passed, the wet nurse grew old; she summoned many women until there were five hundred, and each of these women further purchased maidservants, so that the number of variously adorned attendants reached eight thousand.
At that time, the king fell ill and passed away, and the crown prince succeeded to the throne. A wise minister addressed him, saying:

"The late king, in his desire to repay her kindness, gave this old slave-woman free rein; she has caused the kingdom to become like a village of courtesans, and the damage to our national reputation is indeed no small matter."
"What is the use of this?
You should be banished at once!
Having said this, he went outside, set fire to the high tower, and drove out all the women.
The women, filled with terror, went to the kingdom of Śrāvastī. Having arrived in Śrāvastī, they established brothels at the crossroads and practiced their seductive arts as before.
The great kingdom of Śrāvastī was populous; it was decreed that anyone staying overnight at the women's quarters must pay a fine of two hundred gold coins.

In the kingdom there was an elder named Yuludata, who had accumulated a fortune of ten billion. The elder had a son named Huade; the three brothers were dissolute and unrestrained, vying with one another to frequent brothels. At their first visit, each of them wagered fifteen gold coins, and night after night they constantly wagered more than twice as much as ordinary people, until within one month an entire treasury of gold was exhausted.
The father, the elder, went to inspect the various treasuries and saw that one treasury was empty.
He asked the keeper of the treasury, "Where is the gold in this treasury? The treasurer replied:
"The sons of our great household go every day with gold to the courtesan’s quarters; if you do not restrain them, the gold will be exhausted.
Upon hearing this, the elder beat his breast and wept aloud:
"Alas! My wicked sons are ruining my home!"
He seized a large staff and struck his son’s mother on the head. The wife wailed and cried out: “Alas, you wicked son!
To have fathered you has been of no benefit; you have stolen the gold and exhausted the storehouse. Since our father lacked instruction and was never stern in his commands, why do you strike me now?”
The elder, filled with rage and weeping aloud, went before the king; prostrating himself with his chest against the ground, he addressed him, saying: "Great King!
The kingdom is in chaos and turmoil. Rākṣasīs from the country of Mathurā have come to dwell in this city and destroyed my household estate."
The king said to the elder:
"Even your vast wealth and gold treasuries are already exhausted; how much more so for other commoners—would they not surely suffer from want?
The elder addressed the king:
"May Your Majesty swiftly execute this evil man.
The King said to the elder:
"I have received the Buddha's precepts; I would not even harm an ant, much less kill a human being."
Upon hearing this, the elder raised his hand and struck his head, saying:
"Great King! Your servant has heard that when a king executes and punishes evil people to eliminate calamities for the sake of the state, what crime could there possibly be?"

"Today the Great King has taken evil as his companion; by indulging these lewd women, he brings ruin and disorder to the True Dharma. The land lies desolate and the people are impoverished—how can the precepts remain secure?

The King said to the elder: "The Tathāgata appears in the world to tame many beings. He has transformed Aṅgulimāla, the Candāla who breathes fire, the powerful ghost-king, the rākṣasas, and the executioners—all have been converted. We shall now go to the Buddha and report this matter; you may wait a moment."

Having comforted the minister, he mounted a famous elephant and, accompanied by his attendants, proceeded to the Jetavana. He paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and with palms joined and kneeling for a long time, addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"The courtesans of the kingdom of Mathurā have now come here to seduce the young men; we pray that the Buddha will transform them.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Seven days from now, the Buddha shall know of it himself."
Then King Prasenajit prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.

The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa: "Go to the home of the great elder Sudatta and say to the donor: [The Buddha has said: 'If you wish to make offerings to the Tathāgata, you should first offer them to the Saṃgha.'"
"Seven days from now, the Buddha will go to the debating hall to transform the courtesans.

Upon hearing this, Sudatta was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he prepared various offerings and fashioned a flower of the seven precious gems eleven *zhang* high to place at the Buddha’s seat. He hung silk canopies, sprinkled fragrant liquid upon the ground, and when the appointed day arrived, the King struck the golden drum, commanding all the masters of debate within the kingdom to proceed to the debating hall.
The elder Sudatta invited the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; they all assembled, and he was about to provide them with offerings.

When the time arrived the following day, the King and his retinue proceeded to the debating arena. The elder, like Raudrākṣa, dispatched a caṇḍāla to summon the courtesans, and the elder Sudatta likewise announced that the time had come.
At that time, the Tathāgata commanded one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus:
"O bhikṣus! Each of you, according to your meditative concentration, manifest great supernormal powers."

The Elder Kauṇḍinya and four bhikṣus manifested a single cave as large as Mount Gandhamādana and filled with hundreds of thousands of lotuses. Upon each lotus sat five bhikṣus in the full lotus posture, their bodies emitting golden light that rendered them golden-hued; they were so upright, dignified, and lovely that they resembled Maitreya.

Furthermore, there were emanated beings who performed the eighteen transformations; within each transformation were eighteen bhikṣus performing the eighteen transformations of supernatural power, which were worth beholding. Among them, some entered samādhi, while others recited the sūtras. Radiance whirled about like a mountain of gold, producing various precious flowers. The bhikṣus remained within their caves with body and mind undistracted, flying to the examination hall and taking their seats at the head of the row.

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa leaped into the air and transformed himself into six dragons; they coiled their bodies together to form a seat for the bhikṣu, and upon that seat he performed eighteen miraculous transformations as he flew to the place of examination.

The two brothers, Gayanādi and his sibling, leaped into the air and transformed themselves into a great stone cave; entering the fire-light samādhi, they performed eighteen miraculous transformations and flew to the site of the trial.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, wearing a robe of a thousand patches and holding an alms bowl in his hand, maintained his majestic deportment as he walked through the air;

with every step, he manifested a precious tree, and beneath each tree appeared a manifested Kāśyapa, performing the eighteen transformations while walking in meditation within the grove, until they all arrived at the place of examination.
"O Śāriputra of Great Wisdom!

Leaping into the air, he performed eighteen transformations: from his upper body issued the brilliant radiance of a thousand suns, shining so intensely that they did not obstruct one another; from his lower body issued a thousand moons, as full and lovely as the autumnal moon. Having performed these eighteen transformations, he flew to the examination hall."

Mahāmaudgalyāyana leaped into the air and manifested eighty-four thousand lion thrones; each lion closed its eyes and crouched upon the ground, white as the Snow Mountains. Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat upon the back of one, performed the eighteen transformations, and flew to the place of examination.

Venerable Upāli leaped into the air and, while suspended in mid-air, spread out his *niṣīdana* mat and sat cross-legged, entering the *maitrī-samādhi*. From all the pores of his body, golden light flowed forth as he performed the eighteen transformations and flew to the place of examination.

Mahākātyāyana leaped into the air and manifested himself as fifteen Maheśvaras; each of these devas rode upon a bull-king, with a flower growing from his head. Mahākātyāyana sat upon this flower-throne and, performing eighteen miraculous transformations, flew to the examination hall.
Subhūti leaped into the air; he became invisible, yet his voice was heard as he spoke these verses:
"All dharmas are of the nature of suchness; There is no self and no sentient beings.
There is also no notion of lustful desire— Whom, then, should one go on to transform?"
"All phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, and they likewise lack the characteristics of names;
since desire arises from attachment, whom should I go on to teach?
Having spoken these words, he performed the eighteen transformations and flew to the place of examination.

At that time, Aniruddha leaped into the air and manifested ten thousand Brahmā kings along with their various Brahmā palaces; the bhikṣu stood in their midst and performed eighteen transformations as he flew to the place of examination.

Rāhula and Nanda! At that time, the two bhikṣus leaped into the air and manifested a jeweled pavilion; dwelling within it, they entered deep meditative concentration and performed the eighteen transformations as they flew to the place of examination.
In this manner, these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus each manifested various transformations and, performing the eighteen kinds of supernatural powers, flew to the site of the trial.

At that time, the World-Honored One took Ānanda alone; holding his *niṣīdana* and grasping a water pitcher in his hand, the World-Honored One went in front and Ānanda followed behind. From within the Buddha’s alms bowl, six lotuses emerged, and from each lotus there radiated golden light, illuminating the city of Śrāvastī and turning it entirely golden.
Within the water of the ritual pitcher was a great golden banner, at the top of which were five hundred rays of light;
from each ray of light emanated a thousand transformation Buddhas, all fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, who stepped through the void and flew to the place of examination.

King Prasenajit and the great assembly scattered flowers and burned incense, prostrating themselves before the Buddha; hundreds of thousands of celestial instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, as they sang praises of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits.
King Prasenajit knelt with palms joined and entreated the Tathāgata to convert the courtesans.
The Buddha sat upon a lotus throne for the great assembly and briefly expounded upon suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and the various pāramitās; yet the women did not accept it.
At that time, among the assembly of women, there was a courtesan named Kāmagavī who addressed the other women, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."

By nature you are without desire; people say you are not a man. Therefore, among the assembly, you preach suffering, emptiness, and the impurity of desire. If you possess all the male organs in their entirety, you should cast off shame and modesty before this great assembly like the Nirgranthas and step forth to show them to me.
If these characteristics truly exist, we shall submit to you and become your disciples;
if they do not exist and you falsely claim that [the body] is impure, then since this rootless person is by nature free from desire, why do you not declare desire itself to be impure?

Having spoken these words, the Tathāgata then manifested a transformation elephant, like the Elephant-Treasure of a Cakravartin King. From between the legs of this elephant, white flowers emerged, appearing like the elephant's limbs gradually touching the ground.
Upon seeing this, the women laughed joyfully and said to one another, "This śramaṇa is a master of illusion; he has conjured this up!

The Buddha then further manifested the form of a horse-king, with a horse-king’s sheath appearing like a tube of lapis lazuli that hung down as far as his knees. When the women saw this, they spoke all the more of it being an illusion.
When Queen Mallikā saw this manifested transformation, she said to the bhikṣuṇīs and upāsikās:
"We women should each withdraw and return; what the courtesan has spoken must not be heard."
"The World-Honored One possesses great compassion; now that he intends to transform them, he will surely manifest extraordinary transformations. We should withdraw.
Having paid homage to the Buddha, they withdrew.
The Buddha then commanded Ānanda:
"Tell King Prasenajit and all the bhikṣus that each of you should go about your own affairs.
King Prasenajit addressed the venerable ones:
"The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, wishes to transform this courtesan; we should now each depart to a distance."
Having spoken these words, he stepped back and withdrew; only these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus remained standing in attendance behind the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"Lead your followers for a walk through the forest."
The five hundred bhikṣus, with the great wisdom Śāriputra as their leader, continued to stand in attendance by the Buddha’s side with palms joined.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“You too may, according to your own inclination, engage in discussion with these masters of debate on whatever is appropriate.”
The five hundred bhikṣus followed after Śāriputra to the flower grove and preached the Four Noble Truths once more for King Prasenajit.
Only Ānanda remained, and the Buddha said to Ānanda:
“You leave your sitting mat behind; it is fitting that you also depart.”
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One went alone to where the women were.
At that time, seeing the Buddha alone, the women laughed loudly and said:
"Śramaṇa, do you now have any sexual organs or not?"
The Buddha said,
"I possess a male body and am a great man (mahāpuruṣa).
When the women heard this, they covered their mouths and laughed.

At that time, the World-Honored One spread out his sitting mat; the Vajra Earth Deity transformed herself into a golden couch with legs made of the seven treasures positioned beneath the mat. The Buddha sat upon it, laid aside his saṃghāṭī robe, and donned his saṃkakṣikā undergarment, revealing the svastika mark on his chest for the woman to see.
When the women saw the letters, they were like seeing hundreds of thousands of young men in the prime of their vigor, with extraordinary countenances that greatly pleased their hearts;
the Buddha then removed his inner robe (nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī), and they beheld the Buddha’s body, perfectly smooth and full, radiating a golden light like that of a thousand suns.
When the women saw this, they all said, "Gautama is a man without genitals.

When the Buddha heard these words, he manifested gradually according to the manner of the Horse King; when he first appeared, his male organ was like that of an eight-year-old boy, and it gradually grew larger until it took the form of a youth.
When the women saw this, they were all filled with joy. At that time, the secret organ, like a lotus banner, gradually grew larger; within each successive layer there were ten billion lotuses;
each lotus had ten billion precious colors;
and within each color there were ten billion transformation Buddhas.
Each of these transformation Buddhas was attended by ten billion bodhisattvas and immeasurable multitudes as their retinue.
At that time, all the transformation Buddhas, with one voice and in unison, condemned the faults and afflictions of women’s evil desires, and spoke in verse:
“If there were men, All fifteen or sixteen years of age;”

"Though they were in the prime of youth and possessed great strength and power, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, they offered themselves to serve her, yet they could not satisfy her for even a moment.
When the women heard these words, they were filled with shame and distress; they fell to the ground, beat their heads with their hands, and spoke thus:

"Alas, how evil is desire! It causes the Buddhas to speak such words as these. We harbor malicious hearts and cling to defiled desires, unaware that they are a source of affliction; thus we cause the Buddhas to hear of such depravity, as if a blazing fire were burning us!"
When these words were spoken, she saw all the emanated Buddhas in the void extensively teaching the contemplation of impurity to the women, namely:
the nine perceptions, the ten perceptions, the thirty perceptions, and the counting of breaths (ānāpāna).
Upon hearing the discourse on the contemplation of impurity and the joy of the dharma and meditative concentration, the women no longer took pleasure in sensual desire.

At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his bodily radiance and sat upright upon the golden throne; the great assembly, having gathered like clouds, returned to the Buddha’s presence, and King Prasenajit addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world brings great benefit; he has manifested such a great radiance even at this place, let alone from his other limbs which possess immeasurable merit!
All the devas in the void also praised the Tathāgata’s hundred thousand pure practices:

"The Tathāgata’s pure conduct has resulted in this: his superior horse-organ (aśvakośa) has vanished without a trace, and countless golden lotuses and transformation Buddhas have appeared—this is the towering merit and reward of upholding the precepts."

When the women heard these words, four thousand of them resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; two thousand women became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and two thousand women were destined to attain the path of a *pratyekabuddha* in succession after twelve kalpas in a future life.
“Householder, just as Ruruda saw the Buddha manifesting the transformation of the evil Māra’s women and praised him, saying:
‘Excellent, excellent!

In the past, the Tathāgata shattered the army of Pāpīyas; now he has transformed these women so that they are no different from their original state. When this sign appears, immeasurable devas resolve upon bodhicitta.’”

The five hundred men in King Prasenajit’s retinue sought to leave the household life under the Buddha; their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, the garments they wore were transformed into *kāṣāya* robes, and they immediately attained the state of an Arhat.
At that time, when the great assembly beheld the concealment of the Horse King, those whose hearts were filled with joy had the karmic offenses of birth and death for fifty billion kalpas eradicated;
they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, during my summer retreat, there was a brothel in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. On the upper floor of the building was a woman named Citramati, who had a profound karmic connection with me from former lives. I, along with Nanda and you, went to this courtesan’s house every day to beg for alms. This woman never showed me respect, but she harbored a particular attachment toward Nanda. After seven days had passed, the woman thought to herself:"
"If the śramaṇa Gautama would send his younger brothers Nanda and Ānanda to follow me as I wish, I shall provide various kinds of offerings to the śramaṇa.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Nanda:
"From this day forward, do not go to that village."

The World-Honored One personally carried his almsbowl alone and went to the woman’s tower; from one day until the third day, he emitted golden light to transform the various devas and humans, yet this woman did not awaken.

On a later day, the World-Honored One was again walking on the terrace with Ānanda and Nanda. Because the courtesan cherished and respected the two bhikṣus, she scattered many flowers from afar over the Buddha and the two bhikṣus.
Ānanda said to her, "You should pay homage to the Buddha."
The woman, out of affection for Ānanda, immediately paid him homage.
At that time, the World-Honored One transformed himself into three youths, each fifteen years of age, with countenances so upright and handsome that they surpassed all human beings in the world.

Upon seeing this, the woman’s body and mind were filled with joy; in order to transform the youth, she prostrated herself with her five limbs touching the ground, paid homage to him, and said: "O Noble Sir!

This house of mine is like the Goddess Guṇakāśikā, adorned with various jewels through the sovereign power of my merit. I now offer my body, along with my male and female servants, to you, O Noble Sir, to serve as attendants. If you would deign to accept me, I shall provide everything according to your wishes, without any sense of attachment or stinginess.
Having spoken these words, the conjured man sat upon the couch. Before even a meal had been consumed, the woman approached him and said:
"O Noble Sir! I pray that you fulfill my wish."
The transformed person did not refuse, but approached him immediately according to his desire.
For one day and one night, his mind felt no weariness;
by the second day, his feelings of affection gradually subsided.
When the third day arrived, she said to him:
"O Noble One! Please arise and eat."
The conjured person immediately rose up, his entreaties never ceasing; the girl felt weary and remorseful, and said to him:
"O man! Are you truly such an extraordinary being?"
The transformed man said, "According to the custom of my former lives, whenever I have intercourse with a woman, I must wait twelve days before I may rest.
Upon hearing these words, the woman was like a person choking on food; she could neither spit it out nor swallow it down, and her body suffered pain as if being pounded by a pestle.
On the fourth day, she felt as if she were being crushed by a carriage;
on the fifth day, it was as if iron balls had entered her body;
on the sixth day, all her limbs and joints ached as if arrows were piercing her heart, and the woman thought to herself:

"I have heard people say that the Prince of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu possesses a body of purple-gold color and the thirty-two marks; out of compassion for those in blindness and darkness, he rescues those in suffering. He always dwells in this city, constantly performing meritorious deeds, and emits golden light to save all people. For what reason does he not come today to rescue me?"
Having formed this thought, he was filled with remorse and reproached himself:

"From this day until the end of my life, I shall never again crave form; I would rather dwell in the same lair as tigers, wolves, lions, and other fierce beasts than, out of craving for sensual desire, undergo such suffering."
Having spoken these words, she rose again to eat and drink; as they walked and sat together, there was nothing he could do about her. The transformed man also became angry and said:

"Shame! You wicked woman, you have ruined my business. It would be better for me to die early than to remain in this same body and place with you. If my parents and kinsmen come to search for me, where shall I hide myself?"
"I would rather die than endure such shame.
The woman said, "I have no use for this wretched thing; you may die as you please."

At that time, the emanated person took a knife and pierced his own neck; blood flowed in torrents, drenching the woman's body as it pooled on the ground. The woman could not withstand it, nor could she escape it.
After two days of death, the body becomes livid, blackish, and foul-smelling;
on the third day, it swells;

on the fourth day, it rots and breaks open, with excrement, urine, various worms, splattered blood, and pus smeared all over the woman's body; the woman feels extreme loathing and revulsion, yet she cannot leave it.
By the fifth day, the skin and flesh gradually rot;
by the sixth day, the flesh has completely fallen away;
by the seventh day, there remains only stinking bones, as sticky as glue or lac, adhering to the woman's body.
The woman made this vow:
"If the various devas, as well as the rishis, and the son of King Śuddhodana can spare me from this suffering, I shall take all the precious treasures in this house and bestow them as gifts."

While he was reflecting thus, the Buddha, accompanied by Ānanda and Nanda, proceeded toward this woman’s tower. Śakra stood before him, holding a precious incense burner and burning priceless incense; Brahmā followed behind, holding a great jeweled parasol. Immeasurable devas played celestial drums and music. The Buddha emitted his usual radiance, which illuminated heaven and earth, so that the entire assembly beheld the Tathāgata approaching.

At that time, when the woman saw the Buddha, she felt deep shame and remorse; having no place to hide the bones, she took various white cotton cloths and immeasurable quantities of incense to wrap around the putrid bones, yet the stench remained as before and could not be concealed.

When the woman saw the World-Honored One, she paid homage to the Buddha; out of shame and remorse, her body became transparent so that her bones were visible, and the stinking bone suddenly appeared upon her back. Overwhelmed with extreme shame and remorse, she shed tears and said:
"The Tathāgata’s merit and compassion are immeasurable. If you can enable me to leave this suffering behind, I pray to become your disciple, my mind never to retreat."
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the stinking bones did not appear. The woman was filled with great joy; she prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All that I now cherish, I shall give as an offering to the Buddha.”
The Buddha offered a blessing with a flowing and resonant Brahma-voice; hearing this blessing, the woman’s heart was filled with great joy, and she immediately attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

When the five hundred handmaidens heard the Buddha’s voice, they all resolved to attain the unsurpassed mind of *bodhicitta*. Upon witnessing the Buddha’s supernatural transformations, an immeasurable multitude of Brahma-devas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Among the sons of gods led by Śakra, some resolved to attain *bodhicitta*, while others attained the stage of *anāgāmin*.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the past, when I first attained enlightenment, I was staying by the side of the Nairañjanā River near the city of Gayā. There were five Nirgranthas there;
the first Nirgrantha was named Sājāta, who had a following of five hundred disciples."
Each of the other four had two hundred and fifty disciples.

At that time, the Nirgranthas, who claimed to have attained the Way, came to where I was; they encircled my body with their own bodies seven times, approached me, spread grass down, and sat, saying these words: "Gautama!..."

"Because I am free from desire, the marks of the holy life (brahmacarya) are perfected; my faculty of the body is thus capable like that of Maheśvara. My supernormal power now exceeds that of the śramaṇas by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; while the śramaṇa creates one, I shall create two."

He immediately manifested a tree from the earth, coiled his body around the tree seven times, and caused the tree to emit clouds and mist like the breath of a dragon king; then, raising his hand, he cried out in a loud voice: "Gautama!
“My manifestation of the marks of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is verified in this way; you call yourself a man, a great being (*mahāpuruṣa*), but by what do you provide proof?
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a jeweled collar. On both ends of the collar were fourteen pearls, and each bright pearl emitted a thousand rays of light.

Each ray of light transformed into a manifested Buddha who performed eighteen miraculous transformations while standing in mid-air. As the World-Honored One displayed this manifestation, he stood inverted in the air with his feet upon the collar.
At that time, from the two feet of the Buddha, a thousand lotus flowers emerged; each lotus flower possessed ten trillion rays of light;
within each ray of light were ten billion jeweled terraces;
and within each terrace were countless manifested Buddhas.
Each of the manifested Buddhas grasped one of his own feet, just as if rolling up a piece of lapis lazuli so that the foot was no longer visible.

All the manifested Buddhas and Śākyamuni likewise suspended one foot each and remained poised upside down in mid-air. Only the Nirgranthas saw the Buddha standing upside down; however, immeasurable devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, and spirits saw the World-Honored Buddha sitting peacefully in the lecture hall, expounding the Great Dharma—namely, the teachings of signlessness, selflessness, and so forth.
At that time, a voice from space addressed the Nirgranthas:
"The Buddha has already performed one; you may perform two.

Thereupon, the Nirgranthas leaped up by themselves, grasping tree branches with their hands and standing while clinging to the trees; yet, despite exhausting all their Nirgrantha arts, they were unable to stand on their heads.
The tree deity manifested her form and struck him on the ear with her palm, scolding him: "Madman!
You are like a tiny insect to dare to fight against the lion, the king of beasts!"
"You previously shouted loudly:
'If the Buddha acts as one, I shall act as two.
Now that the Buddha has already established himself in great supernormal power (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), why do you not do so?"

After the tree deity had finished reviling him, the earth deity Dṛḍhā emerged from the ground and stood in mid-air. She bound the feet of the Nirgrantha with great iron chains and suspended him upside down in the air. Five yakṣas then struck him with clubs. In his intense agony, the Nirgrantha struggled to pull himself free and fell to the ground; before he even reached the ground, another Nirgrantha cried out: "Namo Buddhāya! (Homage to the Buddha!)
The World-Honored One received the Nirgranthas with his hand so that their bodies felt no pain.
When the Nirgranthas had reached the ground, their jealousy did not cease; they spoke to the Earth Deity, saying:

"You have no heart of compassion and show partiality toward Gautama. Because of your past sins, you have received the body of a yakṣa here beneath the earth. Today, you again lack universal compassion and love, but instead afflict us for the sake of Gautama alone."
Then the goddess of the Ganges flew up into the air, grasped a large rock in her hand, and said:

"Nirgranthas! You fools who consume cow dung, smear your heads with lime, cause your hair to fall out, and wander naked without shame—you are like donkeys and horses, and like poor dragons that cannot provide any moisture or benefit."
"The Tathāgata is the Buddha-sun that shines universally upon all; how can you now, with a body of darkness, contend for light with the sun?
When the Water Deity had spoken these words, he exhorted the World-Honored One to subdue the Nirgranthas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Nirgranthas:

"You do not know the physical form of the Tathāgata; if you wish to see it, observe it as you please. Throughout kalpas of accumulated practice in the Brahma-faring, while I was still a householder, I harbored no thoughts of improper desire. Because my mind was untainted and free from worldly entanglements, I have obtained this retribution. Just as a precious horse may appear or disappear unpredictably, I shall now manifest a small portion of my body for you."

At that time, the World-Honored One descended from the sky and immediately manifested upon the ground four bodies of water like the four great oceans. Within these four seas stood Mount Sumeru; beneath the mountain, the Buddha lay flat on his back, emitting golden light. This radiance was so brilliant that it dazzled the eyes of the devas. From his secret organ (aśvakośa), he slowly produced [light] that circled the mountain seven times like a golden lotus. These lotuses followed one after another, ascending as far as the Brahma-world. From the Buddha’s body emerged a hundred million nayutas of various jeweled lotuses, which, like floral banners, covered and concealed the secret organ.

This Lotus Banner has ten billion tiers; in each tier are hundreds of thousands of immeasurable transformation Buddhas, each of whom is attended by ten billion Bodhisattvas and countless bhikṣus as their attendants. These transformation Buddhas emit light that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions.
Upon seeing this, the Nirgranthas were greatly startled and their hearts submitted in reverence, thinking:

"The Buddha’s marks of pure conduct are thus inconceivable; his form is not ugly but is like a lotus flower. We now prostrate ourselves before the ocean of the Buddha’s merit; the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless and inexhaustible—may he accept our repentance and take us into his care."
Having spoken these words, the five hundred Nirgranthas joined their palms, pressed their hands together, and knelt long upon the ground,
requesting the Buddha for ordination. The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣus!"
The Buddha commanded Kāśyapa to prepare robes for him; at that time, Kāśyapa went to the place of the seer and said to the great seer:
"Today the World-Honored One has subdued all the Nirgranthas!"
"I only pray that you, O Rishi, will grant me a few garments.
Then the various ṛṣis took fine tree bark and tāla leaves and sewed them together to make clothes.
At that time, the teacher of the ṛṣis, named Jyotiṣmati, joined his palms in reverence and addressed his disciples:
"The Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable and his great vows are all-pervasive; he has thus accepted and taken under his care even those who cling to false views.
I ought to prepare robes for those who are naked, and by revering the Jewel of the Buddha, I may likewise be liberated from all sufferings."
Having spoken these words, they followed behind Kāśyapa and approached the World-Honored One.
The five hundred rishis saw a lotus pedestal emerge from the Buddha’s body, like a multitude of lotuses surrounding Mount Sumeru and ascending as far as the Brahma world.
At that time, when the various rishis had witnessed this event, they rejoiced and, with palms joined in reverence, paid homage to the World-Honored One.

They gazed intently at the World-Honored One without averting their eyes for a moment. Seeing the light of the white tuft between the Buddha’s eyebrows curling to the right, and beholding all the marks of the Buddha’s body, they reflected:

"These marks and signs must have arisen from the pure *dānapāramitā* of previous lives—characterized by being unbound and unattached, without self or agency, without mind or consciousness, without person or thing, and without giver or receiver—and they also arise following the great wisdom of emptiness, the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is equal and signless in all things."
Having contemplated this meaning, he immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Before the five hundred Nirgranthas had even raised their heads after donning their saṃghāṭī robes and paying homage to the Buddha, they immediately attained the path of Arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges (*traividya*), the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Each of the Nigaṇṭhas made a vow that they would cross over [to liberation].

When these five hundred Nigaṇṭhas manifested such signs, immeasurable multitudes of devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, seeing the pure fruit of the Buddha’s Brahma-conduct, felt joy in body and mind and resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the assemblies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, śramaṇas, and brahmins will ask the Blessed One: ‘In past lives, what was the fruit of the pure and desireless cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya) that he attained?’”
You should answer:

"The Buddha possesses the horse-king’s *kośa* mark, which is level with his body, sevenfold and full; like a vajra vessel, it is pure both inside and out. This mark has appeared for the sake of delivering sentient beings, and the clouds of radiant, wondrous lotuses of the transformation Buddhas are immeasurable in number. Such a body as this is born from the unblemished, peaceful, and well-maintained precepts, wisdom, and *śīla-pāramitā* throughout countless lifetimes."
The Buddha commanded Ānanda: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
all the disciples of the Buddha who wish to contemplate the Tathāgata’s mark of the sheathed male organ (kośagatavastiguhyatā) should perform this contemplation."
To contemplate in this manner is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the Buddha’s disciples focus their minds on right mindfulness and contemplate the characteristics of the Buddha’s pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), the transformation Buddhas, and his radiance, they will constantly see the Buddhas of the ten directions in their dreams. Such a person will always cultivate pure conduct throughout successive lifetimes and shall eliminate the sins of birth and death for two hundred thousand kalpas.

When these marks were being described, eight thousand yakṣas among the assembly of yakṣas rejoiced in body and mind; they praised the Tathāgata’s immeasurable virtues and immediately, at that very moment, resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Scroll Eight.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: On Past Deeds (9) Chapter Eight: On Past Deeds The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

“The Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics. His body is of golden radiance, and from each ray of light issue infinitely many transformation Buddhas. From every pore of his body, all manner of manifestations appear; yet even this is but a most concise summary of the Buddha’s physical form. Now, for the sake of the great assembly gathered here and for King Śuddhodana, I shall briefly describe these marks and characteristics.”

The Buddha was born among humans to manifest the same activities as human beings; because he shared these human characteristics, he is said to possess the thirty-two marks. Because he surpasses all devas, he is said to possess the eighty secondary signs. For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he is said to possess eighty-four thousand excellent marks and signs; yet these are merely the Buddha’s manifest marks and signs, for his true marks and signs are such that when I first attained the Way at the site of enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha, I already extensively expounded them in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for the great bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Bhadramukha.

The reason this Honored Dharma is explained in brief is for the sake of ordinary people and the four classes of disciples who slander the Vaipulya sutras, commit the five heinous crimes, violate the four grave prohibitions, steal the property of the Saṃgha, engage in sexual misconduct with bhikṣuṇīs, break the eightfold precepts and fasts, perform various evil deeds, and hold all manner of false views. If such persons as these can, with a sincere heart, for one day and one night, focus their mindfulness before them and contemplate even a single mark or excellence of the Buddha Tathāgata, all their evil karmic obstructions will be completely extinguished.

For this reason, the Tathāgata is named Bhagavat; he is named Arhat; he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is named Sun of Merit; he is named Full Moon of Wisdom; he is named Pool of Coolness; he is named Jewel that Removes Sin; he is named Treasury of Radiance; he is named Mountain of Wisdom; he is named River of the Precepts; he is named Guide on the Path of Delusion; he is named Lamp of False Views; he is named Destroyer of the Thieves of Affliction; he is named Father and Mother of All Sentient Beings; and he is named the Great Refuge.

If there are those who take refuge in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, or even those who merely invoke his name, they will eliminate the heavy obstructions of afflictions accumulated over hundreds of thousands of kalpas; how much more so for those who, with a correct mind, cultivate the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the past, throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Tathāgata burned the fuel of afflictions with the fire of wisdom and cultivated the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) without realizing it at an improper time. For this reason, he has obtained such supreme marks; within each single mark there are immeasurable transformation Buddhas, let alone in many marks."
If one can fix the mind to contemplate a single pore, such a person is said to be practicing the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Because of this mindfulness of the Buddha, the Buddhas of the ten directions will always stand before them and preach the True Dharma for them; such a person is thus able to give rise to the lineage of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time—how much more so when they fully possess the mindfulness of the Buddha’s physical body?

“The Tathāgata also possesses immeasurable dharmakāya, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the samādhis, the liberations, and the various supernormal powers; such sublime states are not the sphere of what you ordinary persons can study, but you should simply give rise to thoughts of sympathetic joy with a profound mind.”
Having given rise to this perception, one should further fix the mind upon the merits of the Buddha. As for these merits of the Buddha, they are:

morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the golden body with its thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness.

If there are sentient beings who hear but once of the Buddha’s body—its merits, marks, and signs, and its radiance—they shall not fall into the evil realms for billions upon billions of kalpas; they shall not be born in places of wrong views or impurity, but shall always attain right view and cultivate it diligently without ceasing.
"If merely hearing the name of the Buddha yields such merit, how much more so for those who focus their thoughts upon the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha?

At that moment, as the World-Honored One spoke these words, a pavilion made of the seven treasures appeared in the void; atop each pavilion were billions of jeweled canopies, and the heavens rained down precious flowers as an offering to Śākyamuni Buddha.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī sat cross-legged within a jeweled pavilion, and together with ten billion bodhisattvas dwelling in mid-air, he praised them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
Śākyamuni, World-Honored One of Great Compassion!

You have spoken of the marks and signs of the Buddha’s body, displayed the majestic deportment of the Buddha, and manifested the radiance of the Buddha to reveal all the transformation Buddhas, acting as the cause for future beings of ignorance and folly who do not see the Buddha to actually behold him.
Excellent, Ānanda! Son of the Dharma, endowed with compassion!
Your name is "Joy."

Rely on the names to ascertain the reality; uphold the Buddha’s words well and be careful not to forget or lose them. Future sentient beings who hear what you say will see the Buddha; those who contemplate this meaning will fully behold the subtle and wondrous form-body of the Buddha.

At that time, after Mañjuśrī had spoken these words, he and his retinue of bodhisattvas descended from the sky, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"O Son of the Buddha!
When you were seated here and performing this contemplation, lotus flowers sprang up from the earth, equal in length and breadth, filling one yojana."
Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas sat upon lotus flowers. At that time, having finished sitting, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now wish to speak of the causal conditions of my own past births; I only pray that the World-Honored One will empower me with his majestic spiritual authority!
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Speak quickly without hesitation!"
Mañjuśrī addressed the great assembly and spoke to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Ānanda, you should know that I recall, from incalculable kalpas in the past—indeed, many times more than that, beyond thought and measure, during asaṃkhyeya kalpas—a Buddha who appeared in that world named Ratnatejas Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

When that Buddha appeared in the world, the depravity of sentient beings was no different from that of today; that World-Honored Buddha was likewise sixteen feet tall with a body the color of purple gold, and he preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles just as Śākyamuni does.

At that time, there was a great elder in that land named Sarvadatta. The elder had a son named Śīlarakṣita; while he was still in his mother’s womb, because of the mother’s faith and reverence, she had already received the Three Refuges on his behalf.
Once the child was born and had reached the age of eight, his parents invited the Buddha to their home to provide offerings.

When the boy saw the Buddha walking with peaceful and slow steps, with lotuses springing up beneath his feet and emitting great radiance, he was filled with joy and prostrated before the Buddha. Having prostrated, he gazed intently at him without averting his eyes for even a moment; having seen the Buddha but once, he was immediately able to eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas.

From that time forward, he constantly encountered as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in ten billion nayutas of Ganges Rivers. In the presence of these Buddhas, he planted the roots of all manner of virtues; all those World-Honored Ones preached this very Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha and praised the light of the mark of the great man’s white tuft of hair, exhorting many sentient beings to repent and maintain mindfulness.
"After this has passed, he will again encounter a Buddha named Maṇiprabha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!"
When the Buddha Maṇiprabha appeared in the world, he constantly emitted radiance to perform buddha-work and deliver sentient beings.
Thus, twenty thousand buddhas all shared the same name: Maṇiprabha.
At that time, all the World-Honored Ones received and guided sentient beings with the subtle, wondrous radiance of their transformation buddhas.
Next, there was a buddha named Candana-maṇi-prabha, fully endowed with the ten titles;

likewise, there were ten billion such buddhas, all named Maṇi-prabha. By the power of their vows, these World-Honored Ones used the light from the white tuft of hair between their eyebrows to protect sentient beings and eliminate all their transgressions.
"Furthermore, there appeared a Buddha named Candanasāgara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; likewise, one million Buddhas all shared the same name, Candanasāgara."
These World-Honored Ones! They transformed and delivered sentient beings through the light of the *svastika* seal (*śrīvatsa*) upon their chests.

At that time, the youth attended these Buddhas personally, without a moment’s interval, prostrating, making offerings, and joining his palms in gazing upon the Buddhas. By the power of the causes and conditions of thus contemplating the merits of the Buddhas, he further encountered ten million *asaṃkhyeya* Buddhas. These World-Honored Ones likewise transformed and delivered sentient beings through the radiance of their physical forms. From then on, he immediately attained hundreds of thousands of billions of *buddhānusmṛti-samādhis* (Buddha-remembrance samādhis) and obtained ten million *asaṃkhyeya* *vartanī-dhāraṇīs*. Having attained these, the Buddhas appeared before him and preached the Dharma of signlessness (*animitta*), and in a mere instant, he attained the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

"At that time, because that youth received the three refuges and, having prostrated once to the Buddha, contemplated the Buddha’s marks with a mind free from weariness, he encountered countless Buddhas by virtue of this cause and condition; how much more so for one who fixes their mindfulness and fully contemplates the Buddha’s form-body?"
"Was that boy at that time anyone else?
He is none other than my own self here now!
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!
Because you once prostrated to the Buddha in the past, you have encountered this many countless Buddhas; how much more so for my disciples in the future who diligently contemplate the Buddha?”
The Buddha commanded Ānanda:

"Bear Manjusri’s words and proclaim them throughout the great assembly and to all sentient beings of future ages: 'If there are those who can prostrate, those who can recollect the Buddha, or those who can contemplate the Buddha, you should know that such persons are no different from Manjusri himself. When they cast off their bodies in another life, Manjusri and the other great Bodhisattvas shall serve as their preceptors.'"

When these words were spoken, there was among the assembly of bodhisattvas a son of the Buddha named Vasumitra. He rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha seven times, and paid respectful homage. He also prostrated at the feet of Mañjuśrī and scattered celestial māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjūṣaka flowers over the Buddha, as well as over Mañjuśrī, and also over the Venerable Ānanda.
These celestial flowers shall transform above the Buddha into flower pedestals, within which the Buddhas of the ten directions sit in the full lotus posture.
The Buddha Śubhavyūha of the east addresses the great assembly, saying:

"You should know that I recall that in the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. When that Buddha appeared in the world, he likewise preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles as is done today."

At that time, in the world of that Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who had nine disciples. Together with his disciples, he went to a Buddhist stūpa to pay homage to a Buddha image. There they saw a precious image, magnificent and beautiful to behold; having paid their respects, they gazed at it intently and praised it with verses. Then, according to the length of their respective lifespans, each passed away.

Having passed away, he was reborn in the eastern buddha-field of the Buddha Jewel Majestic Virtuous Sovereign (*Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja*). He manifested through miraculous birth, sitting cross-legged upon a great lotus flower. From that time forth, he constantly encountered immeasurable buddhas, where he purely cultivated the brahma-faring. He attained the ocean-like samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha; having attained this, the buddhas appeared before him and immediately bestowed upon him the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that he would become a buddha at will throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha of Good Virtue in the east is none other than my own self!

The Buddha of Sandalwood Virtue in the south, the Buddha of Immeasurable Radiance in the west, the Buddha of Marked Virtue in the north, the Buddha of Sorrowless Virtue in the southeast, the Buddha of Jewel Bestowal in the southwest, the Buddha of Flower Virtue in the northwest, the Buddha of Practice of the Three Vehicles in the northeast, the Buddha of Vast Multitude of Virtues above, and the Buddha of Bright Virtue below—these ten World-Honored Buddhas attained Buddhahood in the ten directions solely because they offered a single verse of praise at a stupa. Could these have been anyone else? No, they were not.
"We are the Buddhas of the ten directions!

At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions descended from the sky, emitting a thousand rays of light and manifesting the radiance of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) upon their physical bodies. Each sat upon the seat of Śākyamuni Buddha and, extending his right hand, stroked Ānanda’s head, saying:
"O Son of the Dharma!

Your teacher, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, through hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices and immeasurable diligence, sought the wisdom of a Buddha and attained this body as its fruit. I shall now describe for you his radiance and physical marks; you should uphold the Buddha’s words for the sake of future generations, and extensively expound upon the contemplation of the Buddha-dharma and the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* for the great assemblies of devas, nāgas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Having spoken these words, they then inquired after the well-being of Śākyamuni Buddha, asking,
"Are you dwelling in peace and security?
Once they had made their inquiries, they emitted great radiance and each returned to their own land.
At that time, the great assembly saw the Buddhas of the ten directions and the various bodhisattvas, as well as their lands, large and small, like seeing myriad forms and images in a clear mirror.

The flowers scattered by the Bodhisattva Wealth Chief, upon reaching the crown of Mañjuśrī, were transformed into a four-pillared jeweled pavilion. Within that pavilion sat four World-Honored Ones, radiating bodily light and sitting in solemn dignity: Akṣobhya in the east, Ratnaketu in the south, Amitāyus in the west, and Gadgadasvara in the north.

At that time, the four World-Honored Ones scattered golden lotus flowers over Śākyamuni Buddha; before they had reached him, they transformed into a flower canopy with ten trillion petals. Within each and every petal were hundreds of thousands of manifested Buddhas, and these manifested Buddhas emitted light.

Within the light there were also countless manifested Buddhas. Once the jeweled canopy was completed, four World-Honored Buddhas descended from the sky and sat upon Śākyamuni Buddha’s seat, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Śākyamuni! You are indeed able, for the sake of sentient beings in the turbid and evil world of future ages, to expound upon the mark of the white tuft of light between the eyebrows of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, enabling all sentient beings to extinguish their transgressions and faults.

Why is this? I recall that in the past, under the Buddha King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*), I left the household life to study the Path. At that time, there were four bhikṣus who were my fellow students; we practiced and studied the True Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. However, our minds were shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*), and we were unable to firmly uphold the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma. Having committed many unwholesome karmas, we were destined to fall into the evil realms.
A voice from the sky spoke, saying:
"O you four bhikṣus!

Although the Tathāgata Śūnyarāja has entered parinirvāṇa, regarding the offenses you have committed as being beyond salvation, you should now enter the stūpa to behold the Buddha; it will be no different from when the Buddha was still in the world."
Following the voice from the void, I entered the stupa and beheld the image between the eyebrows, where a tuft of white hair was visible; I immediately thought:
"How does this differ from the radiant physical body of the Tathāgata when he was in the world?"
"O Buddha, Possessor of the Marks of a Great Man, I pray that you may remove my transgressions.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground like a great mountain collapsing, repenting of all his sins while contemplating the space between the Buddha’s eyebrows.

By virtue of these causes and conditions for repentance, from this point forward for eighty billion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I shall not fall into the evil realms. In every birth, I shall constantly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions; under those Buddhas, I shall receive and uphold the profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. Having attained this samādhi, all the Buddhas will appear before me and bestow upon me their prophetic declaration (*vyākaraṇa*).
In the east there is a land called Abhirati; in that realm there is a Buddha named Akṣobhya, who is none other than this first bhikṣu!
In the south there is a land called Saṃtuṣita; the Buddha there is named Ratnaketu, who is none other than this second bhikṣu!
In the western direction there is a land called Sukhāvatī; the Buddha there is named Amitāyus—this is the third bhikṣu!
In the northern direction there is a land called Padmavyūha; the Buddha there is named Sutejoghoṣa—this is the fourth bhikṣu!
At that time, the four Tathāgatas each extended their right hands, stroked Ānanda’s head, and said:
“O Dharma Prince!
"You shall uphold the Buddha’s words and extensively expound them for the sake of all sentient beings in the future.
Having spoken this three times, they each emitted radiance and returned to their own lands.

The flowers scattered by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra that remained above Ānanda transformed into clouds of flowers that filled the ten directions. Within each cloud were countless transformation Buddhas, each extending his right hand to stroke Ānanda’s head and declare:
“O Prince of the Dharma!
All the emanation bodies of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are just like us, equal and without distinction.

You have now seen them with your own eyes; you should extensively explain and analyze this for all sentient beings of the future, so that all those beings may practice the recollection of the Buddha.”

If one recollects the Buddha, they shall behold the transformation buddha no differently than they do now; if there are sentient beings who hear what you have spoken, they will thereby see the Buddha and eliminate immeasurable sins.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dhanapati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, also named Śākyamuni."
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a prince named Suvarṇadhvaja who was arrogant, held false views, and did not believe in the True Dharma.
A bhikṣu known as Samādhisvatantra said to the prince:
"In this world, there is a Buddha image adorned with various jewels that is exceedingly lovely; you should enter the stūpa for a moment to behold the form of the Buddha."
Then the prince followed the words of his good friend and entered the stupa to behold the image. Seeing the marks and signs of the image, he said to the bhikṣu:
"If the Buddha image is already so majestic and dignified, how much more so must the Buddha’s true body be?"
Having spoken these words, the bhikṣu said:
"If you are unable to prostrate before this image now, you should instead recite: 'Namo Buddha!'"
At that time, the prince joined his palms in reverent salutation and cried out,
“Namo Buddha! Upon returning to the palace,
he focused his mind exclusively on the image within the stupa, and during the final watch of the night, he saw the image of the Buddha in a dream.

Because he saw the Buddha image, his heart was filled with great joy; he abandoned wrong views and took refuge in the Triple Gem. At the end of his life, due to the merit and causal conditions of having previously entered the stupa and recited "Namo Buddha," he constantly encountered nine million billion nayutas of Buddhas. In the presence of these Buddhas, he always applied himself with diligent vigor and attained the profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. By the power of this samādhi, the Buddhas appeared before him and conferred predictions upon him. From that time until today, for a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he has not fallen into the evil realms, and has now attained the profound *śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
"The prince at that time was none other than I, Dhanapāla, the foremost in wealth!
Thus did these and other great bodhisattvas, immeasurable in number, each recount their own past causes, which were attained through mindfulness of the Buddha, as described in the *Jātaka-sūtra*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:

"I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Candanaguha-vyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān!

Endowed with the ten titles, he dwelt among the various virtuous mountains of Jambudvīpa; within those mountains, he left the household life to study the Way and, after a full seven kalpas, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, there were two youths in that world who, insatiable in their learning, traveled through the kingdoms inquiring of various brahmins.
At that moment, a brahmin named Raudrakṣa addressed them, saying: "O youths!"
"In this world there is a Buddha named Candanaguhya; you two may go to his place and seek the Dharma of debating doctrines.
