At that time, the two youths—the elder named Sarvadarśanābhirāma and the second youth named Parākramasaṃnāha—went together to the Buddha’s abode, each holding celestial flowers which they scattered over the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in tranquil meditative concentration, entering the Samādhirāja-samādhi with body and mind unmoving; he universally manifested the form-bodies of all Buddhas, with immeasurable radiance as described in the Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, when the two youths beheld the physical body of the Buddha and his radiance, they immediately transcended the karmic offenses of birth and death accumulated over *koṭi-nayuta-gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-asamkhyeya* kalpas. They constantly encountered immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and in the presence of those Buddhas, they practiced the profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. They directly beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions, who expounded for them the Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression.
At that time, was the first youth anyone else?
He is none other than the present Maitreya Bodhisattva!
The second youth is none other than I, Śākyamuni!

I and the bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa once, in the past, heard this ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha’s Transformation of the Form Body from the presence of the Buddha Candanaguhya. By the power of the merit from these causes and conditions, we have transcended the offenses of birth and death for nine hundred trillion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and shall successively attain Buddhahood within this Bhadrakalpa; finally, the Tathāgata Ruci will also preach the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha at this very place.

The Buddha told Ānanda: “This Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha is the medicine for all sentient beings who have committed offenses; it is the protection for those who have broken the precepts; it is the guide for those who have lost the Way; it is the eye for those in blindness and darkness; it is the wisdom for the ignorant; it is the lamp for those in the gloom; it is the valiant general amidst the thieves of affliction; it is the playground of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; and it is the place where the great samādhis, such as Śūraṅgama and others, first arise.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You must now uphold this well and be careful not to forget or lose it. The Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—all these World-Honored Ones have taught this very same *Nien-fo Samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi). By the power of this *Nien-fo Samādhi*, I and the great Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa attained the sovereign majesty and spiritual power of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Likewise, the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions have all realized *samyak-saṃbodhi* through this Dharma."
At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the Venerable Ānanda personally recollected the events of countless kalpas from his past lives and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, countless billions of kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One named Candrasūryapradīpa, who was fully endowed with the ten titles.”

In that world, I saw the Buddha-Tathāgata emitting a great radiance; that light shone everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions, making them all the color of gold. Within each ray of light were various transformation Buddhas. Having seen this, my body and mind were filled with joy, and I cried out: "Namo Buddhāya!"

"From that time forth, I have constantly encountered hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and heard their preaching of the Dharma; just as water poured from one vessel into another, I have retained it in my memory without forgetting. Therefore, I am now able to see the World-Honored One and personally attend upon him."
Having spoken these words, he recited various verses in praise of the subtle and wondrous form-bodies of all Buddhas.

At that time, countless Buddhas appeared in the air, all manifesting radiance; from every pore of their bodies issued transformation-Buddhas identical to Śākyamuni, all of whom addressed Ānanda, saying:
"O Son of the Dharma!

"You should now uphold this Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha and explain it in detail for the sake of the entire great assembly, causing all ordinary beings to plant the causes for seeing the Buddha.
Having spoken these words, the manifested Buddha disappeared.

At that time, for the sake of entrusting this matter, the World-Honored One stood poised in mid-air with sovereign dignity, performing the eighteen transformations to manifest all-encompassing light, and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who wish to contemplate the Buddha, they should contemplate him in this manner."
When the Buddha spoke these words, twelve billion devaputras attained the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi and received their prediction of enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha.
Chapter Nine: Contemplating the Image (The Ninth Chapter on Contemplating the Image).
At that time, there was in the assembly a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Maitreya. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and prostrated himself before the Buddha.
He removed the necklaces from his body and offered them to the Tathāgata; he then scattered pearl flowers over the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and Mañjuśrī.
The necklaces he scattered spontaneously leaped up and remained suspended in mid-air, transforming into eighty trillion jeweled terraces.
Within each terrace were ten billion Śākyamuni Buddhas, all of whom emitted—
The Light-body that Universally Manifests Colors appears within all the wondrous forms of mountains, forests, rivers, oceans, and all sentient beings;
it likewise manifests within the stars, the sun and moon, all Mount Sumerus, and the palaces of the devas, nāgas, and spirits.
It also manifests the five supernatural powers of the rishis, their billions of incantations, and the ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths of false views.
Medical arts, crafts, technical skills, and literary compositions—all these matters are manifested within a single hair;
even those things longed for by worldly beings of wrong views and defiled desires likewise emerge spontaneously from the radiance.

The hells, the animal realm, the various asuras, the eight difficulties, the four inversions, and all such inauspicious matters—as well as the beauty or ugliness of the retributions one receives—are likewise naturally perceived and known through these signs.
The pearl flowers scattered that remained above the Buddha transformed into ten billion white rays of light;
those that remained above Mañjuśrī transformed into hundreds of thousands of billions of subtle and wondrous colored lights.

These various radiances interlace with one another like the coiled bodies of great nāga kings facing each other. Within each ray of light are five hundred million jewel-lights, clearly demarcated like the cut-and-sewn patches of a *saṃghāṭī* robe; they are held together by golden light as seams, and at the points where the threads enter and exit, four-jeweled flowers arise. Within each flower, a Bodhisattva of the Bhadrakalpa sits in the full lotus posture.

The Buddhas of the ten directions and their emanation-Buddhas sit upon precious lotuses, preaching the profound *pratyutpanna-samādhi* for the great Bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa. They also praise the primary causal conditions for contemplating the Buddha, namely the *samādhi of non-existence*, the realm of mindfulness of the Buddha, and the diamond-like concentration.
Having spoken this Dharma, all the Tathāgatas each extended their right hands, stroked Ānanda’s crown, and said:
“Son of the Buddha!
You should now skillfully uphold the Buddha’s words and be careful not to forget or lose them.”
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

We pray that the World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, will take pity on all sentient beings in future ages who will commit unwholesome deeds; for when the Buddha is not present, upon what can they rely to eliminate their transgressions?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"Ajita! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!"

After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, there will be many sentient beings who, because they do not see the Buddha, commit various evil deeds. Such persons as these should be led to contemplate the image; for if they contemplate the image, it is no different from contemplating my own body.
When these words were spoken, flowers appeared in the air, and the Buddhas of the ten directions stood in the sky with their hands joined in reverent salutation, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha!"

You have asked an excellent question. Only Śākyamuni, the savior from the sufferings of the world, has taught the method of contemplating the image for the sake of sentient beings who are blind and ignorant at the end of the age; now is precisely the right time, so do not harbor any doubts.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again earnestly and repeatedly exhorted the World-Honored One to teach the method of contemplating the image.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted his usual radiance, which illuminated the Nyagrodha Monastery and the lands of the ten directions, making them all golden in color. By the Buddha’s spiritual power, this golden ground was divided into two parts; within each part, five hundred billion Buddhas emerged from the lower realms, appearing spontaneously and standing in mid-air with palms joined, praising Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, saying:
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha!"

"Thus, out of compassion for future sentient beings who will be born in the age of the final dharma, you should entreat the World-Honored One to explain the characteristics of the contemplation of the image.
When all these manifested Buddhas had spoken these words, they leaped into the void and performed the eighteen transformations.

Śākyamuni Buddha then smiled of his own accord; as he smiled, a great lotus flower emerged from his mouth. That flower possessed a radiance like that of a hundred billion suns, moons, and stars combined. Amidst the various constellations and moons, there were a hundred billion transformation Buddhas, sitting cross-legged upon lion thrones.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!

The Tathāgata now, for the sake of sentient beings of the future world who suffer the five kinds of suffering, bhikṣus who violate the prohibitions, unwholesome and evil persons, those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma, and those who practice the sixteen kinds of evil disciplines— for such as these, I shall preach the method for the eradication of their offenses."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these foolish people will be without support, without protection, and without a place of refuge. How can the Tathāgata preach the Dharma for the removal of their offenses?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In your mind, you have not yet fully understood the Buddha-dharma. As long as I am in the world, those who take refuge in me are said to take refuge in the Buddha, to take refuge in the Dharma, and to take refuge in the Saṃgha."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this age of turbidity and evil, if sentient beings wish to eliminate their transgressions, wish to attain the stages from srotāpanna to arhat in the present life, wish to give rise to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*, or wish to understand the twelve links of dependent origination, they should diligently practice the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

While the Tathāgata is in the world, sentient beings see him directly; yet even when they contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs and contemplate the Buddha’s radiance, they do not perceive them clearly. How much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha is no longer present—how should they contemplate him?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is present before one, one should contemplate the image of the Buddha.

Those who contemplate the Buddha-image—whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, or any sentient beings—who wish to contemplate the image, should first enter a Buddhist stūpa and cleanse the ground by smearing it with fine fragrant mud and various clay and earth. According to their capacity, they should burn incense and scatter flowers as offerings to the Buddha-image, recount their own transgressions and evils, pay homage to the Buddha, and repent. In this manner, they should subdue their minds for a period of seven days."

Furthermore, he went among the assembly to sweep and clean the monastic grounds, removing all filth and impurities, and confessed before the Sangha while prostrating at the feet of the monks; he continued in this manner for another seven days.
Thus making offerings with a mind free from weariness or fatigue, if he were a renunciant, he should recite the Vinaya until he had mastered it thoroughly;
if he were a layperson, he should provide filial support to his parents, show reverence to his teachers and elders, and discipline his mind to make it supple.
If the mind is not supple, one should forcefully subdue it to make the mind compliant and harmonious, just as one trains an elephant or a horse so that they do not escape control.
Once the mind is made pliant and obedient, dwell in a quiet place, burn various kinds of famous incense, pay homage to Śākyamuni, and speak these words:
"Namo to the Great Virtuous One, my Great Preceptor, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion!"
"I pray that you will shelter this disciple with clouds of compassion.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself on the ground before the image, weeping tears. Rising from the earth, he adjusted his robes and sat cross-legged, fixing his mindfulness on a single point according to the beings before him: he fixed his mind on the tip of his nose, fixed his mind on his forehead, and fixed his mind on his toes.

In this manner, bind your attention as you wish and fix it intently upon a single point; do not allow it to wander or cause the mind to waver. If the mind wavers, press the tongue against the palate, close the mouth and eyes, and sit upright with hands crossed. For one day up to seven days, bring the body to a state of stability; once the body is stable, then engage in visualization.
Regarding "joyfully practicing reverse contemplation":

one contemplates upward from the toes of the image's feet in succession. First, one contemplates the toes, binding the mind to them so that it is single-minded; for one full week, taking the Buddha’s toes as the object of focus, whether with eyes closed or open, one causes the golden image’s toes to be seen clearly.
Gradually, one further contemplates the two insteps of the feet until they are seen clearly.

Next, one contemplates the hocks of the deer-king; once the mind has become concentrated, one proceeds in order to the topknot. If the face is not clearly perceived while contemplating from the topknot, one should again repent and exert oneself with redoubled austerity. Because of the purity of the precepts, one beholds the face of the Buddha-image, as distinct and clear as a mirror of pure gold.

Having performed this contemplation, one contemplates the hair-tuft between the eyebrows, which is like a crystal bead, curling gracefully to the right. When this mark appears, one sees the Buddha’s eyebrows and eyes as if they were painted by a celestial artist. Having seen these things, one next contemplates the light of the crown of the head until it is clearly manifest; such a series of marks is called "contemplation in reverse order."
Regarding "contemplating the image in forward order":

one should fix the mind upon each of the *śrīvatsa* swirls on the crown of the head and observe them with clear discernment, until the mind clearly perceives the Buddha’s *śrīvatsa* swirls as black threads twisting and curling to the right.

Next, observe the Buddha’s face; having observed the Buddha’s face, observe the body in its entirety, gradually moving downward until reaching the feet. Repeat this process back and forth fourteen times in total. Observe a single image with such precision that it becomes perfectly clear. Once the observation of one image is complete, whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, you will constantly see the standing image before you.
When the single image is clearly perceived, further imagine a second image; having seen the two images, next imagine three, and so on up to ten, ensuring all are clearly perceived.
Having seen the ten images, imagine an entire room filled with Buddha images, with no gaps or vacancies between them.

Having filled the entire chamber, he further applied himself with diligence to burning incense and scattering flowers; he swept the stupas and smeared the ground with plaster, and bathed the assembly of monks. For his parents and teachers, he massaged their bodies to relieve them of fatigue, bathing them and anointing their limbs with fragrant oils. When begging for alms in the four directions and obtaining fine and delicious food, he first offered portions to his teachers and presented them to his parents.
Having performed these practices, he made this great vow:
"I now behold the Buddha; by means of this merit, I do not wish for the realms of humans, devas, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, but desire solely to seek the path to the Bodhi of a Buddha."
Having made this vow, if one truly seeks the Mahāyāna with a sincere heart, one should practice repentance;
having practiced repentance, one should next practice the invitation of the Buddhas;
having practiced the invitation of the Buddhas, one should next practice sympathetic joy.
Having practiced sympathetic joy, one next practices dedication;
having practiced dedication, one next practices making vows;
having practiced making vows, one sits upright with the body straight, binding mindfulness before oneself, and contemplates the realm of the Buddha so that it gradually expands and grows vast.

Within a single monastery, he causes it to be filled with Buddha images, each six feet tall with square bodies, lotus flowers beneath their feet, and circular halos one fathom in diameter; including the pervasive body-radiance and the mani-jewel flame-marks, as well as the various emanated Buddhas and their attendants, he causes all their lights and myriad colors to be clearly manifest.
Having accomplished this within one monastery, he further expands his mind so that an area of one *qǐng* of land is likewise filled with Buddha images.

Once this visualization is accomplished, the mind attains tranquility and the body experiences joy. Whether walking or standing still, because the mental visualization is sharp, one sees a field of land—measuring one *qǐng*—filled with Buddha images, along with incense, flowers, offerings, and various banners and streamers, all following the movement of the images. Because the mind is so keen, one perceives the movement of the images throughout the left, right, front, and back.

The mind gradually expands and broadens until one sees a hundred *qing* of land filled with Buddha-images; whether opening or closing the eyes, one maintains this mental visualization, with each thought succeeding the next in an uninterrupted flow, like a thirsty person longing for a drink.

Once this visualization is accomplished, one sees Buddha images filling a *yojana*; gradually increasing in scale and range, they fill a hundred *yojanas*, and all these images are seen with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, all vividly manifest.
When this visualization is accomplished, one visualizes the continent of Jambudvīpa, eight thousand yojanas in extent, entirely filled with images of the Buddha.
When this visualization is accomplished, one next visualizes the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, eighty-six hundred yojanas in extent, entirely filled with images of the Buddha.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one further visualizes the western continent of Aparagoyānī, measuring eight thousand nine hundred yojanas in extent, filled with Buddha-images.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one further contemplates the northern continent of Uttarakuru, measuring sixteen thousand yojanas, filled with Buddha-images.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one further perceives a hundred Jambudvīpas filled with Buddha-images.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one perceives ten billion four-continent worlds (cāturdvīpaka) filled with Buddha-images.

Once this visualization is accomplished, except for the times of eating and the times of attending to excretions, at all other times one constantly perceives Buddha-images; the void and the earth are filled with Buddha-images, each image following the next without any intervening gaps.

Once these contemplations are accomplished, one’s body and mind shall be filled with joy; one should redouble one's diligence, revere and honor the twelve divisions of the scriptures as if wearing them upon the crown of one's head, and regard the teacher of the Dharma as a great master.

One should regard the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha as one's own parents, making the mind supple and gentle so that thoughts of anger do not arise. Should anger occur, one must prostrate oneself before the Prajñāpāramitā and sincerely repent. One should practice the five dharmas in the sequence described above.

Having completed this visualization, he closes his eyes, joins his palms, and sits upright in meditative absorption; he then forms a further visualization of vast scope, seeing all images filling the worlds of the ten directions, his body being pure gold in color and emitting great radiance.
If there are those who have violated the precepts and committed unwholesome deeds, whether in a previous life or in this present life, they will see various Buddha-images as either black or white;
through the power of repentance, these images gradually appear red; having seen them red, they gradually appear golden;

having seen them golden, their body and mind rejoice, and they entreat the images to emit radiance. When one gives rise to this visualization, because the mental focus is sharp, one sees all the images, and every pore of the body emits light, with each ray of light possessing ten billion jewel-like colors.

Within each and every color, immeasurable variegated colors emerge spontaneously as subtle and wondrous objects; when this mental visualization is perfected, it is called "contemplating the established image.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Contemplating in this manner is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation."

If other signs appear, they arise from a different realm; you should swiftly eliminate them. One who performs this contemplation eradicates the sins of birth and death accumulated over sixty billion kalpas; this is also called "seeing the Buddha.

Because their mental resolve will be sharp in future lives, they shall encounter the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, serving as their preceptors. They will successively leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma, seeing the physical marks of each Buddha with perfect clarity. Hearing the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they will remember and uphold it without forgetting. Under the Buddha Prabhūtaratna during the Tārakakalpa, they will receive a prediction of enlightenment in his very presence. If even contemplating the image with a coarse mind yields such immeasurable merit, how much more so when one focuses the mind to contemplate the light of the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows?
When these words were spoken, the Great Brahmā King and his immeasurable host of Brahmās took various celestial flowers and scattered them over the World-Honored One;
they removed the necklaces from their own bodies and offered them to the Buddha.

The flowers remained suspended in the air like clouds; the necklaces they were strung upon transformed into golden pedestals. Within these golden pedestals there was golden light, which further transformed into the honored images of the seven Buddhas, majestic and sublime, complete in every physical feature.
The Brahma King Śaṅkhakeśa knelt with palms joined and entreated the World-Honored One, saying:

"The Tathāgata, out of great compassion and pity for sentient beings, prays that for the sake of the blind and ignorant beings of future ages, you will fully expound the method for contemplating the marks and signs of the Buddha’s image. By causing all sentient beings to rely upon what the Buddha has taught, may they always encounter the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and attain the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). Through the power of this samādhi, may all sentient beings remain far removed from evil; and because their offenses are extinguished, may they manifestly behold the Buddhas."
The Buddha told the Brahma King:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said."
At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of all sentient beings of future generations, further explained the method of sitting while contemplating the image:
"As for sitting while contemplating the image:
with a sincere mind, fix your mindfulness so that flowers grow beneath the feet of the standing image before you. When these flowers grow, you should give rise to this thought:"
"May this great earth become the color of yellow gold and the colors of the seven treasures.
As he thought, so it appeared; each of the treasure-colored regions was bounded by gold, and between each region grew precious lotus flowers.
When forming this visualization, a precious lotus flower with a thousand petals shall appear as one visualizes it.
Once the flower has been seen, one should invite the various visualized deities to sit upon the precious lotus.

When the multitude of images are seated, the great earth spontaneously emits a vast white light, as brilliant and pure as the color of lapis lazuli, lovely to behold. Amidst this white light, ten billion bodhisattvas—white as snow mountains—emerge from the pores of the visualized bodies. From each and every pore of these bodhisattva bodies, golden light issues forth, its radiance like a mountain; hundreds of thousands of Jāmbūnada golds blaze with such splendor that their number is beyond reckoning, appearing according to one’s visualization.

Upon each mountain peak stands a visualized image, lofty and magnificent to behold, with a Jāmbūnada golden body and a light so intense that it illuminates the worlds of the ten directions, turning them all to gold. One sees the earth and the sky likewise turned to gold, filled with golden images, golden light, golden canopies, golden pedestals, golden flowers, and golden banners.
One should visualize the Bodhisattva Saṃjñā as the color of pure white jade, holding a white fly-whisk or a white flower; one should form this mental image until it is exceedingly bright and white.

If other miscellaneous thoughts or different objects appear, they must be swiftly eliminated. If they are not eliminated and one pursues those other thoughts, following after external objects will cause wind-disorders (vāta-roga) to arise.

This contemplation of the Buddha is a great ambrosia that benefits sentient beings; it is the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha. Just as taking excellent medicine benefits the four elements, those who take this medicine neither age nor die.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are sentient beings who wish to contemplate the seated image, they should contemplate it in this way.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation."

If there are sentient beings who contemplate this image while seated, they shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over five hundred *koṭis* of kalpas. In the future, they will encounter the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa; after the Bhadrakalpa has passed, during the Nakṣatra-kalpa, they will encounter Buddhas numbering one hundred thousand. Under each and every Buddha, they will receive and uphold the Buddha’s words, their body and mind remaining peaceful and secure, never again falling into confusion.
Each World-Honored One will appear before them and bestow a prediction of enlightenment, such that after passing through incalculable kalpas, they shall attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If there are sentient beings who, having contemplated the seated image, should then contemplate the walking image. As for contemplating the walking image: [it is as follows...]"
He saw the worlds of the ten directions filled with rows of images; in both the void and upon the earth, he saw each individual image rise from its seat.
As each image rose, five hundred billion jewel-flowers appeared;
within each flower were countless rays of light.

Within each ray of light, countless transformation Buddhas appear according to the thoughts of sentient beings. When the seated images rise or stand, or during the interval before they have risen, as their bodies move, the white tuft of hair between their brows rotates and extends, long or short, just like a true Buddha emitting white radiance. This white light is adorned with hundreds of thousands of colors that reflect golden light; amidst the multitude of white lights, there are countless silver images whose bodies are the color of white silver, along with silver light, silver flowers, silver canopies, silver banners, and silver pedestals—all of which are entirely made of silver.

At that time, the many golden and silver images all stirred their bodies as if wishing to rise; from the navels of each image, a lotus flower emerged, and from within those lotus flowers, hundreds of thousands of countless transformation Buddhas leapt forth. Each of these transformation Buddhas emitted golden light that shone upon the body of the practitioner.
At that time, when the practitioner enters meditative concentration, they see their own body as the thirty-six impure and foul substances.
When these impurities appear, they should quickly eliminate them and form this thought:

"The bodies and minds of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are pure. I am now training in the Buddha’s truly pure Dharma-body; this contemplation of impurity arises from craving and attachment—it is false and useless, so why employ this contemplation?"

Having formed this thought, one should contemplate one’s own body, causing all impurities to transform into white jade. One should see one’s own body as a vessel of white jade, empty both inside and out. While performing this contemplation, it is appropriate to take ghee medicine so as not to leave the body depleted.
When this visualization is accomplished, all the images arise and stand as before. Upon seeing the images standing, one should form the thought of inviting them to proceed.

Once the images have begun to walk, within every step they take, lotuses grow beneath their feet, forming lotus pedestals. One sees the worlds of the ten directions filled with walking images, ritual implements, and musical performances, surrounded by a great assembly of devas in reverent attendance. The walking silver images emit light that illuminates the great assembly, turning them all to a silver color; the white jade Bodhisattvas emit white jade light, turning the great assembly to the color of white jade; and the various multi-colored images emit multi-colored light, adorning the space between them.
Once this visualization is accomplished, one further gives rise to this thought:
"I pray that all the images of the Buddhas will extend their hands and stroke my head.

At that time, each of the images extends its right hand and strokes the practitioner's head. Simultaneously, the multitude of images emits a great radiance that illuminates the practitioner's body. When the light shines upon the body, the practitioner sees his own body as the color of gold.

Once this visualization is accomplished, one emerges from meditative absorption with joy; furthermore, with a sincere heart, one pays homage to all Buddhas and cultivates various meritorious virtues, dedicating these merits toward Bodhi.
"At that time, one should further give rise to this thought:
'I have now visualized many golden images walking and sitting at will, yet I have not yet seen their supernormal powers.
One should then arouse the mind to form the visualization, requesting the various walking images and the Bodhisattva images to perform the eighteen transformations."

Upon recollecting this, he immediately performs eighteen kinds of transformations; one sees him filling the ten directions with all manner of forms, leaping into mid-air to perform the eighteen transformations with sovereign spiritual power, universally manifesting his form-body so that the practitioner may behold it.

Having seen this, they rejoice and entreat all the images to turn the wheel of Dharma; instantly, as they think of it, each of the images, with different mouths but in one voice, praises the upholding of the precepts and praises the mindfulness of the Buddha!

Having heard this, his heart was filled with great joy, and he redoubled his diligent effort. Because of this diligence, his mental visualization was perfected. When the mental visualization was perfected, he beheld the worlds of the ten directions; the entire earth, mountains, rivers, and rocky walls were all transformed into a ground of vajra. From the vajra ground, white light surged forth, and amidst these countless white lights, innumerable transformation Buddhas sat upon precious lotus flowers.
Each transformation Buddha emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light, and each ray of light further manifested hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas.
When this visualization appears, the practitioner sees golden light emerge from all the pores of his own body, illuminating everything;
if other objects arise, they should be swiftly eliminated.

Such mental conceptions are swifter than a violent wind; in a mere instant, one sees countless transformation Buddhas. Just as a person with keen vision holding a crystal mirror observes their own facial reflection, so too does the practitioner observe these forms!
“When this perception has been accomplished, one should form this thought:

‘The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, abide in great quiescent extinction; their body and mind are pure, neither coming nor going. As for my own body, it is a composite formed by the four great elements and the five aggregates; it is like a plantain tree that has no core of solidity within, like foam upon water, like the moon reflected in water, like an image in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like the movement of wild horses, and like the city of the Gandharvas.’”

Having formed this thought, all the images immediately vanished, and a golden light appeared. Within the golden light, there were reflections of golden Buddhas like images in a mirror; within the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—they manifested every form.

"When this visualization is accomplished, one should contemplate the Tathāgata’s body of precepts (*śīlakāya*). While contemplating the body of precepts, one sees the reflections of all Buddhas; the light from between their eyebrows is like white silk, pure in the void, and extends before the practitioner. Having seen this, the practitioner should form this thought:

'Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, adorned himself with the great body of precepts in past lives; therefore, today he has attained morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.'"

While he was forming this thought, Śākyamuni Buddha sat within a lapis lazuli cave; his body was of purple-gold hue, majestic and exquisitely subtle, with a retinue of bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, and a great assembly. Standing before the practitioner, he addressed him, saying:
"Son of the Dharma!

By the power of your cultivation of the Buddha-contemplation samādhi, I have manifested a physical body for you through the power of the marks of nirvāṇa so that you may contemplate it clearly. You must not engage in excessive contemplation while sitting in meditation; for those of future generations who commit many evils, you should simply contemplate the light of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows. When performing this contemplation, the realms perceived will be as described above.
At that moment, his mind was free from attachment and he felt great joy; immediately, he attained the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
As for this Buddha-remembrance samādhi:
he saw the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) with perfect clarity, and he also perceived the Buddha’s mind and all its spheres of activity.
It is also as previously described regarding the contemplation of the Buddha’s mind;
one also beholds all the radiances of the Buddha’s body;
and it is also as previously described regarding the contemplation of the light of the Buddha’s body.

He also saw that from every single pore of the Buddha’s body, eighty-four thousand lotus flowers emerged; within each flower, there were again eighty-four thousand transformation Buddhas, these Buddhas following one another to fill the realms of the ten directions.

"At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha immediately extended his right hand and stroked the crown of the practitioner's head; all the manifested Buddhas likewise extended their right hands and stroked the practitioner's crown. One who attains this contemplation is said to have attained the Samādhi of the Manifestation of the Buddha before One’s Eyes;
it is also called the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha;
and it is also called the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha’s Form Body."

At that time, all the Buddhas, with one voice and in unison, each preached the Dharma for the practitioner. Although he had not yet attained the Way, upon seeing the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma, he maintained it through dhāraṇī without loss; this is called the ordinary person’s nianfo samādhi (Buddha-remembrance samādhi).

One who attains this samādhi will, in every single moment, constantly behold all Buddhas; in every thought-moment, they shall hear the Buddhas preaching the Dharma—namely, the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras—and within a single day and night, they shall attain thorough mastery of them.

Born of their parents’ flesh in this vexing, turbid, and evil world, because they have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, they shall hear the dhāraṇī. After casting off this body in another life, they will surely behold the Buddhas. From those Buddhas, they will obtain thousands of millions of billions of *āvartana-dhāraṇīs*. Having obtained these dhāraṇīs, eighty billion Buddhas will each extend their right hand and stroke the practitioner’s crown.

Each and every Buddha will speak with a definitive word: “Because you have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, you shall attain Buddhahood after the Star宿 kalpa; your physical marks and radiance will be no different from mine!”

Having spoken these words, eight billion Buddhas simultaneously emitted light; within that light there were further immeasurable transformation Buddhas, and each of these transformation Buddhas spoke these same words.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These various dharmas are called the 'Method of Contemplating the Image. When one contemplates the image, there will naturally arise further immeasurable hundreds of thousands of supreme realms."
"To observe in this manner is called right observation; to observe otherwise is called wrong observation.
Thus ends the ninth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*. [Fascicle Ten follows.]
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: Recollecting the Seven Buddhas (10). Chapter Ten: Recollecting the Seven Buddhas.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"If there are sentient beings who have accomplished the visualization of the image, they should next visualize the images of the seven past Buddhas.

Those who visualize the seven Buddhas should apply themselves with diligent vigor; throughout the six periods of day and night, they should diligently practice the six dharmas. Sitting upright in meditative absorption, they should delight in speaking little, except when reciting the sutras or extensively expounding the Dharma teachings. They must never utter meaningless speech. Constantly mindful of all Buddhas with an uninterrupted stream of thought, they shall not for even a single moment fail to see the Buddha. Because their minds are focused and diligent, they shall never be separated from the sun-like presence of the Buddha."

"In the distant past, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin Buddha. His body was sixty *yojanas* tall and majestic; his halo was one hundred and twenty *yojanas* in circumference. His body was the color of purple-gold, possessing eighty-four thousand primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and within each primary mark were eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).
Within each secondary sign were countless rays of golden light;
within each ray of light were transformation Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Each of these manifested Buddhas possesses light-rays as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
within each ray are countless assemblies of devas, śrāvakas, bhikṣus, and bodhisattvas, serving as attendants.

Each person held a great precious lotus flower, upon which were hundreds of billions of radiant nets of precious maṇi jewels; these nets were arranged in succession to a height of hundreds of thousands of zhang, forming the Buddha’s light.

At that time, the Buddha’s body becomes even more manifest, like hundreds of thousands of suns illuminating a mountain of purple gold; brilliant light arises, manifesting countless transformation Buddhas, each of whom is like ten billion suns and moons appearing simultaneously, causing the practitioner to behold them.
Vipaśyin Buddha bared his right shoulder, extended his golden arm, and rubbed the practitioner’s crown, saying:
“Son of the Dharma!

Because you have practiced the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha and attained the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, I have come to bear witness to you. You should now contemplate my true physical body, observing each mark in succession. You must establish a vajra-vow with a sincere heart: ‘When we formerly practiced the path of the Buddha in the past, we were no different from you.’”

At that time, after Vipaśyin Buddha had comforted the practitioner, he immediately manifested a great jewel lotus flower as large as Mount Sumeru. Seated upon the flower in the full lotus posture, the Buddha preached for the practitioner the mindfulness of the Buddha and the mindfulness of the Dharma, as well as the *Bhagīrathī-dhāraṇī* (the Hundred-Crore Revolving Dhāraṇī).
Having seen this, the practitioner’s joy redoubled and he paid homage to that Buddha.
That Buddha said to him:

"If there are sentient beings who hear my name or prostrate before me, they shall eliminate the offenses of birth and death for five hundred billion kalpas. You have now seen me and have had all obstacles removed; you shall attain the immeasurable koṭis of *dhāraṇīs* and, in a future age, you shall become a Buddha."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, because the practitioner saw Vipaśyin and felt joy in his heart, I and the six Buddhas appeared before that person."
The Elder Vipaśyin preached the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha for this Dharma-son.

The World-Honored One Śikhin was forty-two yojanas in height; his body was the color of purple-gold, his halo was forty-five yojanas in circumference, and the radiance of his entire body extended for one hundred yojanas. Within that lattice of light were countless transformation Buddhas, as well as bodhisattvas, the great assembly of śrāvakas, and celestial retinues who surrounded him, following behind the Buddha and circling to the right.
At that time, the practitioner beholds Śikhin Buddha and further increases his attainment of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharanī gates;
he further expands his vision to behold hundreds of thousands of countless transformation Buddhas.
"In future ages, beyond eons that transcend calculation, throughout that interval, you shall constantly encounter the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and be born into the family of Bodhisattvas.

When these words were spoken, there were again countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras who, having heard this matter and beheld the Buddha’s physical body—so dignified, majestic, subtle, and wondrous—all simultaneously gave rise to the mind of *sambodhi*.

The World-Honored One Viśva raised his entire body to emit light and stood before the practitioner; that Buddha was thirty-two yojanas in height, with a halo forty-two yojanas in diameter and a pervasive radiance sixty-two yojanas in extent. His body was the color of purple-gold, and his majestic brilliance and physical marks were no different from those described previously.
Having seen this Buddha, they further advance in the various *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* gates; in future lives, they will certainly and without doubt be born into the family of the Buddhas.

The Buddha Krakucchanda also emits light and stands before the practitioner; that Buddha’s body is twenty-five *yojanas* in height, his halo is thirty-two *yojanas*, and his pervasive radiance is fifty *yojanas*. He is fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks, like a mountain of purple gold.
Those who behold this Buddha will always be born in pure lands and shall never dwell within a womb; at the time of their death, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will surely come to welcome them.

The Buddha Kanakamuni emits a great radiance that abides before the practitioner. This Buddha’s body is twenty yojanas in height, his halo is thirty yojanas in circumference, and the light extending from his entire body is forty yojanas long, fully endowed with radiant marks.
One who beholds this Buddha immediately attains ten billion gates of samādhi and countless dhāraṇīs.

When emerging from meditative concentration, one constantly attains the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas. Because this samādhi serves as the witness for the practitioner, it is named the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas.

Having attained this samādhi, whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one constantly beholds all Buddhas, who manifest their wondrous form-bodies before that person.

“Kāśyapa, the World-Honored One emits a great radiance and stands before that person; the Buddha is sixteen *zhang* tall, his body is the color of purple-gold, and he is fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks.
Those who behold this Buddha attain the Samādhi of the Silent Mark of Quiescent Radiance, and in future ages they shall eternally abide within the ocean of the Great Emptiness Samādhi.”
“The body of Śākyamuni Buddha is sixteen feet tall; emitting purple-gold light, he stands before the practitioner.
The body of the World-Honored One Maitreya is sixteen *zhang* tall.”

In this way, each of these Buddhas enters the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms and appears before that person, causing the practitioner’s mind to feel joy; because of this joy, each of these emanated Buddhas extends their right hand and strokes the crown of the practitioner’s head.

Having seen the seven Buddhas, one sees Maitreya; having seen Maitreya, one sees the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, each in successive order down to Ruci, all emitting light and standing before the practitioner.

At that time, the thousand bodhisattvas each praised the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) and, for the sake of the practitioners, explained the nature of the bodhisattvas, the liberations of the bodhisattvas, and the wisdom of the bodhisattvas; this is called attaining the *nien-fo san-mei* through the mind that contemplates the image.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, among the Buddha’s disciples, those who contemplate in this manner are said to have right contemplation; those who contemplate otherwise are said to have wrong contemplation.”

One who cultivates this samādhi, though still possessed of afflictions, is not driven by those afflictions. By the power of this Buddha-remembrance samādhi, the Buddhas of the ten directions emit great radiance that appears before such a person; this radiance is peerless, and they are uniquely honored throughout the three realms.
After the Buddha had spoken these words, the Brahma King again entreated him:
"May the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
explain the radiant physical marks of the Buddhas of the ten directions as they abide before the practitioner."
Chapter Eleven: Mindfulness of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions (10). Chapter Eleven: Mindfulness of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
“How does a practitioner contemplate the Buddhas of the ten directions?”
Regarding the visualization of the Buddhas of the ten directions:

beginning with the east, there is a world in the eastern direction called Jewel Peaceful Stability (*Ratna-śānta*). It is composed of immeasurable billions of jewels possessing billions of colors. The Buddha there is named Good Virtue (*Sudeva*), who likewise emits countless rays of light that universally illuminate hundreds of thousands of lands;
he also manifests countless billions of transformed bodies of emanation-Buddhas who abide before the practitioner.

His body was golden in color, majestic and peerless; he sat within a great adamantine cave, which was adorned as a hall and pavilion by the radiance of countless diverse jewels. Before each hall and pavilion stood billions of jewel trees, as numerous as the atoms in immeasurable worlds.
Beneath each jewel tree were eighty-four thousand lion thrones.
Upon each lion throne sat an emanation-body Buddha, seated cross-legged in samādhi beneath the jewel tree.

The body of the World-Honored One, the Buddha Śubhavyūha, was two hundred and fifty billion nayutas of yojanas in height; every single pore of his body possessed countless billions of atoms of all the most excellent marks and signs.
Within each mark and sign were countless transformation Buddhas.
Each transformation Buddha was lofty and majestic like Mount Sumeru, emitting great radiance and sitting upon precious lotus flowers as they dwelt in mid-air.
The emanated Buddhas each manifested subtle and wondrous light, revealing countless hundreds of thousands of transformation Buddhas;
each transformation Buddha sat upon a precious lotus flower,
and each lotus flower was adorned with a thousand banners and streamers.
Each individual banner and pennant produces ten billion subtle and wondrous sounds; within these sounds, there is instruction on contemplating the countless Buddha-bodies of the ten directions.

When this sign appears, one perceives the worlds of the ten directions as being like adamant, with ten billion jewel-colored hues that are neither extinguished nor destroyed. Having seen this sign, one receives the rank of Dharma Prince before all the Buddhas; such a state is called the Bodhisattva of the Ground of Nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*).

"To the south is the Buddha Candanaśrī; his physical marks are lofty and manifest. His buddha-field has lapis lazuli for its ground and the colors of the jewels of the sands of the Ganges. Within the light of that Buddha, there are also countless hundreds of thousands of halls and pavilions, with rows of jewel trees arrayed and lion thrones spread upon them. Upon these thrones, the Buddhas sit cross-legged. With precious banners, pennants, and canopies, they proclaim the sound of the Dharma as described in the *Buddhasamudra-samādhi*."

"In the west is the Buddha Amitābha; his land is pure, with ground of gold. His Buddha-body emits the radiance of five hundred billion jewel colors. Multi-storied pavilions and lecture halls are lined with precious trees and jeweled lion thrones. Buddhas who have manifested their bodies sit cross-legged beneath these precious trees, and within the jeweled banners and pennants, they also preach upon the ocean of mindfulness of the Buddha."

"In the north is the Buddha Lakṣaṇaguṇasāgara; his land is the color of crystal. There are five hundred billion jewel lights, with rows of jewel trees, and jeweled lion thrones, multi-storied lecture halls, banners, and radiance no different from those previously described."

"In the southeastern direction is the Buddha Aśoka-guṇa; his land is the color of the seven treasures, and upon each of these colors are seven billion variegated hues. Rows of jewel trees and multi-storied pavilions emit hundreds of billions of kinds of light, and each ray of light proclaims an ocean of the Buddha’s merits, just as the ocean of Buddhas describes them."
"In the southwest is the Buddha Ratnadatta; his land is the color of the five jewels, and upon each jewel are fifty billion rays of light.
Each ray of light transforms into fifty billion clouds of lotuses, and atop each cloud of lotuses are ten billion multi-storied pavilions."
Each successive tiered pavilion was like the palace of a hundred thousand million Brahmā kings;

within each Brahmā palace were countless couches and seats, all formed together from radiant lotuses. Upon these seats sat various emanation Buddhas in the full lotus posture, expounding the Dharma of the great compassion of all Buddhas; their radiant banners and streamers likewise proclaimed the ocean of the Buddhas.
"To the northwest is the Buddha Flower Virtue (Guṇakusuma). His buddha-land is the color of lapis lazuli and crystal; upon each color there are countless hundreds of thousands of rays of light.
Each ray of light transforms into five hundred billion jeweled grottoes, and within each grotto are countless jeweled canopies."
Within each and every canopy are ten billion rays of light;

within each ray of light are countless emanation Buddhas sitting cross-legged and emitting great radiance. Within that radiance, they preach the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), and by means of this *nien-fo samādhi*, one further comes to behold countless Buddhas.

"To the northeast is the Buddha who practices the three vehicles; his buddha-land is entirely the color of white silver with billions of rays of light, each ray possessing a thousand colors. He adorns the realm so that it is utterly pure, with emanated bodies, transformation buddhas, jeweled trees, banners, and streamers arranged in rows in a number beyond reckoning."
"In the zenith is the Buddha Vast Array of All Virtues; his ground is five hundred *koṭi* of jewel colors, and each jewel color emits countless rays of light.
Each ray of light transforms into countless hundreds of millions of manifested Buddhas.
Within the light of each Buddha, immeasurable jewel trees stand in rows, forming a magnificent array."
Beneath each tree were ten billion precious lion thrones.
Upon them, the Buddhas sat cross-legged, attended by countless bodhisattvas, while the entire great assembly dwelt within clouds of the Buddhas' radiant light.

“In the region below is the Buddha Mingde (Virtuous Brightness). His land is golden in color, with golden light and golden clouds. Within these clouds of light are countless golden halls and pavilions made of the seven treasures, adorned with rows of trees made of a hundred jewels.

There were tens of billions of precious banners, pennants, and canopies; beneath each tree were ten billion precious seats, halls, and pavilions, with countless seats shaped like precious flowers. Countless emanations of all Buddhas sat beneath the precious trees upon lapis lazuli thrones, amidst assemblies of countless Buddhas interspersed with the colors of various flowers.
All these World-Honored Ones have fully expounded the dharmas of the bodhisattva practices; likewise, the innumerable transformation Buddhas of the ten directions each manifest radiant light.

"At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions each sat within a vajra cave; their physical dimensions and radiance were like those of the Buddha Śubhavyūha and the various emanation Buddhas. Through their majestic spiritual power, they caused the practitioner to see their lands as clearly as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a bright mirror. Because of seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions with such vivid clarity, the practitioner’s heart was filled with joy; thus, remaining unstained by any phenomena, they abided in the initial mind."

At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions extensively expounded the six semblance *pāramitās* for the practitioner respectively; having heard this Dharma, one will have no doubts or hesitations regarding the ten mental states within the realm of the first stage.

One who perceives this phenomenon will surely hear the Buddhas preach the Prajñāpāramitā; hearing the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), their mind will not be startled or doubtful, and they will attain entry into the śūnyatā-samādhi among all dharmas. This is called the samādhi of the semblance-mark of emptiness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the Buddha’s disciples wish to contemplate the Buddhas of the ten directions, they need only know their coarse marks within the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, and they will naturally come to know their immeasurable subtle marks."
Observing in this manner is called right observation; observing otherwise is called wrong observation.

One who attains this observation sees Buddhas in numbers beyond measure and limit. One who enters this samādhi is said to see the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all Buddhas, and shall also gradually enter the three gates of emptiness.

Those who roam within this emptiness do not become attached to emptiness by virtue of the power of the Buddhas; they shall in future ages attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and reach the stage of non-retrogression. This is called not forgetting the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and being correctly aligned with the Buddha-way.

When he spoke of contemplating the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Buddhas of the ten directions were seated within hundred-jeweled caves on Diamond Mountains; each extended his right hand, stroked Ānanda’s crown, and said:
“O son of the Dharma!

You must uphold the Buddha’s words; for the sake of all sentient beings in future ages, you should proclaim them widely, but take care not to transmit them recklessly. You should speak only to those who have firmly resolved to attain *samyak-saṃbodhi* and who practice the meditative absorption of mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“If this buddhānusmṛti-samādhi is accomplished, there are five causes and conditions. What are the five?
First, upholding the precepts without transgression;
second, not giving rise to false views;
third, not engendering arrogance.
Fourth, to be free from anger and envy.
Fifth, to practice with courageous diligence as if one’s head were on fire.

By performing these five practices, one maintains right mindfulness of the Buddhas’ subtle and wondrous form bodies so that the mind does not regress; furthermore, one should read and recite Mahāyāna sūtras. Through the merit of this and the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, one will swiftly behold immeasurable Buddhas.
"Those who behold the Buddhas should, with a mind uniquely pure and not shared with others, offer worship to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
How should they offer worship?
When this person emerges from meditative absorption, enters a stupa, beholds an image, or recites and upholds the sutra, if they pay homage to a single Buddha, they should form this thought:"
"The wisdom-minds of all Buddhas, the Perfectly All-Knowing Ones, are without limit or obstruction. When I now pay homage to one Buddha, I am paying homage to all Buddhas;
if I contemplate one Buddha, I see all Buddhas;
and when I see a single practitioner before each Buddha prostrating by touching his feet in worship, it is my own self in every instance."
When making an offering of a single flower to the Buddha, one should form this thought:

"The merits of the Buddhas' Dharma-body are immeasurable; it does not abide and is indestructible, remaining eternally tranquil and secure. I now offer this flower to all Buddhas; may the Buddhas accept it."
Having formed this thought, one should further give rise to this visualization:
"The flowers I hold were born from grasses and trees; by holding these as an offering, they may be used for mental simulation.

One should then immediately visualize all the pores of the body, causing each single pore to emit countless clouds of flowers. With these clouds of flowers, one should employ visualization and intention to offer them to all Buddhas. Upon each Buddha, they transform into flower pedestals which the Buddhas accept; within the worlds of the ten directions, they perform the work of Buddhas. When making offerings of incense, it is also like this!

Fragrant smoke and clouds of incense perform the Buddha-work throughout the worlds of the ten directions; having performed this Buddha-work, they return to form a golden platform before the practitioner.

If ordinary persons wish to make offerings, they should hold incense burners in their hands and offer flowers, while also giving rise to the intention to visualize these flowers and incense. They should then make this vow:

"May these flowers and incense fill the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, transformation Buddhas, as well as Bodhisattvas and countless assemblies of Śrāvakas. May they accept these clouds of incense and flowers as a platform of radiance, extensively performing Buddha-work throughout boundless realms."
Whether prostrating before the Buddha or practicing seated meditation, one should give rise to this mind of making offerings and always make this vow.
With silk canopies, banners, streamers, music, and verses of praise, one should make this vow:

"I now provide these meager offerings; may these offerings pervade and serve all Buddhas of the ten directions. May the Buddhas accept them, and from within these banners and streamers, may clouds of radiant light be manifested."
"Amidst music and song, one shall proclaim the sublime sound of the Dharma.
Having made this vow, while sitting, one should visualize that from each and every pore of the body there arise immeasurable banners and streamers;
and within each banner and streamer, one should visualize clouds of immeasurable verses.

When one forms this perception, the mind is like an incense burner, emitting clouds of golden incense smoke; from the pores of the body, like fine flowering trees, there emerge clouds of countless *asaṃkhyeya* varieties of flowers. These clouds of flowers, above the Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions, transform into all manner of articles of offering.
At that time, within the sphere of body and mind, one should give rise to the perception of all requisites for making offerings.

Whether obtaining food and drink or bestowing even a single coin upon another person, one should give rise to the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by emptiness and the absence of self.

All such immeasurable offerings as these should be brought forth by generating the intention and emerging from the ocean of mental imagery to make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called the immeasurable merit arising from the ocean of mental imagery while sitting.

While sitting in this manner, they enter the ocean of various samādhis within the immeasurable realms of profound meditative concentration; yet within their minds alone, the exhalations and inhalations continue in an uninterrupted succession of momentary thoughts.
Within that single mind, they direct their mental faculty to conjure clouds of countless offering implements.
Making offerings to all Buddhas above and bestowing gifts upon all beings below—one who forms such a thought is said to be practicing universal giving.

When this contemplation is perfected, the fetters of all afflictions are gradually diminished and eliminated. One contemplates the signlessness of phenomena, and by the power of this signlessness, one shall attain the profound six pāramitās.
12. Chapter on Contemplating the Secret Practices of the Buddhas (10). Chapter Twelve: Contemplating the Secret Practices of the Buddhas. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"Regarding future sentient beings who attain this Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddhas, who contemplate the marks and signs of the Buddhas, and who attain the Samādhi of the Buddhas Appearing Before One—these persons should be taught to keep their body, speech, and mind secret; they must not give rise to wrong livelihoods, nor should they harbor arrogance."

If one gives rise to wrong livelihood and the dharma of arrogance, you should know that this person is one of overweening pride who destroys the Buddha-dharma; they cause many sentient beings to give rise to unwholesome minds, disrupt the harmony of the Saṃgha, and manifest eccentricity to delude the masses—they are companions of the evil Māra.

Such evil persons, though they may recollect the Buddha, lose the flavor of the ambrosia. In whatever place these people are born, because of their arrogance, their bodies will always be lowly and small; they will be born into base families and suffer from poverty and various misfortunes, with immeasurable evil karma serving as their adornment. Regarding these many kinds of such evils, one should guard oneself against them so that they never arise again.
If one gives rise to such wrong livelihood, this wrong livelihood is like a mad elephant destroying a lotus pond; likewise, this wrong livelihood ruins and destroys one's roots of goodness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha should protect themselves and not allow themselves to become lax.

If those who possess the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha do not guard themselves and give rise to arrogance, the evil winds of wrong livelihood will blow upon them, and the fire of pride will burn away their wholesome dharmas."
Wholesome dharmas refer to all immeasurable meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
All recollections of the Buddha arise from various mental conceptions; this is called the treasury of merit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Suppose there were an elder with abundant wealth and many treasures who had only one son. Knowing that he would soon die, the elder entrusted all his storehouses to his son."

Having obtained it, his son played with it as he pleased; then, at one time, he encountered a royal calamity, and immeasurable bands of thieves came from the four directions, vying to seize the hidden goods which he could not protect.

There was only one piece of gold, which was Jāmbūnada紫金 (Jāmbūnada purple-gold), weighing sixteen *liang* and measuring sixteen *cun* in length. The value of each *liang* of this gold was equivalent to hundreds of thousands of millions of other types of jewels. Being pursued by the bandits and having no choice regarding the gold, he wrapped the pure gold in filthy rags and placed it within a lump of mud. When the bandits saw it, they did not recognize it as gold and trampled over it as they departed.
"After the bandits have departed, the owner of the wealth obtains the gold and his heart is filled with great joy.
The samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha is also like this;
you should keep it secret. "Furthermore, Ānanda!"
For example, suppose there is a man who is poor and of meager merit, who sustains his life by depending on various noble and eminent persons.
At that time, a prince happens to go out on an excursion, carrying a great precious jar, within which he has concealed the royal seal and insignia.
At that time, the poor man feigned intimacy and approached him; having obtained the king’s precious vase, he carried it off and fled.
Upon realizing this, the prince dispatched six great soldiers riding six black elephants, who pursued him swiftly with sharp swords in hand.

At that time, the water-carrier fled into the deep grass of a desolate wilderness marsh, where he saw the vast marsh filled with venomous snakes; from all four sides, they spat forth poison and drew toward the water-carrier.

At that time, the poor man, terrified and trembling with fear, fled hither and thither; the snake followed him, and there was no place for him to hide. In a desolate marsh, he saw a great tree, lush and spreading with foliage, which greatly pleased his mind; he placed a precious jar upon his head and climbed up the tree.

Once he had climbed the tree, the six soldiers arrived again, riding an elephant as swift as the wind; seeing them, the poor man swallowed the king’s precious seal, took the crown onto his head, and covered his face with his hands, for out of greed and attachment, he could not bear to look at them.

Then the six black elephants used their trunks to twist the tree until it fell over; the poor man fell to the ground, his body shattered, with only the golden seal remaining. The jeweled vase emitted light, and upon seeing the light, the snakes scattered and fled in all directions.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The seal of the mind of one who abides in the recollection of the Buddha is likewise indestructible!
Furthermore, Ānanda!”
For example, there was once an elder who possessed abundant wealth and treasures, yet had no sons, only a single daughter.
At that time, the elder was over a hundred years old; knowing himself to be decrepit and that his death would soon be at hand, he thought:
"Since I have no male heir, these treasures of mine shall rightfully belong to the king."
Having reflected thus, he called his daughter and told her in secret:
"I now possess a wondrous jewel, the most excellent among all jewels; I shall give it to you. Once you have obtained this jewel, keep it hidden securely so that the King does not discover it."

The woman followed her father’s instructions, taking the maṇi jewel and various precious treasures and concealing them in filth; neither the members of the household, great or small, were aware of it.
During a time of famine, the woman’s husband said to his wife:
"Our family is so poor that we are destitute for food and clothing; you may go elsewhere to seek a means of livelihood."
The wife said to her husband:
"When my father, the elder, was approaching the end of his life, he gave me these treasures; they are currently at such-and-such a place, and you may take them."

At that time, the husband dug up the ground and obtained a great quantity of precious treasures along with a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). Taking the wish-fulfilling jewel, he burned incense, prostrated, and first made this vow:
"May it rain down food for me."
As soon as these words were spoken, food and drink of a hundred flavors rained down; in this manner, they obtained various treasures according to their wishes.
When the husband had received them, he said to his wife:
"Since you, like a celestial maiden, can bestow such treasures upon me, yet I do not even know where you have hidden these treasures, how much less could anyone else?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The firmness of mind that does not waver in the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is also like this!
Furthermore, Ānanda!”

For example, suppose there is a king who is tyrannical and contrary to the Way; the people suffer from his poison, men resent him, and the deities are incensed. The land suffers a great drought, yet though he prays to the gods and spirits, he cannot obtain rain.
A minister addressed him, saying:

"Great King, you should know that within the forests and marshes of this realm there is a seer who possesses the five supernatural powers without obstruction; Your Majesty may pray to him to cast a spell upon the dragon."
Upon hearing this, the Great King was filled with immeasurable joy and dispatched messengers to the forest to entreat the seer.
The divine seer flew to the front of the Great King’s palace and cried out in a loud voice:
"The Great King is devoid of the Way; all the devas, nāgas, and spirits have dispersed in the four directions and no longer protect the kingdom. How can you expect me to cause rain to fall?"
Upon hearing these words, the king felt profound shame and remorse for the evil deeds he had previously committed.

Knowing that the king’s mind had become supple and virtuous, the rishi recited a mantra; by the power of his supernatural faculties, the heavens sent down sweet dew and springs gushed forth from the earth, moistening and nourishing all things.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"One who wishes to practice the recollection of the Buddha is like a king who abandons evil; one who attains the recollection of the Buddha is like a person skilled in incantations.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
It is like a strongman who, relying on his great strength, repeatedly violates the king’s laws. The king dispatches five men to arrest the strongman and confine him in prison.

Shackled and bound at five points with extreme firmness, he exerts himself in a great rage until blood appears over his entire body; he breaks the shackles, leaps over the wall, and flees. Arriving at the seashore, he unties the bright jewel from his topknot and offers it to hire a boatman.
The boatman says: "Such white stones as these are countless in the sea; what use would I have for them?"
The strongman knelt upright and said to the boatman, "This bright pearl of mine has six colors.
He then wrapped the pearl in yellow silk and placed it in the water; the water immediately turned the color of gold.
He then withdrew the pearl again, wrapped it in white silk, and placed it in the water; the water immediately turned white.
He withdrew it again, wrapped it in green silk, and placed it in the water; the color of the water changed into that of green lapis lazuli.
He withdrew it again, wrapped it in azure silk, and placed it in the water; the water immediately changed into the color of pure refined gold.
Having retrieved it, he wrapped it again in red silk and placed it in water; the water immediately changed to the color of musaragalva.

Having retrieved it, he wrapped it again in purple silk and placed it in water; the water immediately transformed into the color of celestial vajra, and upon the water there appeared the light of a purple mani-jewel.

Having seen this, the boatman immediately took the precious jewel and, using a great jeweled palanquin, carried the valiant hero onto the large ship; then, catching the wind and hoisting the sails, they reached the opposite shore as swiftly as a shot arrow.
Having reached the other shore, his mind was serene, peaceful, and free from fear; he took great treasures to repay the kindness of the boatman.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"One who practices mindfulness of the Buddha is like a mighty warrior who breaks the shackles of the mind-king and reaches the shore of wisdom."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is like when a kalpa is about to end and two suns appear simultaneously; the mountains, forests, trees, rivers, and ponds dry up.
When three suns appear, fires break out from all forms and colors."
When four suns appear, the great ocean diminishes until three parts remain and one part is left;
when five suns appear, the great ocean is completely exhausted;
when six suns appear, Mount Sumeru collapses.

When the seven suns arise, the great earth blazes intensely, reaching even up to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); yet only the Diamond Mountains (*vajraparvata*) cannot be destroyed and remain as they were at their original limit.
The *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is also like this: one who practices this concentration dwells within the ocean of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the Buddhas of the past.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I now wish to repay the grace of the Buddhas of the ten directions for their mindfulness of me through the *nianfo sanmei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these words, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, he entered the *sarvarūpakāyaprabhāsa-samādhi* (the samādhi of the light of all physical bodies).

At that time, from every single pore of the bodies of all the Buddhas, there emerged vast, incalculable clouds of wondrous transformation Buddhas; these transformation Buddhas sat cross-legged, abiding and standing in mid-air.
In this manner, all these countless emanation Buddhas each extended their right hands to stroke Ānanda’s head and commanded Śakra-devānām-indra:
“You two must uphold this sublime Dharma and be careful not to forget it, for the sake of extinguishing the various karmic obstacles of sentient beings in the turbid and evil world of future ages.”
“The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, now speaks of the physical characteristics of all Buddhas within this great assembly.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What should this sutra be named?
How should the essentials of this Dharma be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'The Immovability of Bound Thought'; thus should it be upheld.
It is also titled 'Contemplating the Buddha’s Ūrṇā-kośa'; thus should it be upheld.
It is also titled 'Contemplating the Tathāgata’s Limbs in Forward and Reverse Order'."
It is also titled "The Distinctive Analysis of the Tathāgata’s Limbs and Members within Each and Every Pore";
it is also titled "Contemplating the Wisdom-Light of the Thirty-two Marks and Eighty Minor Characteristics";
and it is also titled "The Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha."
It is also titled "The Gate of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha";
it is also titled "The Adorned Physical Body of All Buddhas with Wondrous Flowers";

and it is also titled "The Sūtra on the Subtle and Exquisite Physical Body Attained as the Fruit of Preaching the Precepts, Concentration, Wisdom, Liberation, and the Knowledge and Vision of Liberation, the Ten Powers, the Four Fearlessnesses, and the Eighteen Unshared Dharmas. You should receive and uphold it well; be careful not to forget or lose it.

When the Buddha spoke these words, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the great assembly of bodhisattvas, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, and all the spirits and ghosts, having heard the Buddha speak of this subtle and wondrous physical form, some attained the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin; some attained arhatship; some planted the causal conditions for the path of a pratyekabuddha; some resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and some attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Their number was exceedingly vast and beyond description.
